The fourth Industrial Revolution has significantly transformed manufacturing systems, incorporating data and intelligence into decision-making frameworks. Despite this, conventional planning models have struggled to accommodate the inherent uncertainties arising from predictive uncertainties in demand, resource availability, and machine functionality. Advanced manufacturing systems can now leverage uncertainty models to mitigate the risks associated with such uncertainties. However, existing stochastic models often fail to account for non-deterministic changes in resource utilization or machine maintenance schedules, which can lead to inaccurate demand aggregation and mask existing uncertainties. This paper introduces a new approach using uncertainty modeling and the Monte Carlo simulation method to address these limitations in practical scheduling problems. The proposed framework is demonstrated through a real-world case study in the textile industry, which involves scheduling a cutting machine in the presence of various uncertainties. The case study highlights the importance of incorporating non-deterministic uncertainty models into existing scheduling problems to achieve more precise simulation results. The method can potentially be extended to various industrial settings and systems.

Cyber-Physical Systems require robust resilience properties to withstand disruptions, including malicious cyber-attacks that can severeely harm people and cause significant economic loss. This paper introduces a resilience framework grounded in Specification Language for a dynamic cyber-physical system environment, which it maintains safe and resilient under attack. A resilience model in a particular environment is defined as a normal behavior model combined with a set of exceptional models arising from critical disruptions, which must be prevented. A key control strategy here involves specifying desired normal and exceptional behaviors through a temporal logic format called STL and using resilience enforcement as an control input to guarantee desired resilience. A specific cyber-physical traffic system is used here as a test case to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

A novel network of advanced quantum-sensing, high-sensitivity accelerometers may be able to detect rare particles by identifying minute changes in acceleration over extended periods and large areas, effectively acting as a sensitive detector for particles that only weakly interact with matter such as dark matter particles. This scenario is inspired by the success of the ALPS experiment in using sensitive accelerometers to detect the oscillations of massive solar particles. If such a network were to be established over a large area, it could have the sensitivity to detect the rare changes in acceleration induced by dark matter particles over a long period of time, and specifically in this study we are exploring the potential of such a large network to measure the rare changes in acceleration over a year and to measure the changes in acceleration induced by dark matter particles over a long period of time to rule out certain models of solar neutrino oscillations and to make predictions for a large number of different half-lives of dark matter particles that only weakly interact with matter such as dark matter particles.

We derive and justify a gradient approximation for the weak solution of a semilinear nonlocal elliptic equation defined on a complete, oriented and connected manifold. This approximation involves expanding the solution as a series of local power series up to the second order based on a reference point. The primary constraint for these local expansions is that they are centered on points where the diffusion function is near a regular, nondegenerate point on the manifold. The local expansions around such points generate a gradient approximation for the solution that represents a diffusion process that is both smooth and non-singular. The findings that establish this approximation leverages previous work on solving the related elliptic equation. The derivation and justification for the gradient approximation involve multiple challenges related to singularities arising from the nonlocal nature of the diffusion process, as well as the issue of solutions that exhibit blow-up on the manifold. One key approach to addressing these challenges involves establishing the existence and uniqueness of the solution for a related problem that involves a normal derivative and exhibits zero boundary conditions on the manifold. This argument demonstrates the consistency of the solution and its supporting estimates with the desired gradient approximation. The solution and its supporting estimates are also shown to be continuous and convergent to the reference point. The proof involves establishing the continuity of solution and its supporting estimates on the manifold and with respect to parameters in an open set. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the solution and its supporting estimates, as well as the local expansions, are harmonics that do not exhibit blow-up on the manifold.

By analyzing 14.5 hours of imaging data from the Low Frequency Array (LOFAR), researchers examined the properties of faint radio sources in the mJC114P1 catalog, using a source flux density threshold of 18 mJy and angular scales ranging from 9 to 300 kiloparsecs. They employed a stacking technique to investigate these sources. The research involved a nearby sample of sources with known redshifts, flux densities, and angular sizes to account for variations in source brightness and distance due to magnification effects. The stacking technique showed that integral galaxy sizes correlated with stellar masses and luminosities, and the research found no link between radio luminosity, host galaxy mass, or star formation rates. The research was completed with a comparison to the Parkes Half-Jy survey, which found differing radio luminosity distributions for bright and faint sources, with a notable turnup in the luminosity function of faint sources. The research attributed this disposition to the presence of hidden sources or magnetic fields, as recent observations indicate faint sources have smaller galaxy sizes than bright sources. The research continued to analyze the relationship between jet magnetic fields and galactic features in more detail.

Quantitative techniques can be applied to some, but not all, formal verification methods. In an effort to bridge this gap, researchers propose a framework that extends the scope of quantitative methods. By defining processes as actions within a specific mathematical structure, the proposed framework offers principles for quantifying behavior and evaluating system properties. In particular, the introduction aims to clarify the concept of Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) as a special case within this structure. Consequently, standard HMMs can be seen as enforcing specific quantitative constraints on state transitions, which are ultimately based on a discrete mathematical framework. In an attempt to expand the scope of applicable models, the authors present a new category of models called abstract HMMs, which incorporate a decoupling mechanism between probability distributions and their underlying domains. However, the process of deciding equivalence between these models remains undecidable, which raises concerns about the effectiveness of applying quantitative methods to the category as a whole. In an effort to mitigate these concerns, the paper suggests an alternative approach, which redefines HMMs to include an additional monadic type for error handling. According to this revised perspective, an HMM can be viewed as an error-free model within a specific mathematical structure. At an abstract level, the error-handling aspect of this new definition can be seen as enforcing specific constraints on the applicability of probability transitions. This approach enables the development of complete and partial decoupling of HMMs, resulting in three categories of abstract HMMs

We analyze the concept of consistency in relation to physical systems, determining its specification and key properties. By applying this concept to the category of dynamical systems, we establish the existence of consistent systems with fundamental properties and prove their relevance to systems with a nonlocal statistical foundation.

We develop a versatile extension of Hidden Valley Models, allowing for the
scattering processes between new particles and their links to standard model particles
to be described through quasi-observables called Vertex Operators. These operators
are based on the concepts of conformal field theory and can incorporate various
scattering processes that go beyond the standard model framework. The
corresponding vertex operators for quarks and gluons involve the quantum field
versions of the standard model's electromagnetic and weak vector bosons as well as
the Higgs field. The proposed model is thoroughly explored in the context of
the LHC's searches for signals of additional particles that appear beyond the
standard model's predicted background levels in the form of quasi-primordial
signals. We demonstrate that this model can accommodate the existence of
particles that are neutral to electric charge and possess masses or energies
characteristic of particles beyond the standard model's framework, potentially
including dark matter candidates. Furthermore, we illustrate that this model
can incorporate the standard model's predicted decay patterns of the standard
model's particles into the decay products of the heavy particles that exist within
the standard model's framework.

A theoretical model for a blackbody in a state of vacuum isolation is developed, incorporating the effects of Casimir radiation. It is proposed that this model follows a modified thermodynamic structure, which in turn enables the derivation of a modified Stefan-Boltzmann law alongside previously reported Casimir radiation relations. Furthermore, a phase transition equation is identified and a phase diagram is constructed to illustrate the emergent behavior.

Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to the significant privacy risk of any shared location pair. To address this issue, our approach utilizes a non-isomorphic transformation of location histories that takes into account the user's past movements and a specified level of privacy safeguard 'epsilon'. By applying the symmetric location privacy problem, location privacy is safeguarded through the creation of a valid location privacy transformer. To achieve this, the location privacy transformer is demonstrated to be possible at any given 'epsilon' greater than zero, despite the inherent difficulties involved. To make our approach more applicable in real-world scenarios where past movements can be unreliable and 'epsilon' not well-defined, we employed a uniform prior distribution for conditional priors. A location privacy transformer was developed under a given 'epsilon' upper bound for any prior distribution, demonstrating its universal applicability.

A key application of 3D point clouds is point cloud localization, where a 3D point cloud obtained from sensors such as LiDAR is matched to a large database of reference maps. The normal distribution transform (NDT) patch is a widely used method for summarized 3D point cloud representation that facilitates efficient localization and mapping. However, conventional NDT patches are incapable of accurately representing noisy or distant features, thus hindering performance in applications such as autonomous driving feature detection. To address this limitation, a novel method is proposed that employs a transformer decoder for NDT patches. This method enhances conventional NDT patches by leveraging self-attention mechanisms to accurately predict pose even in scenarios with noisy or ambiguous features. Furthermore, a novel decoder architecture is introduced that enables accurate estimation of pose from NDT patches even in challenging scenarios with noise, distortion, and ambiguity. Experimental evaluations using both simulated and real-world datasets confirm that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches for LiDAR-based point cloud localization.

Linking brain regions to each other is thought to underlie conscious awareness and consciousness. Mapping these connections using resting-state functional MRI has become a major focus of neuroscience research. Despite the interest in establishing reliable models for predicting individual differences in brain function, it remains unclear how to design multivariate models effectively. We address this question by examining the relationship between the statistical strength of connectivity and the predictive power of models in linking brain regions in individuals. Our investigation of multiple networks revealed that stronger functional connections tend to contribute more significantly to predictive models. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the spectral characteristics of brain function, as revealed by eigenvalues, correlate with knowledge of functional tags such as demographics and cognitive scores, indicating a structured information architecture in brain function where demographic and cognitive information is organized across brain regions in a functional context. Our findings also suggest that the brain functions in a hierarchical manner, with higher eigenvalues corresponding to more abstract concepts located in nodal brain regions, and that these higher eigenvalues are less predictive of lower-level brain activity but highly predictive of higher-level executive functions, indicating a key role for nodal brain regions in supporting predictive models. Ultimately, our study lays the groundwork for a new understanding of brain function, indicating that the accuracy of predictions from multivariate models increases significantly with strong functional connections, and that these connections may hold the key to modeling the complex human brain.

This paper presents a synchronization concept grounded in a single, token-based resource, utilizing the'stomp' operation as proposed by Dung Van Hung et al. in 2021. The name assignment problem is viewed as a challenge requiring global synchronization, with the'stomp' operation providing a means to attain synchronization. It is demonstrated that name assignment issues in a network involving n nodes can be expressed as a set of 'globally synchronized' tasks, each corresponding to a node assigning its unique name through a'stomp' operation. It is also shown that tasks are implementable in the network if and only if they are schedulable. Furthermore, a practical solution is offered for scheduling tasks in a network, allowing for global synchronization and efficient implementation. Specifically, names can be assigned efficiently in a network involving n nodes through a'repeat-and-stomp' mechanism, involving a clock with a O(logn) cycle time, despite running continuously. The mechanism is implementable in a fair, repeat-and-stomp clock, effectively enabling global synchronization. As a result, names can be assigned efficiently in a network, utilizing a'repeat-and-stomp' clock, effectively conserving energy.

Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed social media texts have gained much attention.
Several models using sequential and graph-based methods have achieved impressive results.
Despite performing well, these models struggle with out-of-domain data and require separate training systems for different code-mixed languages.
A new challenge arises from non-sequential positional encoding in social media texts, making it difficult for models to leverage pre-trained neural networks.
To overcome these limitations, we propose the Pairwise Enhanced Sequential Transformation using Switching Points (PESTO) model, which adapts to multiple code-mixed languages with a novel switching point based positional encoding technique.
We test PESTO on Twitter data across three languages - Marathi-English, Marathi-Hindi, and Hindi-English - and compare its performance to leading models, achieving significant improvements and outperforming GPT-3's results while requiring a much smaller data set.

The superconducting H$_{3}$S hydride compound, currently at the forefront of research, has great potential for significant improvements in superconducting properties through pressure alterations. As a result, a wide variety of theoretical models have been developed to illustrate how pressure influences the superconducting impact on the material's behavior. The way that doping the material affects its critical temperature in relation to pressure can be described by the formula $E_k=(\hbar/2m)^(1/2)[k^3-(k_{hv}^3)]$, where $k_{hv}$ represents the density of states and is a fixed value, also indicating a discontinuity in the kinetic energy at $k_{hv}$. The point at $k_{hv}$ constitutes a van-Hove singularity (VHS), with the material's critical temperature closely tied to this point. Our study reveals that the way that doping the material affects its critical temperature in relation to pressure is largely determined by the distance between the VHS and its adjacent saddle point. The distance between these two critical points, in turn, is determined by the structural changes and the elastic constants of the material. The way the material's behavior is affected by its different pressure states can be illustrated by a pressure-induced shift in the position of the material's first brillouin zone electron states. The material's critical temperature is expected to be about 190 K under a 145 GPa pressure threshold, with adjustments to the material

This paper introduces an efficient algorithm for generating motion plans within complex environments that are dynamic in nature. The algorithm, SRGB, is built upon the C-space subdivision approach but with key advancements over the state-of-the-art FSS algorithm, primarily focusing on the speed of both planning and separation times. The study shows that SRGB offers a significant reduction in separation time by taking into consideration the dynamic nature of the environment. Furthermore, SRGB significantly outperforms FSS in planning time by closely approximating initial guess positions provided by fast separation algorithms. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through separation and planning time analyses as well as real-world practical applications in xFSS and xWBB algorithms.

A crucial capability for autonomous robots is determining their position in a known environment.  A promising approach to achieve this is by using a model that accounts for relationships between a robot's observations and the environment's geometric structure, specifically surfaces, making it more resistant to obstacles and scenes containing repeated patterns.  However, existing geometric methods can be computationally demanding due to high processing requirements for 3D geometric data such as coloumns in 3D surfel maps.  This research proposes a two-stage technique that combines a preprocessed step with reduced precision data for more efficiently generating descriptors and performing relocalization, followed by a traditional matching and localization process.  Notably, this method utilizes a dataset with accurately calculated surface normals from a real-world robot dataset to develop a model that simulates and predicts the humans understanding of the robots visual input, making it more effective.  Evaluations of this approach have been conducted using a robot dataset with images and 3D geometric data and the results demonstrate its ability to accurately determine its position in a given environment.

In MIMO systems with multiple users, the problem of determining which users to serve and design precoders to serve them is complex and often involves a large number of candidates. This paper proposes a new method to tackle this complexity by casting user choice and precoder design as a single, mathematically tractable problem. By applying the Group LASSO principle, we reformulate the problem to minimize a combined loss function that accounts for incomplete channel information and the desire to select a limited number of users. We provide conditions under which an optimal solution exists and develop a simple iterative algorithm to find this solution. Numerical tests demonstrate that our method can accurately detect the optimal subset of users with high efficiency, even when there are up to one missing channel per user.

We demonstrate that for any tropical curve $\Gamma$ and its associated semifield $\mathbb{K}(\Gamma)$, there exists a finite set of semifields $\mathbb{K}_1, \ldots, $\mathbb{K}_n$ such that $\mathbb{K}(\Gamma)$ can be expressed as a combination of these semifields through rational functions.

We establish a broad convergence result for the quantile function Q(y/n) as the sample size n approaches infinity, proving that it converges uniformly across a bounded interval of y/n. This convergence is facilitated by a rigorous error bound for the difference between Q(y/n) and its finite sample counterpart, Q*(y/n).

We've reevaluated the significance of the Fox-Hatcher loop in the stable homotopy theory of Lie groups, as described by Borel and Fox-Hatcher. Our analysis specifically focuses on its iterated path-class map, which we find contributes to the development of a Vassiliev invariant of order three via the Dixmier-Morimoto path algebra. This invaraint can also be derived from the iterated path-class map of the top Lie group if all other variables are set to one.

The connection between unconventional superconductivity and magnetic order is still a mystery, especially in materials that can withstand magnetic fields without becoming resonant. The fishbone mode, a type of magnetodynamic excitation found in CeIrInCoAs and BaFe$_2$As$_2$, holds clues about the relationship between these two phenomena. In LiFeAs superconducting crystals, our research shows that magnetic instability does not occur at low temperatures, ruling out the possibility of magnetodynamic excitations similar to the fishbone mode and providing further evidence that LiFeAs and NaFeAs are the only two known superconducting materials without magnetic instabilities. Moreover, our study indicates that these materials do not have in-plane anisotropies in their magnetic characteristics.

This research takes into account two Higgs doublets of different parity, allowing for a unique identification of the lighter Higgs as the known Standard Model Higgs while the other is still an unknown and can take the form of an elementary or composite particle. Two types of 2HDM representations, Type-I-IV, have distinct theoretical underpinnings based on the underlying interactions of the Higgs fields, leading to varying constraints and possibilities for new physics. Our findings reveal that all Type-I 2HDM alignments, where the lighter Higgs mimics the Standard Model Higgs, can be consistently aligned with all available experimental data, regardless of the arrangement of mixing angles. Additionally, our analysis indicates that future experiments like the FCC-eh can further refine this alignment, making it even less susceptible to variations. In a notable contrast, our findings show that Type-II, Type-III, and Type-IV 2HDM alignments, subject to specific constraints and parameters, can only remain consistent with experimental data by introducing an undetectable or inherently blocked secondary Higgs particle. However, when considering the possibility of a parity-blocked or elementary nature of the second Higgs doublet, our results reveal that Type-I 2HDM can even outperform the Standard Model in searching for this new physics, especially through the most favorable conditions at the Future Circular Collider.

We demonstrate through initial trials that a neuroevolutionary method can facilitate the acquisition of assembly strategies among homogeneous, unguided microscopic entities subjected to collide-and-bounce rules in a two-dimensional environment. This approach enables the creation of intricate molecular structures resembling biological cells, such as membrane-bound nuclei and vacuoles. Furthermore, our experiment design allows for automatic production of versatile and efficient assembly protocols, which can be used to construct intricate microscopic structures with specified topologies. The inherent adaptability of the produced assembly methods enables the assembly of various target shapes, and their effectiveness is measured by the proximity of the resulting structures to the desired form. We also find that our approach yields diverse, efficient strategies for forming identical structures and discover that utilizing a large population in the initial algorithm assessment can lead to the discovery of particularly effective and generalizable strategies.

We explore non-thermal, dynamic anomalies in relativistic, chirally invariant gauge theories, with a specific focus on the standard model and its variations. These anomalies manifest when the thermalizing scalar fields behave differently than fermions during the early stages of relaxation. As a result, dynamic anomalies have the potential to significantly impact both real-time dynamics and the initial stages of relaxation. We examine both perturbative and non-perturbative cases and investigate implications for early universe phenomena and associated observational consequences. Furthermore, considering non-hermitian fermion interactions may offer a solution to stabilize the vacuum and prevent significant radiation in the early universe, though this approach raises concerns regarding the reliability of perturbative quantization. We explore this possibility in the context of the standard model with a complex Yukawa interaction and reveal that spontaneous chiral symmetry may have subtle implications for early-time relaxation and the phase structure of these systems.

This study contributes towards addressing a long-standing question posed by Tsurumi (2019) regarding whether stationary Navier-Stokes equations are always well-posed in $B^{1}_{p, \in{nat}}$ for $1 < p < 2$. To this end, we demonstrate the existence of specific functions $v_q$ and $q$, with $v_q$ in $B^{1}_{p, \in{nat}}$ and $q < 2$, such that when these functions are successively added within the framework of the Lie group integration method, the resulting sequence of v_n does not converge to 0 in $B^{1}_{p, \in{nat}}$. As a result, we establish that if the Navier-Stokes equations are modified such that its external force f is allowed to depend on time, then these modified equations become well-posed in $B^{1}_{p, \in{nat}}$ for 1 < p < 2. Additionally, it has been found that the condition of f being time-dependent is necessarily adequate for obtaining this result. Finally, based on an extensive mathematical analysis, it has been clearly demonstrated that the case where p equals 2 is distinct from all other cases.

We develop a theoretical framework for examining how a uniaxial antiferromagnet responds to external temperature variations by analyzing the nonlinear changes in its magnon frequencies before the critical point in a finite magnetic field. Our theoretical framework also encompasses the interplay of thermal fluctuations on the structural order of the material, ultimately yielding an expression for the magnetic correlation length that reflects this interplay. Additionally, our analysis on the specific characteristics of EuO reveals that the primary magnon branch undergoes thermal deformation, resulting in a shift in its frequency, and exhibits thermal squeezing with its spectral width; these phenomena are only possible at low temperatures. Furthermore, our research indicates that the thermal deformations of the two magnon branches are significantly influenced by the magnetic field. To confirm the validity of our theoretical findings, our research recommends conducting a detailed analysis of the ferromagnetic component of the EuTe-EuSe-EuO triple system.

This research paper examines a variant of Loidreau's (2008) code-based cryptosystem,
employing Goppa codes $(g_1g_2)(7,8)$ and $(g_1g_2)(8,9)$ generated by two
irreducible polynomials from $\mathbb{F}_{8}$, produced by the binomial $(x^2 +
\alpha + \beta )^{(3+\alpha + \beta )/2}$ and $\mathbb{F}_{9}/\mathbb{F}_3$,
respectively. We generate public codes $C^*$ as a symmetric code via the matrix
$\begin{pmatrix}A_{1}^T\vert A_{2}^T\Big|A_{3}^T\end{pmatrix}$, then derive
the respective public codes for each system. We calculate the generic
systematization and system efficiency for each system, then compare the
systematization and system efficiency with Loidreau's original system based on
Goppa codes $(g_1g_2)(7,8)$ and $(g_1g_2)(8,9)$ in 2008, using matrices $A_{1}$
and $A_{2}$ respectively.

We introduce Dict-BERT, an innovative technique to improve BERT pre-training
through word dictionary relationships. By leveraging a dictionary, we discovered
that contextualized language models can benefit from the encoded meanings of words.
Our method focuses on reinforcing word embeddings by using connotation similarities
within each word's dictionary entry. To achieve this, we incorporate a dictionary
layer into the BERT architecture during the pre-training phase. Experimental results
confirm that our approach promotes diverse word representations and enhances the
model's general stability. Compared to the standard BERT model, the upgraded
Dict-BERT model achieves superior performance improvements on the GLUE test suite,
ranging from 0.4 to 2.6 percentage points.

The mathematical structures known as persistence diagrams (PDs) in topology have become crucial in modern analysis of complex data. These diagrams essentially represent how persistent patterns within a data set continue to emerge as the level of detail (or threshold) is increased. These patterns can take the form of mountains, valleys, ridges, ravines, loops, and more within a data set. However, studying the vast number of these patterns is a challenge due to their extensive and intricate nature. Therefore, researchers are more interested in understanding the extremum statistics rather than individual pattern occurrences. Mathematical limits such as the minimum and maximum values of certain topological measures, known as betti numbers, are critical in this investigation. These mathematical limits relate to the distribution of certain topological measures, known as extremal spanning acycles, which are formed by minimum or maximum spanning acycles in a simplicial complex. These mathematical limits have model implementations in various real-world scenarios, one notable example being the analysis of valleys or dips in complex data patterns. Valleys are a significant feature in numerous scientific disciplines, as researchers have used them to identify weaknesses in material structures while scientists have used them to understand climate variations. These mathematical limits have critical applications in various disciplines including mathematics, physics, biology, and more as researchers study how the distribution of extreme mathematical limits change in response to varying environmental conditions. These mathematical limits have model implementations in various real-world scenarios, one notable example being the analysis of valleys or dips in complex data patterns.

This study focuses on addressing privacy breaches in Vertical Federated Learning (VFL), where multiple entities collaborate on machine learning projects despite having incompatible datasets. By applying a secure aggregation protocol, they can protect their individual data while jointly generating a machine learning model. We've identified two previously unreported vulnerabilities of the aggregation protocol, revealing how an adversary may derive private user records from shared model components. Our research demonstrates that, in the VFL setting, a curious attacker doesn't need administrative control or access to the actual data; they simply need computational resources and a willingness to conduct trial-and-error attacks to compromise privacy. We've also found that, in contrast to conventional attacks, these privacy assaults can be effectively scaled up without compromising the shared model's accuracy. Moreover, once the attacker has gained control of the shared model, they can use it as a starting point for further attacks, using stolen data along with known model components to guess the remaining data records of victims. Our research aims to raise awareness about the inherent risks in the current VFL framework and propose two practical security enhancements to safeguard against these privacy breaches.

A novel theoretical framework, named light-cone quantum chromodynamics, has been utilising a series expansion method to model rare meson decays. This framework, now paired with a new tool to explore quantum fluctuations in the context of quantum field theory, has enabled the derivation of crucial relationships between decay amplitudes and their underlying form factors. Our analysis focuses on a specific type of decay where a B-meson disintegrates into a proton and a type of antiparticle that doesn't interact with light, and we determine this decay rate to be approximately four times less likely than a comparable reaction producing a neutrino and a pi-meson.

The growing importance of resource management in safeguarding Intelligent Cities (ICs) from socio-cyber-physical threats has been underscored by recent research. This paper presents a dynamic game model that captures IC defense strategy competitions between the defense and offense. Specifically, these competitions center on cyber-socio attacks that target IC's critical infrastructure. Our innovative framework integrates cyber, socio, and physical dimensions of IC defense by utilizing a dynamic programming approach. It enables IC to simultaneously manage operational (physical) and non-operational (cyber-socio) resources to counter enemy forces. In turn, the offense seeks to maximize damage by exploiting IC's exposed resources. Our theoretical analysis and computational simulation validate our approach and offer valuable insights into IC defense strategies.

To analyze the influence of a surrounding cavity on black holes, we utilize the Feiner-Witten complex phase transition as a probe. Our research reveals that for black holes surrounded by a cavity, the complex transition is affected by temperature and radius. We observe that the shift in the phase transition temperature is negligible for large cavities but significant for small cavities. Moreover, our results indicate that the shift in the phase transition temperature is consistent with or opposite to that of black holes surrounded by walls, depending on the radius of the cavity.

Real-world document collections can become contaminated with labeling errors 
which complicate the use of retrieved documents from previous rankings. This 
research addresses the issue of ranking documents under imperfect labels by 
drawing on the information retrieval tradition. It proposes a model that combines bag sampling and group-level cross-entropy loss to learn a consistent ranking from noisy document labels. This approach can be used alone or in conjunction with a neural network and a adapter to leverage the benefits of modern transformer architectures for document ranking. Experiments have demonstrated the effectiveness of this method in extracting meaningful text features from noisy labels and obtaining a ranking consistent across multiple documents and applicable in real-world settings.

Despite the superior performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, these models often require a substantial quantity of node labels, which can be impractical to obtain in many real-world scenarios. To address this limitation, this research explores the potential of pseudo-labeling, a technique widely adopted in computer vision for extracting more informative labels from a classifier. Pseudo-labeling generates a large quantity of pseudo-labels obtained through a trained classifier, eliminating the need for manual annotation. However, the effectiveness of pseudo-labeling in graph-based node classification remains poorly understood. We have experimentally demonstrated that the combination of two advanced techniques, non-ascending Knowledge Distillation and non-linear Loss Function, is capable of producing reliable pseudo-labels in graph domains. These pseudo-labels can significantly enhance the performance of GNN-based models when only a small number of labels are available, outcompeting models trained with numerous labels. Moreover, mixed-type informative pseudo-labels, consisting of both pseudo-input and pseudo-label, provide additional benefits, allowing GNNs to capture local and global structural properties as well as both node features and pseudo-label information. Informative pseudo-labels extracted through this method exhibit consistent accuracy across a variety of graph datasets, with the conditionally-regularized model achieving state-of-the-art results on Cora, Citeseer, and ArXiv datasets.

Betatron radiation spectroscopy in a focused plasma column can serve as an efficient, non-intrusive diagnostic tool for monitoring the dynamics of plasma wakefield acceleration and the performance of plasma wakefield accelerators. This method has recently been utilized in the AWAKE experiment to evaluate the properties of plasma wakefield accelerators using proton beams. However, some aspects of the betatron radiation analysis in AWAKE require clarification. This study investigates and addresses these concerns through a detailed numerical simulation of the AWAKE experiment. The findings highlight the potential issues and constraints associated with using betatron radiation analysis in AWAKE and offer suggestions for improving the analysis in future experiments.

This study introduces a scalable method for Private Deep Learning (PDL) that guarantees accuracy, addressing two main challenges of learning decision trees in a differential privacy (DP) environment: local vs global sensitivity, and noise propagation across tree nodes. To overcome these obstacles, an enhanced mechanism is integrated with the existing BPOD framework, enabling DP to converge towards optimal results without compromising the framework's original convergence properties. To achieve this convergence, a noised-based approach is combined with an adaptive learning algorithm that effectively counterbalances local and global DP mechanisms. In particular, a mechanism is first proposed to demonstrate the equivalence of local and global DP within the BPOD framework, then an adaptive learning algorithm is designed to simulate the propagation of noise through decision trees, ultimately converging towards optimal results by adjusting the learning rate. To validate these claims, comprehensive experiments were conducted, supporting the scalability of the proposed method even in the presence of 1000 nodes. Notably, this technique not only ensures DP convergence but also demonstrates significant real-world performance gains, empirically demonstrating its superiority over existing approaches in non-private decision tree learning.

We focus on the variational inference task of minimizing a R\'enyi divergence-based objective function with additional constraints. This problem appears in a wide array of applications, such as deep learning-based density estimation and integrative and multi-task deep learning. First, we establish the geometric properties of the divergence function, then we devise a Bregman proximal gradient (BPG) algorithm to solve the minimization problem. The BPG is an adaptive algorithm that efficiently resolves problems with constraints like budget or interpretability, as well as those with multi-task setups with conflicting objectives. We compare the BPG with other available methods in numerical experiments, and it outperforms them. Notably, the BPG is a versatile solution that can be used to tackle other deep learning challenges.

This paper presents a chain event graph model with the objective of performing Bayesian model selection by maximizing the model's marginal log-likelihood. To facilitate this selection, we developed a fast and effective algorithm for calculating the marginal probabilities of CHLG nodes and edges. The proposed model selection approach can be combined with both discrete and continuous nodes, allowing for the representation of more complex relationships beyond traditional Bayesian network models. We compared the performance of our model selection method with standard methods based on cross-entropy and Akaike information criteria. Our empirical analysis using real-world data demonstrated the advantages of our approach in determining the optimal model size. Furthermore, we illustrated the proposed method's capabilities using example applications in social network analysis, mental health, neuroscience, and system biology.

In a Hilbert space, we're working with a basic model that uses an inclusion of solutions to stand in for a more complicated problem. Our objective is to investigate the behavior of this model when we take a limit where a particular parameter approaches zero. Since this model is an attempt to solve an otherwise more complex problem, we examine its convergence towards the solution with the least norm in the set of feasible outcomes. By looking at the model's parameter, we find that it converges strongly towards this least norm solution under certain conditions. Firstly, we consider the model's convergence towards the least norm solution in the absence of constraints; secondly, we consider the model's convergence towards the solution in the absence of constraints under Tikhonov regularization; and finally, we consider the model's convergence towards the solution in the absence of constraints with an adaptive parameter that adjusts for constraint violations. In each of these scenarios, we establish the model's convergence towards the solution in the absence of constraints, which is the solution with the least norm under certain parameters.

Our research studies how simple robots making round trips can follow winding paths, especially in environments with obstacles that compel them to take sharp turns. By simulating three different models - a robot moving in round circles, one that changes direction randomly, and one that always turns in the same direction in a fixed radius - we found that as these robots approach an obstacle, their paths start to overlap more and more. With increasing tension in their journey, they begin to take sharper and sharper turns until their trajectories become almost randomly arranged. Interestingly, there's always a stage where a large number of robots start accumulating around the obstacle, forming intricate patterns and moving as a unified unit. This behavior is influenced by the distance these robots keep from the obstacle and can be explained by a robot turning at the last possible moment. These results also illustrate how overcrowding can change the turn-taking habits of these robots, shifting their trajectory and making their journey even more chaotic.

In an experimental study, the effect of doping and frequency on the microwave conductivity of a cuprate family compound was investigated. By introducing impurities for copper, we analyzed how the conductivity varies with frequency and temperature, giving us the in-plane and c-axis conductivity while taking into account the role of LO phonons. Experiments were conducted on five specimens prepared using the MLCO technique and sintered at different temperatures to create varying levels of doping. By scaling the conductivity graphs for LO phonon contributions, we were able to determine the relevant parameters such as the product of conductivity and temperature, its exponent, the characteristic LO phonon frequency, the product of the plasma frequency squared and a screening length, and a dimensionless parameter related to the cuprate's extension.

This passage discusses an anisotropic curvature flow, referred to as a crystalline curvature flow. A comprehensive review of this type of flow will be provided, focusing primarily on the initial value problem's solvability and well-definedness.

Our training method for plant care robots is founded on observational learning.
A human care-giver and a robotic substitute interact with a plant in an interconnected space, allowing them to exchange experiences. As these robots are equipped with a camera, they record the plant's condition as well as any tools required for its maintenance. Data on how to treat the plant is then gathered by observing the robotic assistant's actions. By combining these observations, a compact instructional set is created that describes the necessary steps to care for the plant. When a new plant is introduced, this instructional guide is used to guide the robotic assistant, which is now enabled to provide adequate care. Our research demonstrates that this approach to automated houseplant care is effective, requiring minimal human input and supervision. Additional studies have shown that robots which closely resemble the appearance and movements of humans are particularly successful in this endeavor.

It has been established that the SLE loop ensemble that we defined satisfies the properties of a random loop measure that appears naturally within the context of quantum Liouville CFT. Specifically, the conformal field theory description involves the spectral parameter-dependent universal amplitude which remains unchanged, as well as the associated operator product constant, for both the simpler quantum disk conformal welding case involving Liouville CFT through quantum dilaton Witten's formula, and the more complex instance involving full Liouville CFT through quantum Liouville Witten's formula. Building upon previous work by the first two authors, this new conformal welding method provides a novel approach to examining the loop correction term in the conformal structure equation relevant to the SLE segmenting the quantum cone, and may also have broader implications for Liouville CFT and conformal field theory in general.

The Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative seeks to streamline research, develop guidelines, and develop metrics to increase accuracy and compatibility across studies, while promoting transparency and open data sharing in biomarker studies.

We have calculated the probability rates for $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ production 
in reactions where a photon collides with a nucleon, taking into account resonances 
with 3/2 and 5/2 spin. Our research reveals that these rates are heavily influenced 
by specific intermediate states, particularly the high-spin nucleon and delta resonances, 
which have significant model-dependent characteristics varying across different parametrizations.

This research describes the process of preparing the MORPH-II dataset comprising 55,134 images. The methods used for data pre-processing, as implemented in the MorphyII package from OpenCV, include normalization, averaging, and image alignment. The average age of the dataset subjects spanned from 26 to 67 years, with a majority being Caucasian. The MORPH-II dataset is significant for its classification into multi-racial groups - White, Black, Asian, and Others. The  variabilities present in the dataset led to a need for data pre-processing using the OpenCV framework to ensure consistency and feasibility of tasks for automated processes. The MorphyII package utilizes OpenCV to facilitate a uniform image dataset, thereby easing the complexity of tasks and improving efficiency.

Building on the curvaton model, we explore the possibility that our universe was formed by primordial black holes created during the inflationary period. The curvaton's residual motion after being suppressed during inflation can result in a density peak that can transform into primordial black holes. Our analysis investigates how various parameters affect the primordial black hole mass spectrum. The constraints on this phenomenon are evaluated based on LIGO's binary black hole events data and cosmic microwave background observations. The curved space-time caused by the curvaton's influence can potentially increase the gravitational wave background intensity, thus providing more stringent bounds. The failure to observe a signal from gravitational waves after LIGO's first two years has placed a significant limit on this model. The obtained constraints from LIGO and CMB observations indicate that primordial black holes with masses between $10^{17}$ and $10^{19}$ grams are possible, but a wide mass distribution is disfavored. The existence of such dark matter can potentially be validated by future experiments that demonstrate the curvaton model's signs, such as the second-scale phase transition's impact on the large scale structure. The model's predictions, particularly regarding the properties of dark matter, offer testable outcomes with upcoming experiments.

This study applies various models, including the Mixture Distributional Model and the Multiple Random Effects Model, to analyze a large dataset of higher education students in the United States, with a focus on predicting student attributes using academic outcomes and factors such as high school type and first semester GPA in college. By differentiating between models that assume a normal distribution from those that do not, the research investigates the benefits of each approach for understanding student outcomes. It further explores the impact of specific college factors, such as financial aid and attendance, using a linear model. The findings indicate that considering the presence of different student populations with varying characteristics is a more suitable approach to modeling these factors. Additionally, the research reveals that financial aid and first semester college grades have the most significant influence on student attributes.

The increasing adoption of Connected and Automated Vehicles calls for novel research into more sophisticated control strategies. This study explores the use of security measures in Connected Vehicle formation control, with a particular focus on recovering from hostile actions. A differential game-based control strategy is presented, showing its ability to form structured vehicle clusters and recover from disruptions that alter the predetermined formation design. It is demonstrated how this control strategy can be operationalized in real-world applications with reasonable computational requirements and feasibility. Furthermore, simulations conducted using a typical vehicle dynamics model reveal the effectiveness of the proposed approach, with clusters resembling regular geometric shapes and resilient to abrupt changes in state or input.

Interacting features can be leveraged by machine learning models to predict outcomes more accurately, yet using interaction terms comes with increased risks of overfitting. In scenarios where data is limited, it's often advisable to avoid interactions to prevent exacerbating the model's overfitting issues. 

Predicting binary response variables using logistic regression is an efficient approach, and when factor variables are involved, considering their interactions necessitates a thorough assessment of risks and benefits. Interestingly, utilizing R's data.frame data structure and vec2num function, coupled with appropriate programming techniques, makes it possible to avoid interactions within logistic regression's negative binomial link function without employing penalization techniques or semi-sufficient sets. 

This concept's applicability extends beyond the negative binomial link to other logistic regression models as well, particularly those utilizing the cumulative, probit, and partial log-likelihood links. A thorough exploration of this concept and its underlying principles will be provided in a paper featuring the implementation details, along with a examination of its efficacy through experiments and analysis of publicly available data.

The widespread use of generative models in natural language tasks has led to significant research on their applications and limitations. This paper explores the potential of transformator models, particularly the BERT and XLNet architectures, in creating informative and readable headlines. By leveraging existing models trained on vast amounts of text, we evaluate their capacity to automatically generate headlines and identify the key factors influencing their performance.

Research on frustrated two-dimensional quantum antiferromagnets has been very successful in identifying and studying unconventional states of matter, such as spin liquids. A particularly appealing state is the chiral spin liquid, which has been theoretically confirmed to exhibit significant chiral properties in its energy spectrum. In order to explore this concept further, researchers have been studying a fractional spin liquid developed from a $d$-wave short-range ordered state, which can be achieved through perturbation theory. This theoretical model yields a precise expression for the full spectral weight, demonstrating that the spin liquid displays chiral properties in two forms, one being dominant in the center of the Brillouin zone and the other in the gaps of the spectrum. By applying the power of scale-dependent calculations and analyzing the crossover from the mean-field ground state, scientists have been able to accurately reproduce the known results and gain valuable insights into the properties of spin liquids in the fractal regime. Moreover, the study suggests the existence of two states: an amorphous phase at lower scales and a polycrystalline phase at higher scales, which exhibits multiple domains with $d$-wave symmetries. In the process, researchers have developed a new method to evaluate spectral weight using a Gaussian distribution of density and have established a scaling formula for spectral weight based on the density of states. These breakthroughs are expected to enable experimental communities to manipulate and identify the chirality in 2D systems by using magnetic impurities as probes. In addition

In interferometry, comparing observed signals with simulated data helps uncover hidden sources and determine their characteristics. The success of this correlation-based approach relies on accurately accounting for signals from background noise and establishing a uniform scale for measurements. Wide-field radio interferometers, encompassing a full sky sector (~20-30%), can achieve this with ease due to their uniform data distribution and the regular grid design. The outcome yields an N-log-N complexity, making it scalable even with a large number of antennas (N>1000). Two main issues arise with implementing this approach: calculating the correct weight for data processing and removing redundant data points from the analysis. The regular grid design simplifies these processes, as calculations for both corrections now require only an order of N-log-N resources, regardless of the grid size and grid spacing. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this new approach in a practical implementation and shows that it can handle a large number of antennas, up to thousands, and even an extremely large number, such as tens of thousands, with ease.

In investment, portfolio diversification reduces risk, and this project demonstrates an innovative method using an autoencoding method within the context of a Conditional GAN framework to create diversified portfolios based on historical data. The goal is to generate a portfolio return distribution comparable to a benchmark return distribution, and this novel approach can construct a portfolio on either Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs) or Mutual Funds. The efficacy of this method is validated through numerical experiments utilizing historical data on ETFs, and the created portfolios are evaluated for their historical performance using metrics such as the Sharpe ratio. Additionally, the study examines the differences between using ETFs and Mutual Funds as the underlying assets of the constructed portfolios.

We have derived the polarized massive operator matrix element (POME) $A_{gq}(N)$ to $O(\alpha_s^3)$. This result is based on the light-cone gauge and includes both the standard and twisted-mass method (TMM) approaches. Notably, the $O(\alpha_s^3)$ contribution of the $N=1$ POME in the medium polarization scheme (MPS) and its corresponding TMM can be obtained by differencing with the $O(\alpha_s^2)$ term at $O(\alpha_s)$. This finding provides the basis for calculating $A_{gq}(N)$ up to $O(\alpha_s^3)$ across multiple values of $N$. This information will be used to determine the polarized massive splitting functions and express them in terms of the MPS. This enables us to evaluate the $O(\alpha_s^3)$ splitting functions to third order in $\alpha_s$ for values of $N$ between 2 and 4$. These findings will be incorporated into the PDF4PDF framework.

A newly trained Bayesian neural network event classifier was put to the test by processing nearly five years' worth of data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope, a powerful high-energy X-ray satellite observatory. This network was trained on simulated 3GAMMA events from nearby (within 10 degrees) sky areas and used to analyze 3 years' worth of real Fermi data. Subsequently, it was used to distinguish between 3GAMMA events and those initiated by cosmic background or residual point-source interference. To further refine its capabilities, the classifier was also trained to identify and filter out known Blazar events from the Fermi data.

Despite the rising need for accessible social media, its content authoring remains 
encumbered by complications. Our research involved interviews with twenty users 
from three countries to investigate why accessible social media content is not 
often created. Our findings indicate that inaccessible social media platforms 
hinder accessible content production due to multiple obstacles. To enhance 
accessibility on a large scale, we recommend the implementation of clear 
accessibility guidelines, as well as incentives for both content creators and 
platforms to encourage widespread use.

A subgraph of a hypergraph, connected by a single edge, is called a branch. Two branches with no common vertices are considered distinct. The transformation of a hypergraph by uniting branches, resulting in a new hypergraph, is known as tensor merge operation. Properties of a hypergraph are analyzed based on its tensor power, generated by this operation, and its underlying branch structure. Spectra of tensors, a concept developed in the 20th century with important applications, are utilized for classification and analysis of a hypergraph through its tensor, by identifying specific eigenvalues and the rank of the tensor. Several theories and applications are discussed along with examples and on-the-fly computations.

This powerful telescope has a wide range of observational capabilities that far exceeds that of any previously used space-based telescope and is comparable to the most advanced ground-based telescopes with wide capabilities that include: Unbiased surveys with a large observational area that includes: Unbiased surveys with a large observational area for the identification of near-Earth objects or other distant objects from space.  These observational methods will be based on a time series approach that allows the detection of normal or explosive astronomical objects from space. These observational methods will be based on an advanced technology plateable 1k x 1k CCD camera that enables it to surpass the capabilities of the most advanced astronomical observations from space with an accuracy of 9-12 milliseconds for the timing of signals from astronomical objects from space.
