Our results address inference about function translations $\sum_{k=1}^m T_k f_0 (\cdot - x_k)$ with unknown locations $x_1,\ldots, x_m$ using observations of a sum of these translations, for both the case where the locations are restricted to a given set and the completely nonparametric scenario. These findings can be applied in various statistical areas, such as analysis of repeated measures data and wavelet regression sum of squares. Furthermore, we discuss the relationships between minimax and Fenton minimax problems, as well as nonparametric problems, providing connections to $C^k$-smooth and concave convex analysis. Our study is ultimately generalized to the elements of the Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}(X)$ generated by functions on a measure space $(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)$.

Research has indicated the presence of an ultralight shadow matter field in various experimental setups, including those examining the behavior of cold atoms in an optical lattice and particles at the interface between two materials. To reinforce our understanding of this discovery, studies on ultracold $^6$Fermi have been conducted and show that the results are not contaminated by an inaccurate understanding of the system's behavior. The studies using $^6$Li, however, display signs consistent with the presence of the shadow matter field, and open up possibilities for exploring this field's properties, especially its dependence on the spin state. The effects caused by this field have been found to be very slight, and very feasible to detect. The presence of the shadow matter field has also been determined to be difficult to explain using the existing Li-Si interaction, and very feasible to detect. The effects caused by this field have been found to be very slight, and very feasible to explain using the interaction between atoms in a specific type of gas mixture. The researchers have also explored the potential for this discovery to contribute to a broader understanding of the behavior of matter at extremely small scales.

This research introduces the Kernel Mixture Model (KMM) to the field of blind image restoration. The underlying assumption is that image noise follows a mixture of Gaussian distributions with varying numbers of components. The key findings are as follows: Initially, the concept of the Kernel Mixture Model is explained in the context of image processing. It is demonstrated that learning the mixture components' probabilities represents sampling from independent Bernoulli distributions. Next, an adaptation of the KMM is developed for blind image restoration by incorporating a prior model for image patches. The novel KMM-based restoration algorithm is then contrasted with established distribution prior methods such as LAP and Dn-CVAE. Ultimately, the efficacy of the proposed model is substantiated through experimental trials, the details of which are outlined in the study's methodology section. The primary conclusions drawn from these experiments reveal that KMM-based restoration outperforms competing methods by producing more detailed image reconstructions, as illustrated by higher PSNR values and better visual quality. The source code for these experiments has been made available at https://github.com/Argng/KMM_BIR.

A general approximation method for uniform associative Yang-Baxter equations has been previously developed, and this study expands on that protocol to establish a method for non-uniform associative Yang-Baxter equations. The latter evolution is made possible by two new concepts introduced here: bi-parallel and weakly parallel maps between different metric spaces. These novel maps have inherent and characteristic properties that distinguish them from other similar literature. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that bi-parallel and weakly parallel maps form quasi-group structures under composition. Building on this foundation, a new method for solving non-uniform associative Yang-Baxter equations has been developed, and examples illustrating this new approach are presented. The study also reveals that the bi-parallel map corresponds to the discrete timechaos equation known as the iterated map.

Formal verification via Hoare logic has long been acknowledged as a reliable approach for ensuring software correctness, yet its applicability is restricted due to the intricacies involved in crafting formal specifications for non-trivial programs. The overwhelming majority of software applications are written in languages that are easily understandable but formally weak, such as natural language, making it crucial to bridge the gap between Hoare logic and these languages for Hoare logic to be effectively utilized in everyday software development. This research introduces Natural Hoare Logic (NHL), an innovation that employs formal Hoare logic in conjunction with natural language logic to formulate formal specifications for programs, thus circumventing the need for intricate formal descriptions of program code. NHL combines the expressiveness of first-order logic with the natural language syntax of programming languages, enabling formal specifications to be expressed in a natural and concise manner. This paper formally defines NHL, illustrates its application in a concrete example, and estimates the complexity of deciding its satisfiability and validity. Additionally, NFL based on first-order logic is demonstrated to be an exponentially saturated fragment, specifically decided in PSPACE. This paper also explores NHL in relation to S.K. Nicolai's "programming by naturals" system through comparison and contrasts.

Distributed consensus is a foundational concept, with significant real-world applications, having been used to develop distributed consensus blockchain networks. Existing protocols like PBFT rely on unreliable message delivery and device assumptions, making them prone to failure in real-world applications. Our research aims to strengthen the consensus protocol by casting it as a distributed verification problem. This new approach allows us to develop a resilient consensus protocol, RCanopus. This protocol does not require devices to assume reliability or fault-resistance. Our experiment shows the feasibility of RCanopus. This protocol opens up new possibilities for improving blockchain security.

Despite the presence of cholesterol in cell membranes, its impact on membrane elasticity is still not thoroughly understood. To investigate this, molecular dynamics simulations of bilayers containing varying levels of cholesterol were conducted, which enabled the calculation of the storage modulus of the membranes as a function of distance from the phospholipid head. The results showed a significant decrease in the storage modulus just beneath the headgroups compared to the rest of the membrane. By analyzing the membrane's strain-energy density, an estimate of the persistence length was obtained, which corresponded to 0.25 nm per phospholipid molecule at 15.5 mol% cholesterol. Furthermore, the measurements showed that the presence of cholesterol caused an increase in the storage modulus within the membrane's bilayer plane, which was proportional to the cholesterol concentration. By comparing the simulations to the measurements of Sattig et al. using neutron scattering (refer to doi:10.1074/jbc.C117.pdf), it became apparent that the presence of cholesterol brought about a stiffer membrane environment preferentially located near the membrane's surface.

This paper suggests a novel approach to the formation of black holes and stars based on loop quantum cosmology. A cosmological model is developed by investigating the loop quantum gravity phase space and identifying a scale factor invariant that leads to a positive definite Romaniek Hamiltonian. Consequently, this model's analysis indicates that quantum states exhibit instability and tend to collapse, serving as a fundamental cosmological model that describes the initial stages of stellar or black hole formation. Furthermore, this model offers insights into the initial conditions for the collapse of stars or the formation of black holes and may also be applied to the study of modified gravity theories.

The Pierre Auger Observatory, which operates at zenith angles between 18.5° and 54.8.5°, has documented 105 events with energies surpassing 50 EeV between 2004 and 2020. Within this area, 9 events exceeded 60 EeV and 5 reached 80 EeV or higher. None of these events pointed directly at any specific cosmic sources. Among the recorded events, 94 utilized both the water-Cherenkov and surface formular detectors, which are the highest-energy ones documented so far with dual detector strategies. The remaining 11 events were recorded during testing periods with lower levels of data and have not been reported previously. The data for these events is available online at The Pierre Augier Observatory's Event Catalog.

Incorporating uncertainty information into deep object detectors enhances their capabilities for risky predictions. The main objective of this work is to introduce an innovative Bayesian framework for uncertainty estimation in deep object detectors. By utilizing a straightforward distribution mapping approach, our method facilitates the utilization of various detector outputs as standard Gaussian distribution priors. Additionally, we propose an efficient and dynamic parameter updating strategy to capture priors and impose regularization on the posterior. The proposed approach can be easily integrated with existing object detectors to attain excellent results. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method across various detectors and datasets, yielding significant improvements. The proposed BayesOD framework is now publicly available.

Predicting traffic in transportation systems is crucial for various city services. While traffic forecasting has been extensively studied, there is often an emphasis on individual vehicles rather than aggregated traffic patterns. This paper approaches traffic prediction by analyzing sequential images of traffic sections as the primary basis for learning predictive models. It introduces an effective framework for extracting relevant snippets from these images, allowing for the utilization of pre-trained vision models to generate embedded traffic signatures. These signatures enable the prediction of traffic scenarios by distinguishing between dynamic image patterns. The proposed method is evaluated using a large urban traffic dataset and shows significant performance advantages over existing techniques. The research presents results for three primary traffic forecasting tasks: two-category, multi-category, and regression forecasting.

In various categories, a notion of 'coherence' serves as a means to restrict general categories by incorporating additional relationships between morphisms. In the context of gray categories, these 'coherent' relationships can be represented as second-order diagrams, and the category of gray categories equipped with coherence can be shown to be equivalent to a specific category of profunctors. This profession of second-order coherence notions leads to an exploration of revisions in the context of gray categories, and we prove that an initial gray category can be uniquely extended to a coherent one in a specific manner. Furthermore, we apply these findings to several fundamental gray categories, including the free gray category generated by a given category, the gray reflection of a category, and the pseudo-functor gray category obtained from a double category. In each of these instances, our method allows us to determine the free coherent gray category and establish its equivalence to the category of anfunctors. Additionally, our method will be applied to demonstrate that every double category can be gray reflected to a coherent double category.

The use of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) in automatic hippocampus segmentation has become a highly active area of research.  Recent findings have demonstrated that CNN approaches can outperform traditional methods that rely on hippocampal anatomy.  While CNN methods have shown significant potential for use in clinical settings, there is a need for research on their performance in specific patient groups - those with neurological disorders such as temporal lobe epilepsy or Alzheimer's disease.  This study assesses the effectiveness of multiple CNN models when applied to hippocampampe segmentation for patients with temporal lobe epilepsy or Alzheimer's disease using an in-plane resolution of 3DT1 and 3DT2.  Our results reveal that one of the CNN models, which combined an U-Net architecture with additional data augmentation, exhibited high accuracy in hippocampal segmentation - with a mean relative deviation of less than 5% from manual annotations.  Moreover, our findings suggest that hippocampal segmentation is influenced by age in healthy subjects but not in patients with temporal lobe epilepsy or Alzheimer's disease.  This research provides valuable insights into the use of hippocampal segmentation methods for patients with neurological disorders.

We utilize a $N$-qubit system in an arbitrary state to detect a specific property of entanglement using $M$-pilot-modes with $\lambda$ being the wavelength of the pilots. Each pilot corresponds to a specific $x, y$-polarized wave. Our approach doesn't require the prior use of pilots, instead leveraging the property that when two modes are present, the state will occupy a higher dimension if it's entangled. A specific inequality involving $N, M, \lambda$, and the distance between measurements is derived, quantifying entanglement. A scenario involving two-qubit systems, pilots of 4 and an arbitrary initial state being used to demonstrate the validity of the inequality is explored.

This study provides a computational model for predicting the numbers of secondary particles, generated at Low Earth Orbit by cosmic ray albedo neutrons, produced through interactions with the atmosphere and atoms within satellites. These particles are captured and retained in satellites' vicinity. The proposed model has been tested and compared to actual data collected by a sun-oriented detector on a satellite at an altitude of 600 km to check for accuracy and reliability. The results show that our computational model accurately reproduces the experimental findings, indicating its validity and practical usefulness in analyzing data collected from satellites or other spacecraft.

A comprehensive neural network structure for classification tasks has been developed, incorporating a pioneering framework for message passing in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). To address node representation challenges in GNNs, a hierarchical framework is proposed that synergistically integrates global skeleton construction and local edge weight optimization. The suggested framework leverages a Pyramid-like Shrinkage Skeleton (PSS) constructor to capture global skeleton representations, and alters local connections among nodes with similar attributes to enhance topological relationships between nodes. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments on various benchmark graphs, resulting in improved classification performance compared to existing baselines. The research is documented in a scholarly paper and associated code/timestamp are available online.

To protect data subject to various types of privacy risks in matrix completion tasks with low rank, we propose a novel DPMF algorithm based on Huber loss. The Huber loss-led DPMF approach was inspired by previous research on completing individual low-rank matrices from partially revealed components, but its overall method and theoretical validity had not been fully developed. First, we established the theoretical foundation for our DPMF approach by demonstrating its ability to meet differential privacy requirements and maintain statistical accuracy. Additionally, we performed experiments to compare the performance of DPMF from four different matrices, with results showing that it is competitive with other existing matrix completion methods.

We propose a novel approach to modelling interstellar dust where larger grains are comprised of a uniform material, referred to as 'astrodust', and tiny grains are comprised of another uniform material, referred to as 'PAHs'. Our study suggests that a typical ratio between astrodust and PAHs is approximately 1000:1 by mass and that they have similar optical properties. By applying this unified model to interpret spectral polarization and 2D maps of optical extinction obtained with APOGEE, we reveal a universal grain size distribution that is consistent across the galaxy and describes all measured grain sizes. Our findings show that a majority of interstellar dust is concentrated in compact molecular clouds with extremely high density levels, equivalent to 1000 times that of the solar nebula. Additionally, we discover that diffuse clouds only contribute a small percentage of interstellar dust, with most of it consisting of larger grains compared to the more abundant PAHs. Our model's predictions are highly consistent, predicting the observed extinction, emission, and polarization of interstellar dust with great accuracy, especially in the Milky Way's diffuse regions and nearby galaxies. The success of our model is particularly evident in the optical range where it accurately reproduces both the magnitude and color of the 550 nm polarization peak observed in the diffuse interstellar medium. Our model is also consistent with observations of ultraviolet extinction and interstellar gas chemistry. Our model's code is publicly available for research purposes.

The research on exoplanets, particularly low-mass stars, is gaining momentum thanks to the capabilities of ground-based telescopes and space missions like CHEOPS and PLATO. Our research explores the disk-shaping effect of a massive planet in the protostellar disk of CIDA 1, a very low-mass star. We analyzed the disk of CIDA 1 using VLT/PALM-3000 and VLT/SPHERE images to understand its structure. Our research indicates that the CIDA 1 disk is 7.5 mm in radius, 0.08 mm in inner radius, and has a gentle slope from 0.28 mm^-1 to 0.032 mm^-1 in its surface density. We observed a significant deviation from the smooth run-out in the southwest direction. Using the SIBYLL code, a massive planet of 0.072 to 0.15 Jupiter masses per 0.08 mm caused the material deficit in the northeast direction. Our research indicates that the CIDA 1 disk is oriented at around 66 degrees in its major axis, with the north pole aimed at 329 degrees. The southwest direction by 35 degrees makes the CIDA 1 disk by 353 degrees a perpendicular disc. The CIDA 1 protostar is only 0.18 Msun, and the planet mass required to clear its disk of 0.032 to 0.18 Jupiter masses is much lower than the

The Lights Out problem, also known as the Locking Problem, is a well-known issue with binary tap vectors where tapping specific positions leads to adjacent elements having values changing to zero. The Locking Problem has far-reaching implications and has been compared to a theoretical model used by physicists to study phase transitions in random magnetic or Ising spins. Researchers have found that the number of taps required to zero out all elements in a square matrix is maximized when this number is n plus one over two, where n represents the matrix's order, and they have established this result by using a simple algorithm. By examining a matrix's eigenvalues, we can show that the reverse process - zeroing out a matrix's eigenvalues - typically requires n plus one over two steps as well, and this finding validates a broader conjecture regarding tap efficiency that was first observed in certain square matrices containing integer values.

This paper introduces a breakthrough multi-stage image segmentation approach that
combines a powerful new model for image segmentation with a model for image restoration.
The novel segmentation model uses the normal vector of a contour to represent the
orientation of the shape, eliminating the need for sensitive parameter settings.
Rather than using a parameter-dependent solution space for curve regularity, our
model incorporates a straightforward Gaussian process with a built-in Rockette
phenomenon, automatically avoiding undesirable shrunk contours. In addition,
our model generates smooth and smooth-centered first moment constraints and
relaxes the second moment constraints to allow for greater diversity in shape
models. The image segmentation model is fully integrated with an image restoration task,
enabling the reconstruction of degraded images and the simultaneous segmentation of
these images. Our model's efficiency is further demonstrated by its ability to handle
low-quality input images and achieve high-quality results in a relatively short time.

Our proposal for Abstraction Descending (Abd) combines two established techniques - Abstract Interpretation and Leveled Polymorphism - to manage abstraction depth during two distinct phases of program analysis. Typical Galois Connection-based analyses ascend while analyzing a program, generating an abstraction at a predetermined level. However, this approach often struggles with inferring abstractions for code blocks that execute only after the initial level has been established. 

Abd addresses this issue by allocating different levels of abstraction for a program's ascending and descending phases, based on the principles of level polymorphism. This design enables the determination of appropriate abstraction levels for code blocks that execute later in the program execution, leading to enhanced analytical capabilities.

Ultimately, Abd aims to integrate with existing Abstract Interpretation tools, but our initial understanding of its mechanisms comes from the simplicity of a case study rather than a thorough formal verification.

We investigate the topological phonon modes within $ABO_2$ perovskite crystals with $A$ being silicon or germanium and $B$ being a transition metal from group $3-8$. By solving the $k \cdot p$ equation for the phonons, we find the phonon band splitting is directly proportional to the light element atomic number. Through a phonon resolution of identity method, we calculate the atomic force constants and find the $d$-orbital dominance that originates from the $k \cdot p$ theory's characteristic parameters. Furthermore, we discover a correlation between these phonon band splitting and $d$ orbital hybridization quantities, indicating the former can be manipulated to control the latter. Finally, we showcase that phonon engineering not only alters electronic properties, as traditionally understood, of $ABO_2$ compounds as band gap modulators, but also introduces a new dimension of controlling $d$ orbital configurations through phonon induced local distortions.

To effectively identify anomalies in complex data sets, accurate and rapid outlier detection is essential. However, existing methods primarily deal with intrinsic characteristics of the data, often normalized to form a metric space. Given the presence of anomalies, these methods can be optimized for increased speed, as their goal is to reduce detection time. A novel graph-based approach has been developed for this purpose, taking advantage of the unique properties of the data set under the Mahalanobis distance. This Proximity Graph can be built efficiently in O(n^2) time and used for further optimization in anomaly detection algorithms. Our method also allows the integration of optimized subspace outlier detectors, improving performance by reducing distance calculation times from O(n^2) to linear. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this graph-based technique, with detection times up to 50% shorter than current methods.

Our study explores an atomic system moving towards a potential mirror, where the atom is positioned near a point of zero electric potential due to a background potential. As the atom approaches and crosses this point at varying velocities, it experiences an instantaneous change in the local electric field, giving rise to spontaneous emission and an electromagnetic signal that decays exponentially with time. The amplitude and phase of the emitted signal as well as the periodic characteristics of the radiation, including its polarization and dependence on the atomic transition frequency and velocity, are examined in detail. Furthermore, considering an atom oscillating towards a moving mirror, the radiation emitted when the atom reaches its maximum velocity is found to be an exponential decay modified by a periodic modulation whose amplitude decreases with increasing velocity. The intensity of the radiation at the maximum velocity varies as the square of the velocity, while its phase exhibits a linear relationship with velocity that may be challenging to detect due to the oscillatory behavior of the mirror. However, if the atom oscillates with a small enough velocity and the radiation is observed during deceleration, its intensity exhibits a periodic component decaying at a rate greater than 1/t, with a characteristic frequency dependent on the velocity and a correction term dependent on the frequency of the atomic transition.

Graph representation learning has numerous real-world applications in social network analysis, drug discovery, and traffic forecasting. Graph neural networks excel at extracting global graph structure information, but existing methods fail to account for the diverse interests within a graph due to assumptions of uniform node properties. To address this limitation, we introduce localized community fairness to capture both global graph characteristics and local subgraph properties by focusing on fair learning within connected nodes sharing similar interests. By distinguishing nodes based on interests, our approach enhances the fairness and overall accuracy of graph modeling. Building on this concept, we developed a graph neural network that extracts information both globally and within specific subgraphs and at varying distances. Our method involves updating node features by considering nearest neighbors, then aggregating information by combining nearby subgraphs, and finally scaling up to the entire graph. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the fairness and overall performance of graph modeling on real-world datasets.

This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and evaluates the effectiveness of two analytical techniques in obtaining approximate solutions to these models. The first method, developed by Lapidus and Amundson, is applied to enzyme kinetics and expressed using Michaelis constants. The second approach, based on Korovkin's theorem, is more straightforward and doesn't require enzyme kinetics terminology. Both methods lead to comparable approximations and are compared in terms of accuracy. The approximate solutions obtained can be adapted in optimization problems, as demonstrated in a numerical example.

This study conducts a comprehensive supersymmetry search utilizing data collected from 2016 proton-proton collisions at the LHC's 13 TeV center-of-mass energy. A 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ dataset, gathered by the CMS detector, was analyzed for supersymmetry signs in final states featuring energetic jets and transverse momentum imbalance. A diverse cross-section phase space was explored by combining various simulation models based on simplified hypotheses, incorporating different mass specifications for multiple supersymmetry configurations. To maximize sensitivity, a null hypothesis-based assessment was combined with an advanced neural network analysis targeting the advanced gluino model. The research findings present on-the-fly interpretations of advanced neural network output as the most restrictive supersymmetry model limits to date: setting new, more stringent bounds on squark and gluino masses in conjunction with applying enhanced $E_T$ /$p_T$ threshold criteria. The research also presents new, more restrictive supersymmetry model limits based on simplified hypotheses in complex proton-proton collision experiments. Furthermore, the research presents novel, more restrictive supersymmetry model bounds in supersymmetry models with complex particle interactions. The research, utilizing enhanced supersymmetry model limits, presents new, more restrictive forecasts on enhanced supersymmetry model cross-sections where no signal was detected in supersymmetry models with complex particle interactions. The research presents new, more restrictive forecasts on enhanced supersymmetry model cross-sections in supersymmetry models with low particle masses. The research presents

We investigate financial bubbles driven by rational expectations, with participants anticipating an extrinsic stimulus any moment. The bubbles form when a price surpasses a positive, stable asset value, due to expectations of future appreciation exceeding its perceived risk. The asset's price follows a multi-dimensional geometric Brownian motion with a non-linear drift, modulated by mean-reverting co-factors. The bubble persists as long as the asset's expected growth exceeds its inherent risk, a relationship that varies inversely with time. The parameters of this model are estimable: (i) using Option Pricing theories, (ii) via historical backtesting, (iii) by detecting bubbles and predicting their demise using indicators derived from our model. Case studies on Google and Amazon stocks demonstrate the feasibility of our approach.

This study introduces an exact yet computationally intensive method to determine eigenstates of a driven quantum harmonic oscillator by employing the path integral formulation. By discretizing the action and utilizing a Monte Carlo algorithm, the spectrum of the driven oscillator can be exactly replicated. Our implementation relies on a stochastic version of the Myrskog-Ross method and is capable of being further optimized with the introduction of a guiding function. Our primary focus lies on the linear driving case where the presence of resonances significantly challenges computational intensity. By directly extracting eigenvalues from discretized spectra, the impact of discretization parameter can be easily evaluated. These findings serve as a basis for investigating the properties of eigenstates near threshold energies which become essential at the linear driving case. These computational tools may be applied to diverse oscillator types and can also help in extracting non-stationary probabilities from discretized spectra, a fundamental aspect for analyzing quantum phenomena over time.

Recent research has shown that reviews contain invaluable information about the qualities and shortcomings of products, making them an integral component of item recommendations. However, conventional techniques that rely on complex neural networks for text analysis often struggle to account for the diverse perspectives and sentiments expressed in reviews. This paper presents a pioneering approach that tackles review-centered recommendations by tackling two key challenges: aligning reviews with user perspectives and incorporating multiple reviews into a comprehensive recommendation model. An innovative Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network is proposed to achieve this, enabling a direct alignment of reviews and user views and facilitating an interactive modulation of complex and simple sentence representations through a two-way interaction mechanism. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of this model over baseline techniques on public datasets, with full implementation available on GitHub.

Deep learning models' success with natural language Understanding tasks often rely heavily on data augmentation techniques that involve generating and incorporating more data to enhance performance, but these methods can be particularly challenging for code-switched text - texts that combine vocabulary and expressions from two different languages. Several recent studies have explored variations of data augmentation techniques for code-switched texts but have found them to be limited. Our work investigates four different alternatives to conventional data augmentation techniques specifically tailored to Arabic-English code-switched text. We compare the performance of these new methods against existing approaches and conclude by discussing the implications of our findings and assessing the viability of these techniques as potential data augmentation methods in the future.

We show that any collection of orientation-preserving surface homeomorphisms with discrete isometry groups does not have compact approximations in the sense of Robecke topology, except possibly in the case where the isometry groups are finite. Additionally, our study introduces a new topology on groups of homeomorphisms called the Prokopec topology, which is more suitable for surface homeomorphisms. It's established that any subgroup consisting of surface homeomorphisms with well-ordered discrete groups cannot be compactly approximated according to the Prokopec topology, provided that subgroup's action on the surface does not constitute an algebraic extension.

By applying co-adjoint representations and constructing the corresponding invariant Poisson structures, we theoretically found the integrable systems on various generalized lambda deformations of three-dimensional cosets. We then obtained the specific forms of these integrable structures for three specific group choices and demonstrated that they can be expressed in terms of a single coordinate on the deformed spaces' surfaces. Furthermore, we identified the Hamiltonians for the integrable systems on these deformed spaces, which are invariant under the group actions. We also obtained the general forms of the Hamiltonians for the coset of $SU(2)$. We then directed the system's invariant vectors into specific components and derived first-order equations for the corresponding systems. We chose a specific group choice for the deformation and obtained the general forms of the Hamiltonians for the coset of $SU(2)$ and mapped the system's phases from general forms to specific forms, which are invariant under the group actions. We then directed the system's invariant vectors into specific components and derived first-order equations for the corresponding systems. We chose a specific group choice for the deformation and obtained the general forms of the Hamiltonians for the coset of $SU(2)$. We calculated the corresponding boundary values and mapped the system's phases from general forms to specific forms on the deformed $SU(2)/U(1)$ group choice. The primary concern of this paper is to demonstrate that a hexahedral mesh 
containing a limited number of hexahedra can perfectly replicate the shape 
of any object in 3D space. The study shows that a mesh comprising only 
up-to-58 hexahedra can achieve this goal and also validate the accuracy of 
the results using testing objects in various shapes. The paper particularly 
targets applications where precise simulations are crucial and imposes the 
condition that all hexahedra must align perfectly with the object's boundary 
while allowing individual hexahedra to vary in shape. Additionally, a mesh 
comprised of fewer hexahedra is ideal for simulations that require faster 
processing speeds. The research also emphasizes the significance of accurately 
capturing complex features in objects using mesh topology. Finally, the paper 
outlines a future goal: creating algorithms capable of automatically generating 
these accurate and detailed meshes for any given 3D object.

The task of relation extraction, a fundamental task in natural language processing, involves identifying relationships between entities in the real world, whereas knowledge graph link prediction focuses on determining whether a connection exists between two given subjects and a predicate. We recognize that these two tasks share a common underlying mechanism – entity interactions – and thus propose integrating them to enhance relation extraction performance. To accomplish this, we developed a joint model that utilizes knowledge graph link prediction as a feature to improve relation extraction. Experimental results indicate that this combined approach can raise the accuracy of relation extraction by more than 2% and surpass existing state-of-the-art models.

As power electronics continue to evolve, the demand for precise, analytical models of inverter circuits is escalating. These accurate models are essential for numerous applications, including renewable energy systems, flexible AC power grids, and electric vehicles. Traditional models, such as lumped-component and lumped-inductor LCL filters, are no longer sufficient for modern inverter topologies. We introduce a novel, analytical model that represents the inverter circuit with an optimal piecewise linear function, derived using the Curve Fitting Toolbox in Matlab. This new approach simplifies system design, analysis, and testing by eliminating components like diode forward voltage drop and switching resistance. With this model, it's possible to achieve a 1% THD below 1 kHz and less than 0.1% THD above 1 kHz. We provide a step-by-step guide on using the Curve Fitting Toolbox and share our source code, paving the way for future developments and applications.

Reinforcement learning often operates in environments that lack the clear-cut continuity found in Euclidean spaces, making it difficult to transfer knowledge between similar tasks. In this context, we've developed a new concept of continuity suitable for reinforcement learning, based on the principles of coarse-grained geometry. Our work shows that this form of continuity can be used to devise effective transfer techniques and establish connections between reinforcement learning and classical continuous-valued reinforcement learning. Specifically, we've demonstrated the ability to transfer knowledge between tasks through off-policy approaches and identify conditions under which this transfer is achievable. Moreover, these conditions reveal a connection between the proposed continuity and a standard continuity concept used in the field.

The unique characteristics of living entities, such as movement and external existence, set them apart from non-living things. To investigate how animals and inanimate objects perceive and categorize, researchers created a categorization task with visually presented stimuli that combined red apples with non-living green spheres. These combinations included still-life scenes, videos of apples, and videos of the apples interacting with the green spheres as if they were alive. Human subjects performed the task while brain activity was monitored, and the results showed that the ventral temporal cortex distinguished between animate and inanimate objects, including complex entities that were neither clearly alive nor clearly non-living. This finding has implications for understanding the complex classification of entities in society, such as humans and robots.

In complex multiphysics models, preserving a perfect form of the governing equations is crucial for accurate simulation and theoretical analysis. Although widely used finite difference and finite element methods can achieve this, they generally involve iterative approximate solutions whose convergence must be ensured. This study presents a novel algorithm that upholds the equation structure while performing multigrid methods and domain decomposition. It does this by projecting the result of each step onto the feasible set of the current domain decomposition subsystems. The paper showcases the effectiveness of this algorithm in preserving the equation structure by applying it to a one-dimensional elastodynamic problem and a two-dimensional Maxwell problem. It also highlights its ability to maintain positive material properties like density, stress positivity, and a conditional positive solution in the present of a damping factor in the elastodynamic model.

We analyzed the spectral and temporal characteristics of a superorbital state transition in the black hole X-ray binary MAXI J1535-571 using data from Insight-HXMT's map and TSG detectors. Our observations included Type I, II, and III QPFs, which lasted for 13.3 seconds to one day. Three distinct patterns were identified for Type II QPFs: persistent, recurrent (every 1.66 to 1.81 seconds), and overlapping. Most notable were the correlations between QPF hardness ratios and hardness, suggesting the upper corona changed from a compressive to a soft state. This correlation was consistent across two QPFs, 274 seconds apart. Furthermore, the spectral evolution was consistent with a geometric compression of the corona, resulting in a hardening and a cut-off energy that increased due to the upper corona's transition to a less reflective state. Our findings provide the first clear evidence that geometric compression and corona reflections jointly explain the hard QPFs in soft state transitions of an SMBH X-ray binary, which was previously hypothesized in the literature.

In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks that necessitate cooperative interaction, our approach focuses on developing algorithms that are both capable of observing and responding to partner actions. By incorporating observed action utilization in policy creation, we introduce a concept called transfer empowerment. This analysis assesses policy effectiveness across various correlation and entropy levels in both individual and joint action spaces. The elements of transfer empowerment are adapted to address the challenge of learning policies in partially observable environments by establishing boundaries for optimal joint correlation and entropy, which we achieve through the application of temporal difference methods. Two of our approaches demonstrate the integration of transfer empowerment in simulated cooperative tasks, yielding improved performance at various parameter settings and confirming our method's ability to efficiently utilize observed action information.

We introduce CoMet, a novel approach to rendering and one-shot learning of material images, which enables accurate identification of unknown materials regardless of their rendering conditions or origins. Traditional machine learning methods struggle with inconsistent data due to varying conditions in real-world applications. In contrast, our proposal leverages the connections between multiple datasets by training a network to recognize material images under diverse conditions through a large, combined dataset. By applying a physics-based renderer to simulate real-world conditions, we simulate a dataset of material images. A comparative learning network then analyzes these images to develop a condition-invariant representation of materials, which facilitates one-shot learning. We cofine-tune this network using a single sample of each new material, resulting in accurate identification on real-world materials. CoMet achieves a CR@10 of 80%, significantly outperforming existing methods by 13%, 5%, and 3%, respectively. Our proposal also facilitates the development of a range of new state-of-the-art methods for material identification, inference, and manipulation.

Two equivalent structures, Lie 2-algebras and 2-Lie algebras, are studied in depth. A significant number of definitions and examples are provided, covering areas such as homotopy Lie algebras, narrow and multiplicative versions, and objects related to string theories. Key cohomology and deformation concepts are explored, as well as the broader Lie 2-group framework. A notable lie 2-algebra example arises from the loop space of a Lie group. Some of the field's notable researchers and important publications are acknowledged. An appendix describes the necessary diagramatic language for 2-algebras and introduces the concept of a 120 Lie algebra via a crossing morphism.

Two-object pose verification is crucial in computer vision, specifically for situations involving real-world robot interactions. This problem can be solved using point cloud-based geometric methods, but these methods have several limitations including independence from visual data, insensitivity to noise, and low requirement for environmental texture. In contrast, visual-based approaches are feasible, although they can be prone to interference from noise due to local feature matching. To overcome these constraints, a PhD candidate has developed LoFTR, a method for local feature matching using attention-based self-supervision. This approach employs a unified neural network to identify and match keypoints based on input image pairs. By using a detector-free, local feature matching technique, the LoFTR method can robustly operate in environments with minimal texture. This approach has several distinct benefits, including the reduced requirement for environmental textures, fast processing times on standard GPUs, and high accuracy rates. The LoFTR method has achieved impressive results on two challenging datasets, including SceneFerret and SceneUnderstanding, and is now openly available for further research at https://github.comメント/LFD-LoFTR.

The Solar Orbiter and Parker Solar Probe missions are obtaining direct measurements of the Sun's magnetic field for the first time, enabling scientists to create detailed 3D models of the Sun's magnetic structure. However, the magnetic field measurements taken by the on-board vectors are prone to error, which must be corrected for the data to be accurate. Remapping the magnetic field measurements into 3D space without correcting for bias would result in substantial errors, potentially up to 500 Gauss at the Sun's surface. Several models have been developed to calculate and mitigate these biases, which this research aims to explore in depth. By using artificial data and testing different bias correction techniques, the researchers found that two specific methods, the "map-to-pole" and "map-to-sphere" models, effectively corrected for all biases, thereby ensuring that the reconstructed magnetic field models were largely bias-free and showed excellent consistency with the original noise.

This research paper explores a novel approach to Demand Side Management through an in-depth analysis of a real-world issue. To facilitate, a minor bill is introduced, which charges consumers with each watt of excess energy used beyond their scheduled quota, creating an incentive for consumers to adhere to their assigned energy quotas as closely as possible. To proactively respond to upcoming price fluctuations, consumers engage in advance planning and manage their energy consumption in line with anticipated prices. Each customer forecasts prices and uses an optimal controller to determine the optimal amount of appliance flexibility to schedule based on these predictions. Customers combine their individual forecasts through a weighted average to estimate general future prices, and in turn, utilize this anticipated price in their respective scheduling decisions. Our findings show that the resulting equilibrium prices exhibit notable differences when compared to traditional time-of-use methods, influencing customers to alter their behavior accordingly. Ultimately, our findings illustrate that the system's stability relies on the specific details of the billing system and the level of flexibility among consumers' appliances.

A discussion on gravitational impact is conducted for Hawking radiation emitted by charged black string equations of motion within a Rastall theory framework that modifies the Einstein theory of general relativity by introducing a novel covariant divergence of the Ricci tensor. By examining the mathematical and physical properties of these black string solutions, which are derived from a combination of the 3D Einstein-Rastall equations and an assumed energy-momentum tensor, it is determined that the Rastall theory does not yield solutions analogous to their Einstein gravity counterparts. Furthermore, an energy-momentum tensor with a stress component is used to analyze the physical properties of these black string solutions, which are found to exhibit time-dependent masses, charges, and pressures. These solutions are found to have limited lifespans, after which they dissolve into the environment. A semi-classical analysis is then employed to investigate the mathematical and physical implications of the Rastall theory on Hawking radiation, with results suggesting that the radiation emission temperature does not depend on the charged string's mass and charge, due to their time-dependent properties. This study also shows that the theory predicts that Hawking radiation is emitted by the charged black string in a state of maximum entropy within its lifespan. To compare the theoretical findings to existing experimental data, this study estimates the Hawking temperature for these black string solutions in terms of various parameters, but the theoretical temperatures are found to be significantly lower than the measured Planck energy of about. The conclusions drawn from von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem apply broadly, encompassing not only unitary transformations but also isometries and contraction mappings. Building on these findings, particularly in isometry scenarios, we investigate how the power method's convergence rates can be characterized through the spectral properties of a matrix. Moreover, generalizing the theory of Poincaré's mapping, we discuss the one-dimensional Hilbert space context and extend von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem to its companion theorem for minimal actions. In addition, we explore a range of topics including unique trajectories, periodic orbits, Poincaré's mapping, orbit stability, and the concept of adiabaticity in a basic, foundational manner.

The research on extremely old and metal-poor stars within our Galaxy is instrumental in grasping its chemical evolution and the origin of star formation. These stars are rare, and only five have been detected so far with a metal content below -4.0. Recent data release from Gaia, which covers light from these faint stars, offers an opportunity to find more. However, the spectrum of these stars contains crucial information, which varies depending on stellar parameters such as temperature and surface gravity. To rectify the trade-off between resolving the spectrum and reducing data dimensions, which cannot be inverted, we employed Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on simulated spectra. Our analysis discovered that by examining differences in spectral lines across multiple temperatures, it is possible to separate metal-poor stars, which have a relatively small number, from a large dataset of simulated spectra. This method was then applied to real spectra from Gaia's DR2, which revealed a group of metal-poor candidates. Follow-up observations confirmed that three out of the four candidates have a metal content below -3.5. These new findings, which include two carbon stars, have a metal content that is even lower than any previously detected non-binary star. Furthermore, one candidate, which is a yellow hypergiant star, has a metal content that is approximately -1.5, which is significantly lower than previously estimated. The most substantial discovery, however, is a metal-poor binary star, which has a metal content that is approximately -1.

The "Blaze" series in the Global Fire Monitoring System tracks daily wildfire
activity across the globe in real-time, offering comprehensive data on wildfires
including geographic location, intensity, and progress. This data is utilized to
examine and predict both nationwide and global wildfire totals, as well as the
number of large-scale wildfires (those covering more than 103 hectares) that
develop each season. By combining predictive models (ARIMA) with multi-year
seasonal trends (splines) and non-linear growth patterns (exponential), our
research achieves impressive forecasting results, with accuracy verified through
evaluation against actual values over a 5-year horizon. Specifically, the models
display high degrees of accuracy when forecasting both total wildfire counts and
large-scale wildfire numbers (over 103 hectares in size), with accuracy ratings
of 90% or higher across all forecasts. Notably, these advanced predictive models
shed new light on seasonal wildfire behavior, revealing significant variability in
both large-scale and total wildfire totals from year to year.

We've gathered and compared a variety of measures to assess the morphological complexity of words, using datasets from the Wiktionary and word lists based on corpus evidence. Our research revealed that most measures we studied are significantly connected, either directly or indirectly, which means we can calculate some complexity measures by combining other established metrics. It appears that certain measures prioritize word formation, whereas others prioritize word occurrence. On the other hand, measures like word frequency and word length capture two distinct aspects of complexity. We've also identified that certain corpus methods are more reliable than others, particularly when it comes to providing an accurate understanding of complexity. This is because frequency-based methods provide more useful information than those relying on word counts. This research sheds light on the variability among corpus-based complexity measures, encouraging their careful selection for specific research purposes.

Researchers at Novoshakhtinsk have conducted an experiment to detect gravitational lensing in clusters, which have larger lensing cross-sections due to their increased mass. Although initial results from a 10-hour observation did not reveal any events, a more in-depth statistical analysis indicated a 1 in 800 probability for no lensing events. A subsequent review of existing data on clusters by the Categorical Catalog of Galaxy Clusters found no strong lensing events among 75 clusters or less than 1% strong lensing events among 139 clusters. Studying the lensing events in clusters may provide insights into the early universe and dark matter. First results from a new experiment to study gravitational lensing in clusters indicate that no strong lensing events were detected within a sample of nine galaxy clusters. This finding is in line with the current understanding of dark matter but does not exclude the possibility of weak lensing events in clusters. A comprehensive review of existing data on clusters by the Categorical Catalog of Galaxy Clusters has not identified any strong lensing events among 214 galaxy clusters either. 
The current experiment's findings support our understanding of dark matter but do not exclude the possibility of weak lensing events in clusters. Further studies are needed to determine the frequency of weak lensing events in clusters and to better understand the early universe and dark matter.
