Current testing pedagogies often struggle to effectively convey the complexity of software testing concepts to students. To address this issue, educators seek innovative strategies that foster active student learning. Our study evaluates the efficacy of two distinct learning methods: inquiry-based learning, which incorporates conceptual feedback, and a combination of minimal and thorough feedback. We analyzed student performance over three consecutive years using a mixed-methods design that combined quantitative data collection with qualitative data analysis. Our examination of exam results and qualitative assessments of BSc and MSc students indicated that both methods lead to similar understanding of testing concepts. However, when considering various student characteristics, students benefit more from inquiry-based learning from conceptual feedback. Based on student feedback, we plan to modify the testing course to provide minimal and thorough feedback on future assessments.

Hypothesis shift, which changes a classification target with the same label set, is an effective means of adapting models across different datasets without accessing the target dataset. However, existing approaches to hypothesis shift often require partial target data access or a pair of fully accessible datasets with different domains. This work proposes a novel hypothesis shift framework that allows domain adaptation without target data or additional domain information, by changing the classification target itself, which is made possible through the application of a pre-trained model with contrasting object representations. This framework is tested on the CIFAR-100 to Tiny ImageNet adaptation task, demonstrating significant performance gains even with limited training data available. Our findings reveal that degrading a pre-trained model's performance is a viable strategy for facilitating domain adaptation under source-free conditions.

A Gas Core Nuclear Engine is explained as follows. It has an open core, within which fuel and heavy molten droplets mix and burn in a high-temperature plasma with a 700 to 1000 Kelvin surface temperature. The engine generates thrust through a combination of a tailed rocket effect, where xenon gas is expelled from the back, and a Newtonian reaction effect, where mass ejection from the engine produces the thrust. A recent study has found that GMNCs (Gas-Molten Metal Core Nuclear Cycles) could significantly improve the performance of the space transportation system by increasing specific impulse levels. This study will assess the potential for a GMNC engine to power a deep space spacecraft. It starts by reviewing the performance of the GCRE, then outlines the design of a space mission, and finally, presents results from analytical and simulation-based evaluations of the mission with different engine configurations.

This paper proposes a method to train neural networks using information from specific domains in order to optimize and speed up the process of interaction positioning in astroparticle experiments. Typically, experiments in this field involve extensive and costly deployments around the world which enable these experiments to identify rare occurrences of particle physics phenomena with precision. Due to the complexity of these phenomena and the immense time and resources required to build experimental setups, finding accurate and efficient methods to analyze data is of paramount importance. To address this challenge, domain-informed neural networks (INNs) that utilize knowledge from specific domains are trained to model interactions, resulting in accurate and efficient outcomes. Unlike general neural networks (GNs), INNs tap into domain-specific information, such as 3D geometry and particle properties, to adapt and refine their models. The paper showcases INNs and GNs across various particle energies and depths in 50 different benchmark scenarios, with INNs demonstrating an average of 65 millimeters in terms of improved spatial resolution and reduced depth biases while also accelerating processing times by 25%. Moreover, the study shows that INNs can maintain precise outcomes (better than 3 sigma confidence level) even in rare occurrence scenarios.

The EXOPLINES virtual archive of transmission and emission molecular opacity data offers unparalleled precision of at least 15%, updating regularly with newly calculated opacities and enhanced user tools. Opacities for diverse atmospheric conditions of various celestial bodies are provided, with a focus on hot-Jupiter exoplanets and brown dwarfs. The archive's flexible data format is suitable for any atmospheric model, and opacities are available in multiple formats depending on the model's composition, including for extremely line-d Dominated opacities. The archive features detailed line lists for over 20, and 16 gas species sourced from the most current literature, as well as an online calculator for estimated data. The creation of a dynamic archive allows for real-time adjustments based on user feedback and evolving line lists, and other considerations such as chemistry and geometry. The architecture of the archive also enables the inclusion of emerging high signal-to-noise line lists for stars and other relevant stellar sources for brown dwarf and hot exoplanet atmospheres.

This text provides an overview of an ongoing research project that aims to establish a theoretical framework for addressing logic queries within artificial intelligence by building upon the existing ASP modeling language and its associated semantics. The primary objective of this investigation is to develop a logical foundation for grounding ASP programs, and we have identified three key challenges to achieve this goal: initially specifying ASP programs with an unlimited bag constraint, unbound variables, and recursive constructs; determining the subset of these programs that contain models that can be grounded; and developing procedures that can ground an ASP program by transforming it into a solvable logic program. To address these challenges, we have identified two approaches. First, by employing a fixed point operator and set-theoretic techniques, we have specified models that can be grounded in relation to a given program. Second, by leveraging a pre-processing technique known as query-normal form transformation, we have developed a method to ground ASP programs with an unlimited bag constraint, unbound variables, and recursive constructs. However, this transformation technique incurs exponential complexity and memory usage in the size of the program's symbols, which necessitates the adoption of strategies to mitigate these complexities through algorithmic techniques and approximation methods.

Understanding the fundamental principles of any theoretical framework for quantum resources is essential. We develop a mathematical approach to describe the initial conditions for these theories by leveraging the free quantum theories corresponding to arbitrary Hamiltonians. By combining this with a general constraint due to the positive semi-definite nature of density matrices, we establish a necessary condition for the initial states in any quantum resource theory. This is further substantiated with concrete examples of labor, coherence, and entanglement across various systems.

We offer a unified method to estimate key characteristics of a data distribution, including variance, skewness, kurtosis, and the 80th percentile, using only the first four empirical moments. This approach relies on a single parameter model with a variable location and scale, as well as a strategy for selecting the optimal sample size. Our results indicate that, for typical datasets, there's no need for a large sample size to achieve precise estimations for 70% confidence. Moreover, the estimations for variance and the 80th percentile exhibit lower relative errors compared to those of other moments or distribution characteristics. Generally, the proposed method performs favorably next to established techniques such as the maximum likelihood and Bayesian estimation. Our work is inspired by the desire to create AI models capable of making inferences about a data distribution with minimal information available, specifically a few summary statistics.

We analyze multivariate statistical models with high-end tails, focusing on their natural parameters, R$_\alpha$ matrices, which relate to the characteristics of the models' margins and include the portfolio's excess return's heavy-tailed distribution. Our objective is to estimate the matrices under the assumption that only a selected subset of variables is provided. Initially, we will demonstrate under which conditions the subset estimator achieves the most efficient rate when the model's parameters follow a specific, 'nicely structured' form. Next, we will examine a subset of estimators for a class of multivariate models that include heavy-tailed, non-fixed variables and will analyze its convergence, showing that it reaches the same efficiency rate as the most optimal estimator. Our study also extends to the analysis of heavy-tailed models with non-fixed variables in a time series context, specifically looking at multivariate ARMA models. Our primary finding shows that subset estimator reaches the same efficiency rate as the most optimal estimator under specific, structured model parameters. Our work offers a framework to establish the most optimal efficiency rate for estimators in multivariate models that become increasingly complex with an increase in variables. Our results also show that, in many cases, the subset estimator has an analytical expression that can be applied widely to different models. Our study is available at the link below. Our code is available at the link below.

A novel set of quantum low-density parity-check codes is introduced, incorporating explicit designs that enable linear speed decoding. The construction leverages a refined variant of the Pavlovich duality technique originally applied in classical combinatorial contexts, and its stochastic framework is particularly suited for computer-aided design of quantum codes. The maximum likelihood decoder is modified to accommodate the structural simplicity of these codes, and its iterative convergence can be assured at a linear rate. What's more, the codes exhibit optimal performance on typical graphs at a given degree, and our research demonstrates a substantial performance-profit tradeoff.

The distance-$r$ dominating set of a graph is defined as a set of vertices whose shortest paths to all other vertices never intersect with any other shortest paths. A subset of this set called the distance-$r$ dominating group, consisting of vertices whose paths with the shortest distance, can be shortened by adding an edge, resulting in a new dominating set with the shortest distance. We investigate the computational complexity of finding this subset in graphs with specific characteristics and prove that it is NP-hard for graphs with certain properties and some restricted graph classes. On the other hand, we show that it is possible to efficiently solve this problem for some specific graph classes under certain conditions and also provide an efficient solution for finding a schedule with optimal distance-$r$ dominating group for trees. Additionally, we prove that this problem is APX-hard for graphs with certain properties and some restricted graph classes and also for some specific graph classes under certain conditions. Finally, we show that it is possible to efficiently solve this problem for some specific graph classes under certain conditions.

We investigate disordered topological insulators with interacting surfaces and distinguish two types of interactions: one that smooths out surface states and another that introduces depth-dependent properties. Our study shows that while both interactions lead to a logarithmically localized surface mode, they result in contrasting bulk behaviors. A smooth-interaction leads to a fully delocalized bulk state, whereas the deep-interaction produces a disordered system mimicking the bulk properties of a topological insulating thin film. Moreover, our findings suggest that the disorder-driven transition from a topological insulating film to a non-topological one can be facilitated by increasing system thickness.

A comprehensive review of supersymmetry searches by the CMS experiment from 2011 to 2018 is presented. This includes an in-depth examination of various supersymmetry search strategies conducted in distinct final states, including missing transverse momentum with energetic objects, lepton pairs, and boson or tau leptons. Results from 135 supersymmetry search channels are shown, encompassing a significant majority of the supersymmetry search portfolio at CMS. Supersymmetry search results are presented within specific theoretical models such as simplified topologies and specific supersymmetry scenarios including M2LL and Rasberry cases. These findings are interpreted through various constraints on the observable cross section, measured in the unit of picobarns (pb), with limits being established on the supersymmetry parameter space. Where applicable, results from combined zero and high luminosity runs are presented with 136 inverse femtobarns of data, with the exception of the M2LL and Rasberry cases where only data from 2011 to 2016 with 35.9 inverse femtobarns is considered.

While neural rendering has transformed real-time computer graphics, its widely-used implicit scene representations pose challenges for light-related data and bright colors in environments where accuracy is crucial. To overcome these difficulties, a new neural rendering approach has been developed that harnesses the strengths of explicit geometry for bright and light-intensive scenes. This method transforms 3D meshes into a more suitable neural format. To handle complex mesh deformations and intricate lighting in these scenes, additional advancements are made to the mesh deformation technique. This enhanced method predicts vertex positions and textures more precisely than current approaches, and its ability to respond to lighting changes and render colors accurately in high detail is on par with implicit models.

Observations conducted at the SOAR telescope in 2021 along with previously unpublished data, yielded a substantial dataset of 1735 measurements across 1288 pairs and 1177 targets. A significant discovery of this study includes identifying 59 novel pairs or subsystems among nearby dwarf stars, primarily, adding to our ongoing speckle program. Our speckle program aims to monitor orbital movements of binaries within the solar neighborhood, specifically, high-order hierarchies, Hipparcos pairs, and also assess 892 members of young moving groups and associations, of which we resolved 103 new pairs.

We will explore chiral algebras connected to group flags, establish their complete set of higher spin conserved currents, and prove that they can be represented by combinatorial models based on characters of symmetric groups. Our findings will be synchronized by an invariance known as the "hue-kinematics" map, which will be defined and its properties explored, particularly how it intersects with the concept of celestial double algebras. The work will be completed by the demonstration that a specific version of these algebras is applicable to the study of quantum field theories beyond their weak coupling points, with the four-point scattering amplitude calculated as a series of rational functions of the Mandelstam variables.

To stimulate the Sun's outer atmosphere and initiate mass ejection events, powerful explosions driven by shock waves are crucial.  Although theoretical models exist, there has been a lack of observations that directly observe these shocks in the corona.  Our research team has captured the first observations of a coronal shock using the Low Frequency Array (LOFAR) radio telescope, which caught a shock wave propagating through the Sun's outer atmosphere after a jet erupted on its surface.  The shock was detected using LOFAR's ability to resolve interstellar gas, which showed the shock wave had traveled nearly 200,000 kilometers in under 300 minutes.  These measurements matched the predictions of a classic model for astrophysical shocks, which showed how the speed of a moving front changes based on the magnetic field.  This discovery shows that the classic model for astrophysical shocks is valid for describing coronal shock waves, which shows that the Sun's outer atmosphere is more connected to other astrophysical sources of shock waves than previously thought.

The findings of current experimental research on particle physics are compelling enough to suggest that the Standard Model does not accurately represent the physical world. One key area of investigation involves the phenomenon of particle decay where one type of particle decays into another, unlike expected outcomes. With thousands of such decay experiments taking place, our analysis examines six notable cases where the Standard Model's predictions diverge from observed results. Furthermore, we analyze an independent anomaly based on the measurement of a specific particle's magnetic property and consider its impact within the context of the two Higgs doublet model where both light and heavy Higgs bosons can interact with particles. By working within a parameterized framework where relationships between model parameters are known, we determine if the model correctly interprets available data. While the model appears to align with experimental results in most cases, our findings indicate that it fails to fully explain two significant particle anomaly observations. As a result, these outcomes reduce the model's likelihood of correctness by 69% and 34%, respectively. It's crucial to note that our analysis does not involve a statistical fit, but rather relies on qualitative assessment. To support these claims, we analyze data related to particle mixing, an independent measurement of the two-photon decay of a specific particle as well as the observed quantity of certain particles. If the model's predictions hold true, these findings will be confirmed through experiments designed to test for signs of a broader theoretical framework.

We've developed a mathematical framework to study the random movement of certain objects, called vortices, in areas influenced by randomly changing forces. This model complements previous work on the topic, and our main contribution lies in the method we use to solve for the random movement of the vortices in complex conditions. We've demonstrated that by looking at the behavior of these objects in a specific order – from most to least complex conditions – it's possible to precisely calculate the random movement of the vortices even in highly complex situations. Our approach relies on a particular way of describing the movement of the vortices using mathematical equations, and we've shown that it's possible to precisely calculate the characteristics of their random movement. This mathematical framework has been successfully tested on several important scenarios, including the interaction between two objects moving through a medium. Our method opens the door for further studies on a wide range of topics, including the behavior of many objects in different environments and our new mathematical framework that makes it possible to precisely calculate the random movement of the vortices in highly complex conditions.

The entanglement of boson sampling processes is crucial for determining their actual performance capabilities. We identified the complete state vector of boson sampling, which corresponds to any multi-mode quadratic Hamiltonian evolution's final state, with one-particle operators. Through a fundamental proof, it is established that this state is necessarily entangled when defined by a set of distinct eigenvalues. Consequently, a major theoretical hurdle has been overcome, rendering support for the experimental findings that have successfully demonstrated quantum advantages achieved by various devices, including the spontaneous parametric down conversion, the optical lattice, and Fock states. Nevertheless, this study exposes a significant shortcoming of an earlier approach proposing a classical model for boson sampling and identifies an essential property that must be satisfied for any two-mode non-Gaussian state to be accurately represented by that model.

The analysis of temporal sequence data in fields like biology and medicine has been increasingly important due to its diverse applications, though challenges persist from a data representation perspective. Specifically, datasets containing short and high-dimensional temporal sequences pose significant processing problems, hindering the effectiveness of machine learning models. To address these challenges, we've developed a novel guided learning approach for embedded gradient descent that achieves better representation of input data, thereby enabling more precise spatial and temporal relationships within neural networks. Our proposed algorithm is independent of specific neural network structures, making it adaptable to various architectures. Our experiments show that guided learning is a valuable tool in improving the accuracy of short and high-dimensional temporal sequence classification tasks, as evidenced by our successful applications in biology and medicine where it enhanced classification performance of clinical data, thereby allowing for better prediction of disease states and the discovery of biomarkers.

Reinforcement learning efforts for partially observable environments frequently rely on utilizing a belief state, which represents an approximation of the agent's situation based on available observations. Standard approaches typically employ training of a generative model or a belief representation, often with a hidden state structure that serves as the true system state. In the context of the widely used Guwda et al. framework, it has been demonstrated that training a generative model through maximum likelihood does not guarantee the resulting model will accurately estimate the environment's hidden system state. This paper examines this issue further, with a specific focus on two types of environments: one with a true system state accessible through additional information sources, and another without such sources. In environments with accessible system states, it has been found that a particular variation of variational information maximization yields statistically consistent results. In environments without accessible system states, it has been discovered that a variant of variational intrinsic motivation does not converge to a correct system state under all circumstances. This implies that even with access to additional information sources, training models or belief representations is not sufficient on its own; additional motivation towards matching the true system state needs to be incorporated for accurate system state estimation.

This paper addresses the issue of efficiently detecting actions in videos using limited human feedback. Initially, we develop a versatile model called Spatial Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (STGCN), which incorporates a graph convolutional module for processing temporal information and can be easily extended to various temporal pooling methods. By integrating it with a spatial pooling module, it effectively extracts spatial features that inform the model about the occurrence frequency and duration of actions. Additionally, we create an effective training approach called Temporal Transfer of Context (TTAC) that aggregates contextual information from diverse temporal contexts, focusing particularly on inactive contexts to mitigate overfitting. At test time, our model is enhanced with an online pooling method that adjusts temporal contexts according to expert-labeled feedback, significantly enhancing the model's accuracy. Our proposed framework excels on Action Classification, Action Detection, and Weakly-Supervised Action Detection tasks, ultimately achieving superior results over competing methods on UCF101, Kinetics, VCOCT, COIN, and DGD datasets. Code is accessible at a GitHub repository.

A recent competition, the 2021 Image Similarity Challenge, held within the NeurIPS 2021 venue, aimed to evaluate state-of-the-art techniques for visual copy-detection and arts investigation. The winning team presented their methods and outcomes in a series of papers, which are also detailed in the competition's winning submissions. This research paper provides an overview of the competition's findings and the winners' research output.

Our work considers the stability of solutions and their fluctuations in boundary value problems for parabolic equations with localized reaction sites that undergo degradation. 

In specific scenarios with these degenerating reaction-diffusion systems, we analyze the asymptotic behavior of solutions and their fluctuations near the boundary, identify the dominant scale that influences the system, and determine the scaling factors involved. 

The study of fluctuations relies on the construction and identification of appropriate unstable manifolds in the corresponding half-space problem with a small parameter. 

Through various examples, we demonstrate the effectiveness and interpretative value of our approach for practical cases, such as a mathematical model of carbon arrest and degradation in a porous medium.

This research investigates the properties of nuclear matter at zero temperature within the influence of a strong magnetic field by applying the lowest order constraint variational method (LOCV) with the estimated $AV_{18}$ nucleon-nucleon interaction and the estimated parameter $g_s=0.6$. We have derived the energy of nuclear matter across various values of the strength of the magnetic field along with various combinations of the fermion sea quanta. Our research shows that the energy of normal and abnormal quasi-particles is influenced by the strength of the magnetic field, resulting in a decrease in the total energy of the system. The predicted energy of nuclear matter at the zero strength of the magnetic field is approximately  -3.82805981 $^{o}$ MeV, in line with the existing estimates.

Heterogeneous Client Communications in Federated Learning pose significant challenges, particularly regarding efficiency, security, and data protection. To address this problem, we present a communication-efficient method that applies differential privacy, DP-rec, which utilizes data representation learning and a reconstruction mechanism to allow clients to update global models with minimized data transmission. The framework achieves this by requiring each client to transmit only a minimal, privacy-protected representation of the model update, rather than the full update, and instead provides the recreation mechanism to ensure the server can accurately restore the update. By applying this, we guarantee that the server handles client updates in line with differential privacy, and we demonstrate that the applied reconstruction mechanism can be trained differently from the model update, thereby reducing computational complexity. Experimental evaluations on multiple benchmarks indicate that DP-rec delivers substantial reductions in communication costs while preserving competitive performance levels, often matching or surpassing existing methods. The code for this project is available on the GitHub repository, https://github.com/hughmhugh/DP-rec.

A comprehensive far-ultraviolet continuum map of the Taurus-Aquila-Xeuxina complex was created by combining the observations from Gaia, RIPS, and GALEX, which had observed the area with different telescopes. The UV data from GALEX was analyzed over various fields covering approximately 300 square degrees, and the 231 degree squared flux measurent error accounted for scattered light was corrected. The 231 degree squared flux error was further compared to theoretical models and the error range of 0.1-0.2 magnitudes was determined for point source detection, which was determined through a study of flat fields. The UV data was analyzed to distinguish Prostar sources and background stars by comparing the stellar fluxes across different wavelengths and developing a distinction chart that differentiated Prostar sources and the background stars by 0.2 magnitudes. A total of 1,518,652 sources were identified through this process, which were then filtered to eliminate 682,761 sources that did not fit the criteria for point source error. The remaining sources were further categorized into two groups based on their magnitudes, with 644,552 sources having magnitudes under 18 and 464,991 sources having magnitudes ranging from 18 to 21. A systematic study revealed that the majority of the sources with magnitudes under 18 were blue supergiant stars or pre-main sequence sources and the majority of the sources with magnitudes ranging from 18 to 21 were dust

To improve the efficiency of document search, our method enhances table recognition and retrieval by leveraging Graph Neural Networks. Our initial step involves extracting tables from PDFs using an existing method, and then reframing table detection as a node recognition task within a graph structure. Following this, we employ Graph Neural Networks to upgrade table representation and improve matching between query and keywords. Finally, our tables are indexed and ranked through a soft search operation. Our innovative method effectively combines graph-based table enhancement with improved search efficiency, and its efficacy is verified through comparisons with baseline techniques on the Allen Institute for Natural Language's IMGS dataset and the combined PDFs and IMGS dataset.

In dynamic decision-making scenarios, players may have varying levels of knowledge. Some may know the details of the situation, while others only have a general understanding. We've found that players who only have a general understanding can develop specialized plans based on their limited knowledge, as long as they have access to sufficient data. We've demonstrated that, in a specific format of these situations known as Repeated Bayesian Games, players with incomplete information can, over time, achieve the same outcome as if they had complete information, without needing to communicate explicitly. This outcome is determined by a specific model that reflects the likelihood and consequences of different events. We've also discovered that, in a broader range of situations known as Multi-stage Bayesian Games, players with incomplete information may not be able to achieve a desirable outcome, even with an unlimited amount of data. In fact, in a specific type of situation known as Prisoner's Dilemma, players with incomplete information may continuously experience suboptimal outcomes, as long as their opponent continues to make random choices.

The development of sustainable guided automation is crucial for demographics and census operations. In Mozambique, an innovative approach of on-the-go population estimation using IAI's census autonomous unit (CALU), integrated with ride-hailing technology, was tested to optimize estimation processes. By implementing this method in four neighborhoods in Maputo, calibration adjustments increased the system's precision and pinpointed location details of walking individuals. The proposed technique holds promise for scalable applications in demographics and census operations, ultimately contributing to enhanced census planning and preparation.

Over the past decade, substantial advancements have taken place to minimize the occurrence of incorrect positive results in data retrieval systems. These developments led to the creation of novel systems such as cuckoo and xor filters. In general, such improvements came with a significant cost as they often require significant extra storage space or can only be utilized in data retrieval systems that don't involve an explicit search for patterns within data. In this research paper, we explore ways to build efficient data retrieval systems that not only minimize the occurrence of incorrect positive results but also allow for in-depth pattern-based data analysis and require no additional storage space. Our results demonstrate that such systems can be effectively designed by combining the concepts of cuckoo and xor filters in a unique and harmonious manner. In our investigation, we also gathered and analyzed comprehensive data to find patterns and designs that could help reduce the occurrence of incorrect positive results even further. Our experiments have shown that our proposed design is not only scalable but also extremely efficient as it allows for speeds of data retrieval that are within 95-99.9% of optimal rates and occurs frequently in our tested scenarios.

We have theoretically analyzed multi-dimensional solutions for a specific process where three bosons interact under ultracold conditions and resulting in one molecule formed through three-body recombination. Our investigation shows that in an environment lacking symmetry, an overlapping wave function of two atoms can cause repulsion between them, resulting in one molecule comprised of three atoms. Furthermore, application of a specific laser pulse leads to the destruction of this molecule, and in doing so, from its deformed state, three-atom linkage, and orbital alignment, we observe the creation of one particular type of molecule and multiple modes of molecular orbitals. We have found that by adjusting the time at which this laser interacts, the likelihood of forming specific types of molecules (linked with particular orbitals) varies greatly. Moreover, our research indicates that as the number of atoms in overlapping orbitals increases, the separate groups of molecules (with particular orbitals) become less distinguishable. Utilizing detection techniques involving optical projection, we have successfully identified atom-molecule combinations as a result of this process. Our research reveals great potential in understanding similar interactions of three bosons and resulting atom-molecule combinations via laser interaction, and this knowledge could be applied in creating unique multi-atomic structures and multi-particle entanglements.

For simulations requiring high spatial details, particularly in terms of resolution, a method using the SPH formalism with multiple resolutions is introduced. This approach leverages coarse and fine resolution versions of the SPH kernel and smoothing kernel to achieve improved accuracy. In addition to providing a conceptual framework for SPH at multiple resolutions, this research also outlines a formal formulation for integrating multiple resolutions in SPH, with particular focus on fluid-structure interactions involving complex interfaces and multi-component fluids. Several methods for handling multi-component fluids are conceptualized, with the goal of maintaining a consistent framework. Simulation results are also presented to validate and demonstrate the effectiveness and accuracy of this multi-resolution SPH framework, particularly in the context of fluid-structure interactions.

Machine learning is a significant supporter of modern technology, with applications spanning science, medicine and engineering. A key issue with current machine learning techniques is the need to continually label data and adjust algorithms, which can be time-consuming and costly. The development of unsupervised learning methods has eased this burden, enabling self-studying systems to develop their own concepts. However, as the complexity of emerging technologies increases, this type of learning may not be enough. In this research, we demonstrate a hybrid approach - combining unsupervised and guided learning - using a quantum processor based on superconducting quantum circuits. The outcome shows that both types of algorithms can benefit from each other, with enhanced accuracy and reduced requirement for extensive data sets. This breakthrough sets the stage for the creation of complex, self-improving systems.

A recent version of the FastPitch text-to-wave model, specifically its TTS components, tends to have limited pitch variations. To expand its pitch range without compromising its high-speed processing capabilities, researchers developed the Timbre-Preserving Pitch Augmentation method. This method involves altering the input acoustic feature values to drive a pre-trained mean operator to produce a more suitable pitch. When this method is applied to FastPitch, it significantly improves its pitch controllability without affecting its quality or speed.

This study addresses the challenge of building intelligent city models by leveraging city metadata and sensor data to predict future city dynamics. Using a comprehensive dataset from Atlanta, we demonstrate how multi-hop attention graph models can forecast traffic congestion with remarkable accuracy. The proposed city model based on the Hopper graph transformer outperforms existing benchmarks, showcasing enhanced scalability and adaptability for extensive cities. The model's insights reveal that traffic prediction is heavily influenced by specific spatial areas, such as intersection zones, highlighting the value of detailed urban data for informed city planning. The research code, data, and findings are publicly available for replication.

We've examined the leptonic weak boson production process in association with $b\bar{b}$ particles, which will be available for investigation at the Large Hadron Collider's High-Luminosity run. Our research reveals that this process is closely linked to $WW$ fusion and has a significant relationship with $t\bar{t}$ production. These connections allow us to make $W$ boson mass measurements possible. By applying a multi-variable, multi-chanel machine learning technique that takes into account advanced detector information, we were able to determine the $W$ boson mass with a high statistical uncertainty of 0.12 GeV, even with the HL-LHC's highest possible 3 ab$^{-1}$ of data. Our study also shows that $W$ $\ell^+\ell^-$ + $b\bar{b}$ will be the third strongest production mechanism for $W$ $\ell^+\ell^-$ + hadrons after $t\bar{t}$ and $W$ $\ell^+\ell^-$ + jets after HL-LHC, and that this production mechanism at the HL-LHC has nearly twice the coefficients of $t\bar{t}$ and $W$ $\ell^+\ell^-$ + hadrons.

Remote-controlled vehicles called Telepresence robots have gained popularity in various fields due to their affordability and versatility in completing tasks remotely. A crucial factor for these robots' practical application is ensuring users have a satisfying experience while interacting with them remotely. This article presents a quality of experience (QoE) framework for evaluating how remote control delays affect user satisfaction when operating these robots. The proposed framework involves a remote operator and a locally controlled robot, with each party performing a task through a video conferencing interface. The study provides a model for measuring QoE based on performance efficiency and defines KPIs, including the probability of visual and control errors occurring. It also outlines an error classification system with corresponding probabilities and severities. To confirm the accuracy of the QoE model, a remote interaction experiment was conducted involving 35 participants, who operated the robots under different network conditions and their responses were analyzed in relation to the proposed QoE model. The study demonstrates how using the proposed QoE model can help determine when network delays exceed the acceptable threshold for satisfying user experience.

In educational measurement, various fields such as psychometrics, item response theory, and knowledge networks have offered new perspectives on complex data from surveys, quizzes, and multiple choice online questions. Lately, there's been a growing interest in applying novel statistical techniques that extend traditional models like factor analysis to accommodate diverse data sources and understand how different variables, items, or skills relate to each other. One group of models that fit well in modern educational settings is called Bayesian Hierarchical Linear Analysis models. BHILA models are built on a hierarchical structure of Bayesian linear regression models where prior distributions define the relationships between random variables at different levels, similar to other hierarchical Bayesian models such as multilevel and random effects models. Unlike common statistical models for multivariate data, BHILA models can naturally incorporate missing values, reverse predictions, and offer broad fit assessments, including alignment with data patterns like outliers and category effects. Since BHILA models are generally created based on the needs of each specific study, they offer a flexible framework for a variety of applications. Additionally, the models' mathematical underpinnings as latent variable models expand the range of possible uses even further.

The game of Mafia, also known as Werewolf or Assassins, is a party game involving
two opposing groups. Our work develops a basic model for calculating the chances of
winning the game by one group over the other. This practical model can be expanded
to study more complex game scenarios and predict outcomes. It's reasonable to assume
that the probability of one person being a mafia member on any given night is directly
related to the total number of mafia members and the night in question. Similarly, the
number of people killed on any given night is directly related to the total number of mafia
members and the level of detection by non-mafia members. These relationships allow us
to derive simplified equations that solve for the overall probability of one group
winning the game. These simplified equations can be derived by weighting the previous
relationships by the respective survival probabilities of non-mafia members and
identifying the dominant terms. This method yields a straightforward yet mathematically
legitimate way to calculate the chances of one group winning the game. It's notable
that the accuracy of the derived probabilities depends on multiple nights of gameplay
taking place, but the approximation is suitable for a one-night game. Moreover, the
calculated probabilities show that the outcome of the game is largely determined
by a small number of factors. Finally, we present two methods for confirming the validity
of our derived probabilities by comparing them with simulation-based probabilities.

The formation of gas giants via a radial infant planet-planet interaction is a theory that can explain the existence of binary giant planets in circumstellar disks. In this context, two planets are formed in a close proximity to each other, at opposite sides of a disk, and as they grow in mass, their orbits converge. However, if planet migration is hindered, they can remain in their initial orbits while accumulating gas. This study investigates how the ingestion of gas by planets in the absence of migration affects their ultimate size and the appearance of the surrounding disk. Using a simplified model of gas accretion, we analyze its influence on planetary mass in a binary system and replication of observed disk images through combined observations via ALMA. When gas accretion commences, it triggers a radial pressure gradient in the surrounding disk, hindering further gas accretion. However, if gas accretion is terminated early, it leaves behind a radial feature on the disk and a binary planet system in an irregular orbit. In another scenario, planets accrete gas while orbiting opposite sides of a ring-like structure, and when gas accretion concludes, it leaves behind a thin ring around the protoplanet system. In yet another scenario, it's possible for a binary planet system to develop within a resonant configuration, and when gas accretion concludes, it's consistent with observed spiral features. The electrical conductivity of a thin film made from armchair carbon nanotubes was studied through variations in temperature and light intensity. Measured conductivity showed low temperature darkness and photo-conductive properties that could be identified using a reduced Arrhenius equation. This relationship exhibited a significant change in slope at around 140 K, along with a noticeable energy gap at 0.26 eV at low temperatures. These findings matched with a model where intertube conductivity is assisted by the vibration of atomic bonds between tubes. Calculations revealed that the vibrations occur using a heated vibrational model with a critical point at 194 K and an energetic point at 0.19 eV. These observations provide strong evidence for the role of atomic vibrations in conducting heat through thin films made from carbon nanotubes.

This research develops a novel entropy-driven variable feature weighted fuzzy k-means (EVFkM) approach to cluster high-dimensional data with minimal information regarding cluster configurations. By drawing insights from information theory, a measure of inter-cluster distance is developed using the entropy of variable features, which is adaptable to high-dimensional data with mixed categorical and numerical variables. Furthermore, this method handles issues of feature categorization without separation issues and can handle large datasets efficiently due to its computational efficiency. The approach has been validated through several hyperspectral images and comparative analysis with the entropy-driven variable feature k-means (EVfkM) method, demonstrating its superiority in terms of computation time. Moreover, the evaluation outcomes demonstrate the performance of EVFkM is better than that of EVfkM in most cases.

This study addresses the limitations of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, which have inherent issues during training: (1) expert parameter instability and (2) suboptimal performance and inconsistent solutions. To rectify this, two novel algorithms are developed: one that mitigates parameter instability (3) and another that achieves consistent solutions and improves efficiency. We derive these solutions by transforming the MoE model into a linearly-constrained optimisation problem and applying block coordinate descent for practical application. Numerical experiments demonstrate the outstanding performance and consistency of these algorithms beyond state-of-the-art models.

This set of notes offers a standalone overview of the theory of Jacobians of genus g curves, Jacobian types of Prym curves, and a brief exploration of the underlying ideas of steady and stable chip-firing games on the underlying combinatorial structure, known as the Bruhin-Nagel graph.

We analyze the capability of measurement instruments to detect the nematic phase of quantum gravity on a cosmic scale by studying the behavior of light propagation in the early universe. The observation that unpolarized light exhibits double refraction in the presence of a nematic liquid yields an experimentally verifiable signature. Specifically, we consider the impact of anisotropy in the propagation of cosmic rays on stars, observing how this effect leads to a distinguishing feature apart from traditional alignment phenomena that involve beam bending. Though the current precision in measuring double refraction is not sufficient to confirm the nematic phase of quantum gravity, advancements in astronomy may enable the realization of a more comprehensive investigation into the nematic state.

The optimization of observational time allocated to the study of globular clusters, allowing the examination of their underlying stellar populations, is crucial in understanding their composition. Recent findings from the UVIT instrument on board ASTROSAT-2 have identified numerous stellar clusters and key insights in nearby galaxies utilizing FUV observations. Utilizing the optimised time, researchers have conducted a detailed examination of UV bright stars in the globular cluster NGC 4147 with UVIT's NUSPAC instrument. Two bright FUV sources within the cluster have been identified among the 24 tested stars, with corroboration of previously known bright stars and new discoveries reported in this study. Spectra analysis of these bright stars reveals a temperature difference, pointing to a dual population within NGC 4147 consistent with prior discoveries in other globular clusters. The presence of a blue straggler or young second-generation stellar population in this cluster is also a possibility. Further research utilizing ground-based observations is recommended to validate the findings.

This note presents a breakthrough result achieved by revisiting the Morgan-Bavto progression through the lens of the b-principle, a concept developed by Hamilton-Wengenroth. Achieving this required creating a method for converting b-principles into princples of fragile stability.

Deep learning's transferability, a crucial concept influencing how models generalize, is poorly comprehended across various communities. The existing literature offers few in-depth examinations of its essential characteristics, resulting in a fragmented and intuitive understanding of transferability. To address this, we establish two fundamental agreements that underpin transferability, one ensuring that similar training and real-world data distributions promote transferability, and the other stipulating that training data should facilitate better generalization when applying transferability. By formulating these agreements with theoretical frameworks, we provide a novel and intuitive perspective on transferability, enabling us to experimentally evaluate and theoretically validate our findings. The understanding and quantification of transferability from a theoretical perspective can guide future research and offer insights into the design of efficient machine learning models and strategies for enhancing generalization.

In our study on the spread of information within complex networks, we discovered that the network's structural arrangement significantly affects its speed. Specifically, we found that the balance between localized and global network connections controls the rate at which information spreads. By investigating various types of network structures, both artificial and real-world, we determined that the information spread rate is solely dependent on the network's community structure and not on its overall size or the specific information in question. Furthermore, our numerical simulations confirmed that a network with an optimal level of community fragmentation spread information most efficiently. These findings have substantial implications as they provide a theoretical framework for optimizing the distribution of information within complex networks.

We develop a novel measure to quantify the unique characteristics of a Lagrangian homoclinic orbit in a symplectic manifold, based on its relationship with the other connected Lagrangian homoclinic orbits. This metric, called quantitative Thomas-Yau distinctiveness, provides a specific estimate of how drastically the orbit deviates from its variations. The existence of Lagrangian homoclinic orbits is crucial for this calculation. The developed theory is particularly significant because it leads to a concrete, quantitative understanding of Lagrangian diffeomorphisms. Furthermore, we derive an estimate of the unique characteristics of Lagrangian Floer theory of two symplectic manifolds, X and Y, when connected by a series of connected, independently varying Lagrangian homoclinic orbits. The distinctiveness of Floer theory is a crucial aspect, as it has implications for the intersection theory of Lagrangian Floer theory and the properties of isotopy invariant Lagrangian Floer cohomology.

A reliable model for an unamplified optical transmission link, developed by A. Khawaja at et al in [1], has been previously analyzed under a continuous time framework. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of the valid range of parameters for the Gaussian phase noise model, determined through time-domain calculations. Our approach identifies the conditions under which the four performance measures given in [1] remain accurate, taking into account discrete time filtering instead of the existing continuous model.

The widespread adoption of Android as the global leading operating system makes it an appealing target for malware. To counter this threat, security experts have developed Android protection systems, such as sandboxing and security gatekeeping. However, malicious attackers have adapted to these defenses, giving rise to a relatively underexplored area: evasion attacks. These attacks involve evading detection not just by anti-malware software, but also specific security measures like sandboxing. This field study aims to provide an overview of this type of attack, focusing on general evasion strategies, techniques, and countermeasures, as well as the challenges and open issues that remain to be addressed.

Containerization has become a mainstream technology with Docker as its gold standard. Although containers provide lightweight isolation for applications, they don't adequately manage the dependencies between them. This gap leads to complex bootstrapping and setup issues, especially in large-scale deployments with numerous containers. To address these limitations, we've designed Ozy, a novel container management tool, to seamlessly integrate with existing environments. By allowing flexible argument parsing and configuration options, Ozy makes it easy to create uniform workflows for both scripts and services. Additionally, Ozy incorporates innovative features like "parenting" and "children" relationships between containers to facilitate consistent setup and configuration across multiple containers.

Our work involves employing the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) to
examine the many-body interactions of five degenerate Landau levels in a
two-dimensional, five-valley electron system in strong magnetic fields. We find
that an unusual reentrant phase of the quantum Hall phase occurs at moderate
Landau-level-mixing strengths, characterized by unusual sequences of ground
states, which are identified by patterns in the projected density operators.
Upon further increasing the mixing strength, these sequences become more
predictable and eventually align with the natural symmetry of the system.

Our analysis reveals that the recently proposed Thakurta metric, intended to model infant cosmological black holes, inherently contains terms that mimic characteristics of gravitational waves similar to those produced by cosmic string loops. Since these terms dominate the earlier stages of the evolution of such primordial black holes, they transform the properties of the black holes, deviating from the characteristics associated with their eternally spinning, classical counterparts defined by the (3+1) Lorentzian split depiction of general relativity within the Jacobson-Weinberg potential. Consequently, the phenomenon of gravitational wave emission predicted by the Thakurta regime diverges from that of the binary merger of compact objects described by the phenomenological model. Furthermore, the Thakurta regime departs from the optimal, eternally spinning limit of the Jacobson-Weinberg potential in its predictions. Moreover, the analysis confirms that the bounds on primordial black holes imposed by the LIGO-Virgo data remain unaltered; they are unchanged.

The formation of planets through pebble accretion is an ongoing area of research. However, theoretical predictions don't match observations of planets as much as they should. One major factor overlooked in these studies is how density fluctuations affect pebble accretion. Our study used SPH to simulate the evolution of young protoplanetary discs, achieving high resolution through the context of astrophysical fluid dynamics. This allowed us to study the development of density fluctuations in discs and how they impact planet formation. Our results show that density fluctuations affect how planets form from pebbles, leading to either the formation of multiple planets or monolithic ones, depending on how these fluctuations evolve. Our study was the first to theoretically show how density fluctuations affect planet formation through pebble accretion. We were also able to determine how variations in dust parameters influence this process. These findings have implications for future studies of planet formation through pebble accretion.

Recent research has established that overparameterization in machine learning is achievable due to a specific issue with the optimization process. We have found that in a broader context, a different issue - computational constraints - can make overparameterization possible. Unlike the original issue, this computational bottleneck is applicable not only to second-order but also to first-order methods. We demonstrate this by developing a specific loss function and a particular dataset with the property that large models are necessary to achieve zero training error, and this is because the training error is inherently bounded for smaller models despite the optimization method being suitable. Moreover, we show that computational issues can impede generalization in our setup, in contrast to a different loss function and dataset where overparameterization leads to perfect fit and generalization.

Three results were obtained; they can be viewed as extensions of Martin's work with different generation conditions. The first result stipulates that any enumerable set whose sum yields a predetermined Bohr set must have the same measure as the Bohr set, unless both are measure zero. The second outcome reveals that within anabelian group with characteristic not equal to two, the sum of any two measure-rich sets will either be zero measured or have a measure of 1. The third conclusion implies that within anabelian group with characteristic not equal to two, the sum of any two sets of measure-rich and absolutely measurable elements will either be zero measured or have a measure of 1. These findings can be viewed as generalized outcomes of Martin's work with different generation conditions. The defined term 'absolutely measurable' refers to a set whose linear image in virtually every subgroup has a measure equal to that of its subgroup. It is worthy of note that this term 'absolutely measurable' implies the term'measure-rich', which means the set's linear image in every subgroup has a measure equal to that of its subgroup. The defined term'measure-rich' however, is weaker than 'absolutely measurable'. The defined term used in Martin's work however, was'measure-rich', which means the linear image of the set in every subgroup has a measure equal to that of its subgroup. It is however, Martin's and my conclusion, that the terms 'absolutely measurable' and'measure-rich' are the same

This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within large urban settings where residents have multiple transportation options at their disposal. In response to various baseline models, we develop a more comprehensive mixed-integer linear programming model that incorporates new cut techniques to restrict potentially unfeasible solutions. Our model incorporates demands related to multiple destinations, time sensitivity, and various transportation costs. We demonstrate that our model is highly effective with large real-world datasets and outperform previous approaches in terms of both precision and computational efficiency.

We develop E-shop LM, a pre-trained language model tailored for e-commerce platforms like JD.com, which provides in-depth product information and user-generated content. To enhance the model's knowledge acquisition, we incorporate multiple knowledge sources and propose the Knowledge Understood pre-training objective to enhance its multi-modal understanding. With these innovations, E-shop LM excels in retrieving information from user-generated content and achieves top-notch performance in e-commerce tasks such as product information queries and price prediction. It significantly enhances the overall experience of e-commerce platforms by addressing common user inquiries and predicting product prices or attributes upon user demand.

A significant challenge in Alzheimer's research is creating an effective tool to predict whether an individual will develop the disease. Given that normal MRI scans are initially available before symptoms arise, this article proposes a non-invasive method to identify early-stage cognitive decline in patients and their likelihood of progressing to Alzheimer's. Inspired by the capabilities of contrastive learning in self-supervised image classification, a model uses Deep InfoMax to maximize the distinction between selected data sets. Our experiments indicate that treating the cortical-atrophied group as an elevated state enables the model to automatically identify areas of cortical thinning, associated with reduced cognitive capacity. Moreover, our quantitative analysis shows that this method successfully differentiates between individuals who will experience cognitive decline and those who will remain stable or merely exhibit mild cognitive impairment.

This research paper proposes a new approach to understanding the nuances of language by modeling the complex relationships between individual words, their contexts, and the overall meaning of a sentence. The proposed architectural framework relies on a state-of-the-art recurrent neural network modified to incorporate advanced mechanisms for data interaction, replacing traditional linear operations. Performance of the proposed model was evaluated across three datasets commonly used for coreference resolution in languages and compared to a range of baseline models. Experimental results indicate that the proposed model achieves significant accuracy improvements, with a notable boost of 8.8% in our tests, underscoring its value as a basic building block for more intricate language understanding systems.

A sublattice Augmented S-O coupling was recently proposed and has been shown to significantly impact electronic states near a ferromagnetic interface's boundary. This study focuses on the individual components of Augmented S-O coupling and their effect on a half-metallic ferromagnet with an inverse spin Hall effect, resulting in the breakdown of bulk symmetry. Our model reveals that Augmented S-O coupling can be comprised of two distinct parts: a change in the Rashba S-O coupling strength and direction due to lattice asymmetry, and an isotropic S-O coupling component acting on the sublattice. Both new couplings yield considerable corrections to energy states near the interface and prompt Goldstone modes, and these energy state corrections adhere to specific rules based on the type of symmetry broken. In lab-measured capability terms, these energy state corrections can amount up to a 100 millielectronvolt in the case of bulk transition metal monolayers and much larger for corresponding transition metal triplets.

We're exploring the concept of Shadow Matter, a new theoretical framework built upon a set of operators that mimic the behavior of ordinary matter when seen through the lens of a particular scaling transformation known as a conformal frame. While the primary focus remains on Shadow Matter, the model includes an additional type of matter for comparison purposes. Our analysis examines the stability of static black holes within the framework of the Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet theory, where the theory's additional constants are tied to parameters that affect the shift in the conformal frame. The results indicate that static black hole solutions are only stable when they adhere to certain criteria, depending on the shift in the conformal frame and the mass of the black holes themselves. Furthermore, the study reveals that asymptotically flat black holes are only stable when their masses fall below a specific threshold, depending on the shift in the conformal frame. Ultimately, the behavior of gravitational waves and the cosmological implications are also investigated in this theoretical framework.

To ensure that medical services, including AI-based medical devices, operate correctly with continuously evolving datasets, a new framework has been developed to estimate the predictive performance (test efficacy) of these models when their data sets differ. Conformal prediction-based methods enable accurate assessments of model predictions under distribution changes. This approach measures a model's reliability using individualized predictions that take into account both the training data and a specific test case, effectively adapting to shifting datasets. However, the conventional methods for evaluating conformal prediction methods suffer from high variability, making it difficult to conduct cross-validation, a common technique in machine learning. A new framework has been proposed, combining conformal prediction with cross-validation in the context of classification tasks. This development aims to assess the efficacy of AI-based medical devices in real-world settings where models are typically evaluated on datasets distinct from those used for training and model selection. Moreover, our approach facilitates both subjective and objective measures to estimate model performance. By applying this method to cancer classification, where classification of independent image and clinical information is simulated, the estimated accuracy of an AI-based medical device on a dataset known as DS1 is compared to its actual accuracy on a dataset known as DS57, a dataset that differs significantly from DS1. The results indicate a notable variability in the estimation of model performance, underscoring the need for more accurate estimation of model predictions under distribution changes. Ultimately, the efficacy of AI-based medical devices cannot be reliably estimated using the conventional methods for evaluating conformal prediction models

To understand the complex behavior of DNA at a molecular level, it is essential to account for its dynamic and varied structure. We introduce a novel method that utilizes rigid substrate biasing to enhance sampling in atomic-level simulations of DNA-DNA interactions. By combining this technique with multiple forms of energy compensation, such as umbrella sampling and hypernetwork Monte Carlo, we conduct thorough tests on two DNA systems in different conditions. Our results reveal the significance of incorporating rigid substrate constraints to uncover a broader range of DNA configurations, particularly at higher temperatures where flexible substrate simulations fall short. Additionally, the integrated multi-technique approach helps to validate the accuracy of our results by comparing them to existing experimental and theoretical data on DNA configurations. Our research lays the foundation for future improvements in simulating DNA-protein and DNA-methdiant interactions using more advanced sampling methods.

Any-source flow network programming has gained recognition as an alternative to traditional methods like linear programming and quadratic programming due to its reduced computational complexity through algorithmic techniques such as flow packing and arithmetic network coding. Among ANS encoding methods, the category of lossless encoding that is close to arithmetic source coding includes generalized arithmetical encoding, which we found to be particularly effective in this study. Our analysis using the context-tree weighting model showed that the entropy encoding of arithmetic source coding has a linear relationship with time complexity and no lower bound of approximation, confirming its effectiveness.

This study investigates the dielectric behaviour of a model pore solution resembling that found in cement-based materials using different approaches. Simultaneously, the dielectric properties of anhydrite and Portland cement paste with varying water contents are examined through frequency-dependent impedance spectroscopy and presented as a combination of capacitance and conductance values. These results are compared with data obtained from a solution replicating the composition of the pore fluid and an electrolyte based on synthetic calcium hydroxide. Both methods are then used to determine the dielectric constant and bulk conductivity of the pore solution.

We update our previous observations about the pattern $X-Y-Z$ in systems
where a heavy $Z$ particle is composed of other heavy particles $X$ and $Y$,
primarily focusing on systems containing a $B$ or $\Xi$ particle as the
heavy $Z$. The patterns we've identified for $B$-based molecules strongly
suggest that their couplings to the $B\bar{n}$ and $B\bar{K}$ channels are
controlled by $s$-wave dynamics, whereas $D$-based molecules exhibit
$D\bar{n}$ and $D\bar{K}$ couplings primarily controlled by $p$-waves.
Additionally, our analysis reveals that $\Xi$-barotons primarily consist of
$\Xi\bar{\Xi}$ and $\Xi\bar{\Lambda}$ states driven by $s$-wave dynamics,
while $s$-waves in $\Phi\bar{\Phi}$ and $\Phi\bar{\Xi}'$ bound states
dominate their formations. The patterns we've observed for $B$-based molecules
are particularly noteworthy, as they are less prone to being affected by the
$b$ quark's large mass, strongly hinting at their validity for $D$-based
molecules and potentially other heavy hadronic systems. The collective patterns
we've observed for $X-Y-Z$ systems may hold significant practical value in
shaping future $B$
