This paper is a follow-up to our previous research and offers a novel explanation for the creation of high-speed molecular outflows alongside stable star formation, based on the Repellent Gravitational Theory and the E-effect. We contend that the rotational motion of gravitationally repelled gas around newly formed stars produces the observed high-speed outflows, but with gas moving in one direction within the rotational plane and out of the plane moving in the opposite direction. This explanation is testable through models of star formation and by observing the behavior of super-heeled molecular clouds.

We've gathered a vast dataset of 73 fast radio bursts with precise 90% confidence intervals for 64 events, measuring the flux density of optical or UV emission that would accompany their radio bursts. This is the first time such a comprehensive inventory has been compiled; previously existing observations have shown that FRBs rarely, if ever, exhibit sustained emission that can be detected at optical frequencies. 

Our research also analyzed 11 FRBs from the STARE project, finding no evidence of precursor emission and setting new bounds on the logical "OR" of the areas where these emissions must occur, specifically for the precursor emission associated with FRB 200302: it has a width smaller than $\Delta t_p \sim 0.6 t_b^{1.33}$ and has a width of fluxes smaller than $\Delta F \sim 1.3 t_b^{0.71}$ while for the afterglow it has a width smaller than $\Delta t_p \sim 2.3 t_b^{1.47}$ and has a width of fluxes smaller than $\Delta F \sim 45 t_b^{0.35}$. 

Additionally, our research has analyzed 11 FRBs from CHIME, FRB 20181107A and FRB 20190426A both from STARE, 7 from the SRT, FRB 201602025 and FRB 20160225 both from FRB 20151149 both from FRB 201

Over the past decade, there has been an increased focus on advanced high-power laser facilities. Our work is centered around the European Laser Infrastructure (ELI-NP) in Romania, where we have outlined the technical specifications and then enhanced them to optimize the system's performance. By comparing these designs to other similar facilities, we have developed a method to reverse-engineer these systems from available published information. The three stages in our process are as follows: 1) System planning and initial design, 2) performance optimization, and 3) system reversal. We have outlined the details of each step and, for the benefit of future laser infrastructure designers, all supporting documents, including our own experience, have been compiled and made publicly available online.

Fine-tuned language models can create coherent and informative text, but they lack the ability to omit unnecessary information. Existing methods for filtering model output often rely on explicit definitions of relevance, which can be difficult to define or obtain in practical situations. This study demonstrates that a combination of a pre-trained language model and a few optional visual supports is sufficient to produce high-quality text on unfamiliar topics. The proposed method Utilizing Image Data Through Few-Shot Reasoning (UID-FSR) trains a language model to exclude irrelevant utterance parts by presenting it with visual information and accompanying multilingual spoken descriptions during a few-shot learning process. By successfully applying this approach to machine translation and zero-shot text generation, we conduct experiments showing its potential to improve both relevance and fluency in text generation without requiring explicit relevance definitions or visual understanding. Our experiment results indicate a significant average increase in relevance of 46% without sacrificing fluency. Additionally, the code for our approach is available through a link on the GitHub Platform.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports delegated mixing for Monero, allowing users to contribute to a communal mixing pool while maintaining anonymity through a simplified process with reduced dependence on monolithic mixing transactions. The innovative feature of transaction fragmentation in our protocol enables efficient mixing by splitting transactions into smaller components, thereby facilitating quicker mixing times and reduced costs. Additionally, our delegated mixing solution allows for more flexible payment terms, enabling participants to choose their own fees and fees splits, presenting a more practical alternative to non-cash payment methods. To further expedite the mixing process, we developed an automated mixing delegation system, which quickly matches contributors with transactions to be mixed, enabling faster mixing times and increased efficiency. Our protocol was successfully demonstrated in a live environment using Monero TestNet, yielding promising results with decenttrally-organized mixing activities.

A key feature of the EIC's luminosity is achieved through the collision of two high-energy electron beams, necessitating the development of sophisticated beam diagnostics to ensure its success. Brightness scans, which involve adjusting the beam focus to uncover its distribution, initially held promise as a comprehensive diagnostic tool but have proven impractical for the EIC. Although they fail to provide direct access to key parameters like the beam's emittance and intensity, brightness scans can be adapted to serve other crucial purposes. This paper will outline a proposal to use brightness scans for (1) identifying and localizing beam focus errors, (2) detecting and understanding beam load and loss, (3) establishing a rapid diagnostic for beam delivery, and (4) developing new diagnostic tools for the beam.

Multi-faceted modeling of an intricate system like traffic demands an integrated approach. In this context, a previously developed model that combines different perspectives - macro, micro, and meso - is applied to a specific network in and around Barcelona. Each perspective has distinct, detailed information about the network, its nodes, and the flow of traffic. The detailed views, micro and meso perspectives, consider various traffic data such as speed, count, and road characteristics along with a extensive database of the network's attributes. The model uses existing traffic information to generate an initial state and update existing models with new data, focusing on the interaction between vehicles and road environments. The study aims to develop a publicly accessible, detailed model for the network. Furthermore, this research contributes to understanding and recognizing the potential of data-driven modeling for enhancing transportation modeling and analysis.

Recent studies by BESIII and LHCb experiments have identified $\Upsilon(10753)$,
a newly discovered bottomonium state, which decays into $\Upsilon(2S)$ and
$\Upsilon(1S)$ accompanied by various mesons. Notably, its decay channel with
the final state $2\pi^+\pi^-$ is particularly intriguing. We aim to investigate
this specific decay mechanism and provide insights into how it might be realized
through transition diagrams. We suggest that the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(2S)
\pi^+\pi^-)$ transition could be brought about by a dark loop mechanism, which
explains the experimental observations. We further analyze and compare the
theoretical predictions with experimental data. Additionally, we examine
other possible decay mechanisms, such as the resonance decay of $\chi_{c1}(1P)$
to $2\pi^+\pi^-)$. We find that both $2\pi^+\pi^-$ and $\Upsilon(1S) 3\pi$
are crucial in describing the $\Upsilon(10753)$ state. We hope that the
theoretical findings will be verified by the upcoming BESIII's latest run.

This paper presents a novel optimization technique called AskewSGD to efficiently train deep neural networks utilizing quantization. Quantization significantly reduces model size and processing complexity by limiting tensor values to a restricted range of narrow intervals. However, direct end-to-end training with quantized models is impeded by non-differentiable "askew" error stemming from rounding operations. Our AskewSGD method effectively tackles this issue by approximating the quantized target output on each iteration. We take advantage of previous optimization state to improve current estimates and leverage previous error contributions to decrease their magnitude. Additionally, we develop a quantization-projection operator to refine final results. Our proposed algorithm outperforms existing solutions in reducing "askew" error while speeding up training and achieving accurate results on various datasets including CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet.

The Continuum Soft Robot project utilizes fully flexible mechanical systems to achieve robust solutions to complex tasks, offering exceptional capabilities in comparison to conventional robots.  This research offers an in-depth analysis of the methods to control and grasp objects via continuum robots, focusing on the combination of modeling and control as the most effective approach for designing and building these robots.  Key aspects of this paper include a comprehensive review of relevant scientific papers and the development of a unified taxonomy that classifies and defines the essential problems involved, along with the most commonly used techniques and challenges.  Our study will examine the current state of modeling and control for continuum robot applications, assess their difficulties, and make a distinction between well-established and open problems.  Our long-term goal is to provide a thorough overview of the modeling and control problems associated with continuum robots, along with their existing solutions and challenges, in the hopes of inspiring discussion and the exploration of novel strategies to address these issues.

The Jacobi group is a key player in the study of hermitian forms and it has
significant connections with the group $O(n+1,\mathbb{R})$. We find the unitary
representations of the Jacobi group denoted $G=Sp(n,\mathbb{R})\times \mathbb{R}^n$. As an extension of Kirillov's method of calculating
representations, our approach involves introducing a pre-image domain for the
Jacobi group representations. This alternative representation theorem of the
Jacobi group facilitates a more direct comparison with the known results.

Verifying facts presented in a table format can be difficult due to potential issues with language, missing data, and the structure of the statement. To enhance the verification process, we suggest disassembling the statement by splitting it into two parts - one describing the relationship between entities and the other specifying the attributes of these entities. By analyzing both parts, we can identify key entities, their characteristics, and how they are connected. Since the grammatical structure of the statement determines the disassembly, we utilize a parser to effectively handle various language challenges and apply transfer learning to improve coverage and address rare words not present in pre-trained models. By assessing the disassembly using different table understanding models, we can indicate the correctness of the statement and provide additional clarification if needed. Experiments with our approach on the FactCheckNet dataset reveal a remarkable 64.3% average disassembly recall, surpassing the current best method with 57.9% recall. Moreover, our proposed disassembly helps enhance the performance of existing sequential fact verification models by ascertaining the presence of essential table features, resulting in improved results on the FactCheckNet dataset.

Recently, researchers working with high-resolution images have achieved impressive results using Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (cGANs). However, when working with large images, most current approaches face significant memory issues due to their extensive pixel-by-pixel prediction process. To overcome this limitation, we present a new cGAN architecture called Hidden Space Conditioning, which achieves performance equivalent to the current best methods for generating high-quality images while reducing memory usage significantly. Our method achieves this via a conditional encoder that represents image characteristics in a compact format, thus allowing for faster training and generation without compromising quality. We thoroughly tested our approach, evaluating its performance in terms of both visual quality and resilience to adversarial attacks. Our findings are expected to provide valuable insights for researchers working with high-resolution images in fields such as semantic painting and image generation. Additionally, our contribution to open-source software aims to simplify image generation and classification for researchers, enabling faster experimentation and a more unified workflow.

To efficiently conduct Bayesian analysis, the Nested Sampling technique offers a reliable approach by approximating the posterior probability distribution of a model given observed data. This method works by isolating regions of the parameter space with higher likelihood values from those with lower ones. Recent improvements aimed to improve NS performance involved introducing a step selection procedure that chooses specific parameters to simulate next. Our study investigates the efficacy of various step selection procedures across different model scenarios. In addition to evaluating these procedures, we considered the impact of subpopulation models, which often require computing posterior densities for each subpopulation, leading to extremely high parameter dimensions.

In fault-resilient distance labeling, we achieve nearly optimal results for trees and planar graphs under node and edge device failures. Each device is assigned a memory device that stores its distance from a specific node, taking into account faulty components. For trees, our scheme requires $O(\log^2 n)$ bits per device and handles $t$ simultaneous device failures over a time frame of $T = O((t+1)\cdot\log^2(n+1)\cdot\log T)$. This resilience time framework was suggested by Abrahamson in 1988. For planar graphs, our scheme needs $O(\log^3 n)$ bits per device and handles a significantly larger number of failures, achieving a resilience time of $T = O((t+1)\cdot\log^2(n+1)\cdot\log T)$, significantly better than the previously best known result of Abrahamson for trees, while improving the number of bits per device needed by a factor of $\log n$. This resilience time framework was suggested by Abrahamson in 1988.

In this study, we employ quantum fluctuations to model a Bose-Hubbard model subject to an external driving force and controlled by dissipative parameters. Our findings indicate that the model exhibits behaviors reminiscent of the Klitgaard et al. setup in both time-based and frequency-based two-particle correlation functions. However, unlike the original model, our time-based results feature damped oscillations. Meanwhile, frequency-based functions align more closely with the driven quantum Brownian gas model, featuring shifts toward lower frequencies. Additionally, our research involves calculating and analyzing the quasienergy spectrum's imaginary component in the presence of two distinct gaps in the quasienergy spectrum, characterizing quasienergy bound states versus continuum states.

We analyze a general class of elliptic equations that encompass a specific subcase with $H^{1, p}$-growth, based on a 1978 paper by Faber and Manfredi. However, when we consider a smaller class with $L^2$-integrable coefficients, along with an $L^2$ solution, our research provides the necessary existence and regularity results. We define a current in the Borel measure space as $L^2$-regular, which allows us to derive our outcomes. We demonstrate that a smooth solution exists for the equation when both the coefficient divergence and the solution are $L^2$, which also allows us to derive $L^2$ estimates and establish the regularity of the solution under specific assumptions on the current regularity and the equation's structure. Moreover, by building on these results, we prove the regularity of the solution for certain classes of equations that are symmetric or have a unique function $a_{ij}(x, \mu)$ and show its applicability to Riemannian equations with mean curvature and in nonlinear PDEs that involve an intergral condition.

To identify invalid measurements in sensor data from a manufacturing setting, we develop a novel statistical method. It utilizes the variations present in the training data to create a classification system, which categorizes new data based on their likelihood of being normal or anomalous. This approach, called DGPOD, takes advantage of a precise Gaussian process regression model and a approximation that allows it to efficiently handle a wide variety of data. By comparing the observed data to these predicted distributions, the method is able to accurately identify anomalous observations based on their residuals. Moreover, the method is scalable as it only requires computing the Gaussian process once and can easily be extended to higher-dimensional datasets. Experimental results show that our method compares favorably to similar techniques in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. Additionally, we have created an implementation of this method in the form of a Python package called dgpod, which can be used by manufacturing practitioners to solve similar problems.

The application of digital quantum simulation using cold atoms to study the complex behaviors of quantum many-body systems draws significant interest. However, the simulation of open quantum dynamics, particularly those of quantum systems heated by environment interactions, remains a significant challenge. Our proposal outlines a strategy to effectively simulate the open Floquet dynamics of a quantum particle in a driven optical lattice. By adapting quantum-limited amplification to monitor the system's Floquet mode, where heat exchange between the system and surrounding environment predominantly affects this specific mode, we establish a similarity to heat-driven quantum systems theory. Following this, the proposal suggests utilizing local measurements and state engineering to estimate the characteristic features and thermodynamic properties of the driven system's thermal state, mimicking the behavior of a thermalized quantum system without depending on high-precision quantum memory. Our simulation demonstrates how the driven dynamics of a quantum system leads to the coexistence of a zero-point flux and non-zero temperature characteristics along with regular band structure, and further illustrates the potential to induce Bose-Einstein condensation in a specific "scar-like" state of the driven system. Our work provides a roadmap for realizing the digital quantum simulation of open Floquet systems without the need for precise quantum matter storage.

The article explores the convex solution $u$ of the Monge--Amp\`ere equation in an open convex domain with a nonnegative, bounded right-hand side, along with specific boundary data. We establish the convexity of the difference $|u(x)-u(y)|$ with respect to the geometric mean of the distances between $x$ and $y$, which implies H\"older continuity for certain cases. This leads to the finding of a bounded and convex solution in a specific subdomain when the right-hand side remains bounded.

Currently, optical clocks in periodic regimes have demonstrated remarkable accuracy.
It is vital to verify that similar optical clocks in stochastic contexts still exhibit exceptional accuracy.
Although optical clocks are often used in harsh environments, the standard methods for evaluating their performance in chaotic systems are not directly applicable due to their non-linear and fluctuating nature.
To overcome this limitation, this study presents a novel method for evaluating the performance of optical clocks in non-periodic systems by utilizing fundamental nonlinear perturbations as well as fractional dimensional analysis combined with nonlinear perturbations (RSSN) in the time domain.
The proposed method is validated by applying it to a simplified nonlinear pendulum clock and a nonlinear oscillator clock.
Our findings indicate that non-periodic optical clocks can attain high coherence times similar to those found in periodic systems.
This groundbreaking research offers a new set of metrics to evaluate the performance of optical clocks in complex systems with wide-ranging applications.

This research centers on software-defined networks (SDN) to address the issues in managing service-level agreements (SLAs) related to network traffic via the interaction between a controller and a fog layer intermediate between the application and transport layers. The proposed architecture incorporates service-function chaining (SFC) to enable control over traffic flow and service delivery, with the optimization of traffic routing for high quality-of-service (QoS) purposes. To prevent network overload and ensure resource efficiency, the system also implements a mechanism for fault avoidance. Real-time feedback from sensors allows the adaptation of traffic routing strategies for real-time traffic management. The introduction of the fog layer enables the offloading of computations from the SDN control plane, thereby reducing the burden on the control plane and promoting resource efficiency. The system's effectiveness was validated through simulations which showed that the integration of the fog layer results in a 25% reduction in network workload and 15% decrease in traffic delay compared to a monolithic SDN architecture.

Metric learning's pair-wise loss technique is centered around optimizing an embedding that minimizes a measure of distance between pairs of images within a query and a negative example. Two loss strategies, contrastive and away, differ in the type of distances used: contrastive losses use sine of distances and away losses use exponential of distances. Previous investigations examined combined losses but not individual loss types. Through gradient descent-based dissection, this research explores the distinct objectives of contrastive and away losses, demonstrating their optimal points differ significantly, and experiments validate these findings.

In this context, we explore certain classes of unitary transformations that have closed subalgebras within their underlying lattice structure, specifically focusing on the properties of fundamental, projective, and hyper-invariant subalgebras. Building upon previous work by [Calabrese_2019], we expanded upon their findings to demonstrate how certain quantum systems, characterized by their eigenvalue distributions, exhibit a reduction in entropy due to the application of entanglement-blocking transformations. Moreover, we established the connection between these transformations and holographic error-correction codes, with the former serving as a precursor to the latter. To further develop this concept, we propose a specific code known as hyper-invariant Matrix Product Density Operator (h-MPO), and through its application, prove that this code can correct for non-local errors while maintaining fidelity greater than $1-e^{-L^\alpha}$ in systems with $L$ spatial dimensions. Furthermore, the h-MPO code exhibits the ability to correct for semi-local errors with a radius of $L^{\alpha}$ and still maintains fidelity greater than $1-e^{-L}$. We have found that the hyper-invariant code can be represented using the holographic error-correction wheel, and that it possesses certain structural simplicity similar to the HaPPY code. We have demonstrated that this simplicity is not merely a coincidence but rather a reflection of the precise nature in which the hyper-invariant code enforces the principle of semi-homogeneity. We have explored several numerical methods

Our investigation into the filamentary network centered around the Galactic Center utilized Pan-STARRS $y$-band images and identified a network spanning $|l|<$4~kpc and $|b|<$2~kpc. This study focuses on the interconnectivity of the network, revealing a uniform pattern where filaments separate by approximately $45\pm1$ pc on average, with a standard deviation of $9\pm1$ pc. Their orientation exhibits a random distribution, with variations from this average largely attributed to the network's projection onto the plane of the sky. Notably, the average separation matches the average density of high-magnetic-field molecular clouds found within the same region. This similarity in scales suggests that the large-scale magnetic field plays a crucial role in shaping the network structure, with individual filaments likely forming where magnetic flux tubes link and gas flows become diffuse. This scenario is further supported by a nearby spiral arm, with the filaments closely following the magnetic field orientation, indicating that the network is shaped primarily by external factors. This pattern differs from the hypothesis that the Galactic Center network is sustained by diffusive flows, with both components likely existing in tandem but dominating at different spatial scales. This study implies that magnetic fields play a significant role in galactic structures even at the very center of the Milky Way, with observations supporting a magnetic starburst or reformation model. This work provides insights into 3D magnetic field structures and the dynamics of the central galaxy,

This paper investigates a distributed control technique to achieve conservation voltage deployment across unbalanced four-wire distribution networks.
  By linearizing constraints on current and power sharing, we create a convex optimization problem that can be solved in a decentralized manner by primary distribution substations.
  To address communication delays between substations, we propose a stability-based approach to select a control action, ensuring stability even in the presence of delay-induced instability.
  Simulation results on real-demand data from over 6,000 customers demonstrate that our proposed schemes reduce energy consumption by 2.7-4.4% and lower peak demand by 1.9-3.8%, with energy-saving performance comparable to a centralized controller.

We investigate two related problems. First, we examine delayed adaptive advisors. In this setting, an advisor's algorithm is modified so that it processes the arms only after receiving complete information about time intervals of length $\Delta$. It then selects a single arm within each period and incurs a loss equal to the chosen arm's cost until the start of the next period. By developing a linear bandit approach that estimates costs using spectral decomposition, we demonstrate how such an advisor can achieve performance comparable to nonstochastic adaptive advisors, albeit with possible slight decreases in efficiency due to delay. Second, we expand on previous work investigating delayed adaptive bandits. In this scenario, a bandit algorithm is modified to account for scenarios in which chosen armsincurred additional processing time $d_i$ after being selected but before the start of the next period. By integrating existing methods and improving upon them, we show how such a bandit can achieve performance similar to nonstochastic adaptive bandits, again with possible slight decreases in efficiency due to delay. In both scenarios, we maintain optimal regret upper bounds when processing times are uniform ($d_i = d$ for all $i$) and demonstrate how our methods achieve specific regret upper bounds for specific values of $d$. We also illustrate the applicability of these results to various real-world problems involving delays in testing or processing signals.

Current text-generation algorithms in dialogue produce readable text, but often lack the richness and nuances of human conversation. To address this limitation, our research focuses on incorporating discourse structures from spoken language into a neural dialogue system. Specifically, we've developed a system that predicts discourse markers, such as "in addition," “meanby,” and “as a result,” to enhance the coherence and relevance of generated text. Our approach is grounded in an extensive analysis of spoken language, which reveals a vast array of discourse markers across diverse domains, suggesting a considerable hurdle for human-like text production in dialogue. To streamline this process, our system targets a core set of crucial discourse markers, enabling a more manageable pathway for machine output that closely mirrors human communication patterns.

For two decades, significant advancements in the field of Quantum Chromodynamics have been achieved using lattice QCD with imaginary time intervals. This highly acclaimed method remains the only reliable approach for extracting key quantities essential for understanding the QCD phase diagram. This document outlines the fundamental principles of the technique, reviewing current breakthroughs and addressing persistent challenges. Additionally, it highlights the current state of simulations on complex lattices and prospects for future progress within this field.

A two-stage Gaussian Process predictor, termed cGPR, has been developed to accurately estimate the stress of essential offshore wind-turbine components, namely its foundations and blades. By leveraging the results of computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations, cGPR identifies promising reductions in the time and expense associated with uncertainty analysis for these complex systems. Firstly, the predictor identifies the most critical parameters responsible for the uncertainty in stress levels, accounting for approximately 70% of the variability in stress levels across all considered scenarios. Subsequently, the cGPR predicts the stress of a turbine foundation under a reduced set of input parameters, demonstrating compatibility with the outcomes of extensive numerical experiments conducted employing random sea states. Furthermore, the cGPR demonstrates significant efficiency gains, enabling the prediction of the stress of a 900D Sorensen foundation to be approximately 130 times faster than a deterministic approach. Finally, the cGPR is applied in a stochastic analysis of a IEC turbine blade under blade-deforming loads, showing compatibility with established analytical solutions. The cGPR is a highly efficient alternative, providing a 40-fold speed-up compared to a deterministic approach.

Turkey is prone to seismic activities with varying intensity earthquakes occurring frequently, emphasizing the necessity for swift and effective crisis information dissemination. Social media can provide valuable insights into public perception, beneficial for crisis communication and management. This study examines the use of Twitter data to gauge initial consumer reactions to the 2020 Izmir earthquake and its related crises. By combining textual and spatial analytics on Twitter, consumers' primary concerns during the crisis are pinpointed and analyzed. The findings indicate that consumers primarily focused on earthquake-related information, but as the crisis progressed and fatalities emerged, they began to discuss 'death' alongside 'earthquake', revealing the media's significant influence on consumers' perceptions. Moreover, through geospatial analysis, it is evident that consumers living closer to the affected areas discussed earthquake-related topics more extensively. The research indicates that consumers living under crisis-prone conditions are informed, engaged, and responsive to the media and geographical context.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we also explore which automorphisms $\varphi$ yield a countable number of twisted conjugacy classes in their corresponding nilpotent quotients $G/N$, where $N$ is a nilpotent subgroup of finite height. Specifically, for the generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar groups $\Gamma_n$ and its subgroups $\Delta_k$, we investigate which automorphisms $\varphi$ of $\Gamma_n$ result in a countable number of twisted conjugacy classes in $\Delta_k/N$.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a trajectory basis. The underlying equations are solved using a numerical method from the PETSc suite, which allows for an efficient basis that represents solutions to a wide range of conditions and parameters. The technique is tested by recovering the expansion coefficients of an expanding gas from time-sensitive data obtained through X-ray imaging. The space and time dimensions are combined into a single dimension using the matrix-multiply mass transport method, which allows for an efficient numerical approach. The technique is incorporated into an optimization procedure that seeks the best match between simulated data and actual data by adjusting a set of parameters. The technique was able to accurately recover key parameters of the experiment, such as expansion velocity and pressure, even in scenarios where initial conditions varied significantly.

This paper presents SceNDD, a novel naturalistic driving dataset that captures a wide range of realistic scenarios. The dataset was collected on an urban route within the city of Abu Dhabi utilizing a vehicle-mounted 360-degree camera setup. The collected footage was categorized into distinct driving environments and scenarios with manual annotations. Our primary goal in creating this dataset is to facilitate the development of autonomous vehicles capable of navigating various real-world driving conditions effectively. The chosen urban route allows us to simulate diverse driving situations, enabling us to supplement limited existing naturalistic driving datasets with a broader range of scenarios. To further demonstrate its usefulness, we apply a recently created semantic segmentation model, trained utilizing our dataset, to generate labels for a notable naturalistic driving dataset. The resulting outcomes reveal a substantial improvement in fractional pixel precision compared to manual annotations. This research contributes a new naturalistic driving dataset called SceNDD, rich in scenarios and environments, which could enhance the development of autonomous vehicles. Additionally, the creation of manual annotations documentation and the process of collecting the dataset has been made available to the research community for reproducibility purposes.

This work aims to understand how reflected entropy behaves in situations where there's an interface present in conformal field theories. We start by considering a specific instance involving a Majorana fermion tunneling between two separate regions separated by a boundary. For this particular case, the reflected entropy splits evenly between the two regions, which makes sense given that the fermion can only be created or annihilated. We then explore a more general situation involving an interface in models with conformal symmetry by examining either scalar or fermionic fields. For scalar fields, the reflected entropy is directly proportional to the interface's geometric length. Interestingly, in situations involving interfaces in models with spin, the reflected entropy depends on both the interface's length and the temperatures in the respective regions. As a final point of discussion, the behavior of the reflected temperature in situations involving multiple boundaries in models with or without tensions was investigated.

Our work involves research on an advanced extreme learning machine (ELM)-based channel estimation method for reciprocal multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems aided by reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS), which operate without sufficient cyclic prefix (CP). The estimation reliability of these systems is compromised due to delayed optimisation of the RIS optimal reflecting matrix. To improve this, an enhanced ELM approach has been developed for combined optimization tasks. The enhanced ELM method consists of two parts: the first generates a more effective training matrix by optimising its parameters, while the second enhances sparse representation using a tailored function. The performance of the enhanced ELM method is demonstrated through simulations, which show significant improvement over existing techniques.

The integral variation theorem in quantum mechanics independently confirms the formulae for the van Leeuwen-Gaudin model, the Jacobi tau-function, and the quantum Lax combination, which had previously been derived using coordinate measurements. Furthermore, it confirms a general formula previously established by B. C. Hall and the first author for energy observations. A key finding is that the first author's proof relies on projective measurements, a restriction that is not necessary for the theorem itself. In fact, the proof demonstrates that the theorem holds for non-projective measurements as well, which has significant practical implications for quantum information theory since many relevant experiments cannot be classified as projective measurements.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2-structures and real Killing 3-forms, which in turn creates a suitable framework for our analysis. Considering these factors, we find that deformations of G2-instantons are inherently trivial when accompanied by real Killing 3-forms. Consequently, no deformation exists for G2-instantons on manifolds with a Ricci flat connection, which is a direct result of the triviality of the and 2-form. More generally, when hypercomplex, hyperKahler, or Calabi-Yau structures are present with a non-trivial vector field killing the G2-instanton, a 1-parameter solution can be found.

The rapid spread of COVID-19 has forced governments to implement measures to slow down the infection rate, with the national contact tracing COVID-19 through mobile app being one such measure. As countries strive to contain the outbreak while maintaining their commitment to user privacy, the development of COVID-19 contact tracing apps necessitates an assessment of their inherent privacy characteristics. In this context, the present study introduces a formal model for contact tracing COVID-19 through mobile apps, building on the established Corsi et al.'s framework. It specifically examines the British NHS COVID-19 app, revealing a vulnerability that compromises its ability to safeguard against an attacker who has been infected. Furthermore, this study explores two methods to enhance the app's privacy: augmenting the encryption type used and incorporating a privacy-preserving mechanism, known as the 'drop-in time' variant. In particular, an enhanced variant of the NHS COVID-19 app is presented, called NHS COVID-19$_\mathcal{E}_{AEAD}$, which incorporates lightweight encryption mechanisms. In addition, another enhanced variant, NHS COVID-19$_\mathcal{E}_{AEAD}^\mathsf{P}$, is developed by integrating the 'drop-in time' concept into the previous variant, thereby reducing the duration of unencrypted periods. In contrast to other contact tracing apps, this study's analysis reveals that both NHS COVID-19$_\mathcal{E}_{AEAD}$ and NHS COVID-19$_\mathcal{E

The transition from classical to quantum world occurs naturally in many biological systems, particularly where electrical neural activity is concerned, even if it's been overlooked for decades. Quantizing the fundamental components of neural networks, we demonstrate how quantum properties can emerge in complex nerve cells and associated networks. This development enables novel quantum effects to surface or become more pronounced in brain tissue that wasn't previously thought capable of exhibiting them. With a focus on input layers, we show how quantum effects can occur extensively within neural systems. Our analysis indicates input layers possess a significant number of parameters essential for processing information. Our study shows that neural systems, particularly input layers, are suited to process information through multiple computation methods, including both classical and quantum techniques. This work sheds light on a long-standing puzzle in neuroscience, the pyramidal cell dominance in the cerebral cortex, and reveals potential applications for quantum computing in medical imaging techniques such as MRI.

This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying its correctness through the creation of accompanying ACL2 theorems.

A notable feature of asteroid observation involves the process of spectral
reflection, as scientists study the light reflected off these planetary bodies'
surfaces to gain insights into their composition. However, the information they
receive is often clouded by light waves from other sources, both on the asteroids
themselves and in the surrounding space, which distorts scientific findings.
Gaining accurate knowledge of these light waves, or "scintillation," is a major
concern for astronomers working with this type of data. Researchers recently
detected and analyzed the first known example of light wave fluctuations within
the Ichornia asteroid family - a specific family of asteroids that reflect light in
the L-type, and are characterized by their dark surfaces and L4 Gaussian
distribution. These fluctuations, known as "R-ring-like structures," were found
to be caused by the interaction between two specific Ichornia asteroids and a
resonance zone within our solar system - a specific area where the gravitational
pull of other bodies causes a specific increase in the orbit of other objects.
This new information provides further evidence that light waves, or scintillation,
can greatly impact astronomical observations and data. Studying these waves and
their sources is crucial for astronomers seeking clear and accurate data about
the information reflected off asteroid surfaces.

Ramanujan noted that odd zeta values satisfy a specific continued fraction, and we have found a new connection between this and Hurwitz zeta functions. Our result also leads to novel modifications of Ramanujan's continued fraction, yielding additional insights that were previously absent. Additionally, we have derived new formulas linking odd zeta values with integer partitions, infinite products, and the coefficients of continued fractions.

We establish a ring isomorphism between $z$-equivariant elliptic cohomology ${\mathbb{E}}_{t, z}^{*}(C^0(\mathbb{T}^2), \text{Sig}_2(\mathbb{T}^2))$ built on a ${\mathbb{Z}}$-linear torus ${\mathbb{Z}}\hookrightarrow C^0(\mathbb{T}^2)$ and the action of the rotation circle ${\mathbb{T}}\times{\mathbb{Z}}\rightrightarrow C^0(\mathbbak{B})$ for any tachyon ${\mathbb{B}}\in \text{Spec}(\text{Mod}(\mathbb{E}_t(\mathbb{CP}^1})).$ This comes from determining that the action of ${\mathbb{T}}\times{\mathbb{Z}}$ on ${\mathbb{CP}}^1$ is trivial when it operates via ${\mathbb{B}}$ in ${\mathbb{CP}}^1$ and that ${\mathbb{CP}}^1$ has the point of infinity as the fixed point under the given action. Moreover, we show that the ring isomorphism comes from the ${\mathbb{Z}}$-action being free and the action of the rotation circle ${\mathbb

We employ algebraic topology, the study of persistent patterns in size, as a means to analyze complex objects and encode our knowledge. By integrating $p$-persistent analysis into a machine learning pipeline that utilizes persistent diagrams, we can fine-tune our models and enhance their understanding of data. In this paper, we explore the application of algebraic topology in machine learning through the example of physics. The interplay between these two fields gives rise to new research questions that allow us to better grasp our surroundings.

To determine the ratio $R_{\eta J/\psi}$ of two-part cross-sections, we must calculate the differential angular distributions for the reactions $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \eta_c$ and $e^{+}e^{-} \eta J/\psi$ and then compare their magnitudes. This comparison allows us to accurately measure the probability of $J/\psi$ production in conjunction with an additional light hadron, thereby assessing the small-chromomagnetic field generated by the light hadron's contribution to its alignment. By incorporating Borel transformation into our model, we can obtain the Isgur-Wise function and relate it to the angular distributions of the $J/\psi$, providing a direct link between the confining potential and phenomenological observations. Moreover, our findings can help resolve discrepancies in experimental measurements of the ratio $R_{\eta J/\psi}$ by incorporating next-to-leading-order (NLO) corrections.

Our online survey with 235 Signal users revealed that users can be divided into two categories: those who need additional security through PINs and those who view PINs as an unnecessary complication. Our study involved conducting in-depth interviews with 22 Signal users in Nigeria and found that users who don't use PINs consider them to be an obstacle that hinders the enjoyment of other features. Conversely, users who adopt PINs utilize them for either an increased sense of security or to protect themselves from others. Notably, users who use PINs are in the minority; our results indicate that 88% of our respondents don't utilize PINs.

This study presents a method for calculating the integral of product functions over the surface of a unit sphere using Gaussian quadrature, which can be applied to calculate the average value of a function over a spherical surface. By determining the integral of product functions, we can precisely compute the average value of a function, enabling the evaluation of Gaussian curves, solar-energy distributions, and other applications. A software package is provided for generating quadrature rules tailored to different functions, which can be accessed via arviz.quad.spherical.

The curvature formed by the Hessian matrix or its generalized Gauss-Newton approximation holds significant value in understanding training dynamics and achieving generalization. However, current methodologies for analyzing the curvature are model-dependent and discrete, thereby limiting their applicability to diverse models and frameworks. To bridge this gap, our research presents ViViT, a novel algorithm for accessing curvature through the generalized Gauss-Newton's low-rank framework. By rephrasing the Newton approximation as a spectral problem, ViViT enables continuous and real-time monitoring of the curvature. This capability facilitates the development of enhanced training strategies, enabling users to allocate gradients according to the characteristics of the curvature. Notably, our experiments show that ViViT can accurately replicate the discrete curvature obtained from the theoretical derivation of the Hessian and generalized Gauss-Newton for various network architectures, highlighting its versatility and effectiveness.

We're investigating the impact of grammatical gender on word embeddings, particularly in languages that assign gender to nouns. Unlike languages with limited gender numbers, many others have a myriad of gender classifications, which can pose a challenge for neural networks addressing gender-based issues. Several investigations examine the impact of grammatical gender on part-of-speech specific to nouns, yet the effect of this factor on overall noun representation is still unclear, especially when multiple gender classifications are involved. 

To address this knowledge gap, we've conducted a large-scale study analyzing how grammatical gender affects noun representations in 50 languages, including varieties such as Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese. We utilized several pre-trained word embeddings and evaluated their accuracy in predicting the gender assigned to a noun based on other surrounding words. Notably, our research discovered a uniform pattern where a given noun's gender can be accurately predicted using the context in many languages, regardless of the number of assigned gender classifications. 

Moreover, we evaluated the impact of this context-based prediction on a range of sensitive domains, including hate speech and gender classification. While having access to a noun's context improves performance in these domains, the gender classifications assigned to base words remain the primary indicator. Notably, although data imbalance affects the models' performance in languages with multiple gender classifications, the largest class consistently receives the most attention. Our study provides valuable insights for developers of gender-aware NLP models and social media monitoring tools, highlighting the importance of incorporating contextual information in models designed for languages with

The charmability char(G) of a Lie group G is the supremum of values t such that G has a t-charming homogeneous submanifold. Our work demonstrates that for a finite generation of groups, including nilpotent and solvable groups, charmability and stiffness share key properties but distinct definitions. We then establish specific values for char(G) in groups resulting from outer actions on nilpotent Lie groups. Moreover, we prove char(G) equals 1 in solvable groups with real rank two and one in solvable groups of real rank three or higher. Additionally, we show char(G) can exceed one in cases of complex Lie groups.

Estimating an object's position is a critical element in numerous AI applications such as robotics, human-computer interaction, and image recognition. In our work, we focus on developing a method for calculating an object's position based on a single image, without any prior knowledge or training, given a category-level classification of the object and its location (either in the foreground or background of the scene). We establish two basic evaluation tasks: one focuses on determining the object's location in the image when its presence is also indicated, and another aims to identify the object's location when its presence is not visible. We create a dataset comprising real-world images sourced from Google's dataset without any prior annotation of object locations. We use state-of-the-art image recognition models to design accurate, category-agnostic models for various baseline levels of implementation complexity. Our results show that our method outperforms other object estimation techniques in both tasks with relatively minimal increase in model complexity. Additionally, we use human feedback to fine-tune the models using the dataset (although this step is restricted by ethical considerations due to human involvement).

Predicting short-term traffic conditions is an complex task due to the considerable volume of associated data and uncertainty involved in forecasted values. We present an efficient Sparse Traffiic Forecasting model that takes into account known characteristics like road types, speed limits, and surface types to provide accurate predictions. Since actual traffic conditions are often missing from existing databases, we rely on historical traffic data and employ an extraction method to derive useful spatial correlation data. This approach leverages archival data with newly collected traffic records to generate a comprehensive and structured knowledge base. Furthermore, we develop an efficient Similarity-based AttributE (SAE) model to estimate the current traffic conditions for unsupervised locations by identifying similar sites based on their attribute profiles. To this end, we adopt a knowledge-based memory network with pre-defined rules that attribute weights based on the considered attributes. Experiments conducted on real-world data demonstrate the exceptional performance of our model in traffic forecasting, with results that outperform existing approaches across multiple scenarios.

This study presents VACA, a new model that uses variational graph autoencoders to generate causal graphs from data and make interventional and contrafactual inferences. By representing uncertainty in probabilistic circuits, VACA's objective function aims to closely mimic the test environment's causal structure. Interventions are represented by domain experts and contrafactual analysis occurs automatically. VACA considers cases where observed variables may not encompass the entire causal graph, and its parameter optimization can be viewed as a restricted case of learning Bayesian networks in an unsupervised setting. We demonstrate VACA using two complex natural language commands: one involves coauthoring short, creative stories, and the other generates dialogue based on a given premise. In the first case, VACA employs a graph structure that represents the story's narrative, while in the second, it uses graphs to represent the conversation hierarchy. VACA successfully infers relationships between variables, demonstrates its ability to generate interventions and contrafactual responses, and outperforms alternative models.

The department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering at UE has developed a computing technology capable of carrying out intricate simulations in hardware form. This engineering technology has been converted into a radio processing device called REALTA and has been successfully integrated with the LOFAR facility in Ireland. Initially powered by 2048 CPUs covering a 304 MHz frequency spectrum and spanning a 8 second data collection period, REALTA is an innovative device, facilitating in-depth scientific research. Research conducted using REALTA has demonstrated a complex signal pattern in the time domain, allowing the identification of unusual radio waves connected to a flare-induced galaxy explosion, a rare scientific occurrence. Furthermore, analysis of REALTA data has also revealed a unique pattern of noise-like signal changes connected to a planet in the binary system of BPSR 1305, showcasing the scientific potential of this innovative technology.

A comprehensive understanding of light propagation in complex systems relies on analyzing individual photon behavior as well as its interaction with neighboring photons. Machine learning, particularly with the help of genetic algorithms, has been found effective in determining the configuration of system parameters that achieve the desired light propagation characteristics. Once the initial configuration is established, the inverse design process enables the optimization of free-form surfaces to refine light propagation. This approach is highly versatile and can be applied across various metaphotonic structures, including traditional and unconventional designs.

The high-stakes business of the film industry heavily relies on identifying which movies to produce, when to release them, and how to market them to maximize revenue and minimize losses from poorly received movies. Using a large dataset of 10,000 movies, our research examines the influence of various factors, including movie genre, production budget, runtime, and score on box office revenue. Additionally, we aim to find out how the release dates and pre-released attributes affect a movie's revenue. By applying machine learning, we can predict a movie's revenue based on its attributes before its release, enabling more informed production decisions. An online application is being developed to provide real-time recommendations for movie producers, producers of TV shows, and streaming services, aiding them in optimizing their content strategies.

The growing disparity between renewable and traditional energy sources necessitates innovative solutions for managing the fluctuations in the power grid. Alternative frequency control presents a promising approach by leveraging distributed energy resources to mitigate frequency fluctuations. However, the widespread adoption of this control strategy requires the analysis of its impact on grid stability to address potential vulnerabilities. In addition to frequency management, alternative frequency control also influences voltage dynamics, which can lead to unstable voltage conditions. In this research, we investigate the relationship between frequency and voltage control, focusing on the dynamics of system zero and critical damping to assess the impact of alternative frequency control on voltage stability. Furthermore, we demonstrate the application of this control strategy in enhancing the stability of power grids by stabilizing voltage oscillations through the use of a zero placement technique. Ultimately, the findings of this study provide valuable insights for the implementation of alternative frequency control in contemporary power grids.

To ensure the effective analysis and control of large-scale industrial systems, it is crucial to equip cyberphysical systems with intelligent capabilities. This can be achieved by transforming the underlying information, making it more valuable through data analysis, and embedding logical structures that facilitate automated decision-making processes. By doing so, it becomes possible to detect complex patterns and provide real-time insights in distributed systems. Several examples are used to demonstrate the benefits of intelligence augmentation, including optimized network resources, enhanced cyberphysical system security, and the ability to detect anomalies and human-driven systems. Furthermore, it is possible to leverage intelligent features to support the planning and management of critical infrastructure in emerging fields like space exploration.

Blazars with spectral energy distributions featuring non-thermal, double-humped patterns are largely attributed to various radiative processes, particularly inverse Comptonization of photons. To model these patterns, researchers consider a quantum electrodynamic (QED) comptonization, which has been theoretically developed for both purely polarized and partially polarized photon fields. This study employs a Monte-Carlo code (MAPPIES) for the partially polarized case and investigates its role in reproducing the UV/soft X-ray bump in blazar spectra. Utilizing a dynamic spectrum model, the code generates simulated spectra in the 10^3 - 10^5 eV range from a power-law electron distribution with two distinct spectral indices. This yields a satisfactory agreement between observed and simulated data for a substantial number of sources. Consequently, the partially polarized comptonization process is substantiated as a potential explanation for the UV/soft X-ray excess in blazar spectra.

Quantum field theory complexifications, where the coordinate fields become complex, offer insights into both the field theories themselves and their extended forms. By extending polynomial functions like polynomial landscapes, we can create new landscapes based on operations such as substitution, differentation, and algebraic manipulation of the previously used variables. Various techniques like extending the property of being almost periodic, conformal mapping, and analyzing spectral data can help us understand how field theories behave in this extended space. Moreover, we find that many properties of original landscapes are preserved in their extended forms, providing the necessary basis for extending quantum states without limitation.

This study investigates the ability of Haar-measure unbiased quantum detectors to identify symmetric pure states correctly, and we establish two key no-conjecture results. Firstly, we conclude that no such unbiased quantum detector can distinguish all symmetric pure states. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound on the probability threshold above which a given unbiased quantum detector can correctly identify all symmetric pure states, and this threshold depends solely on the number of qubits in the system. Notably, this result contradicts a previous finding by Avesar et al., who designed a specific quantum detector that could correctly identify all symmetric pure states with a probability exceeding 90 percent, but their results do not generalize to larger systems.

Baryon formation is explored through the quantization of QCD strings. When QCD strings fragment, the quantized QCD algebraic structure remains intact, leading to the creation of baryons consisting of three linked quarks. Utilizing the complex generalized Kaluza-Klein theory, QCD strings with helical characteristics can be derived from the fundamental space-time. The necessity of introducing a caesura factor arises due to the helical nature, resulting in the formation of a quantized helical QCD string. The fragmentation of this string and subsequent baryon formation confirm the quantized structure. Consistent with the traditional particle physics process, the fragmentation of QCD strings does not exhibit quantization, albeit when infused with caesura factor it displays characteristics of Generalized Kaluza-Klein theory quantization. The study reflects the inherent properties of QCD and the necessity for three linked quarks to constitute a baryon. The study proposes a potential new direction in quantum gravity, quantized QCD strings.

The study investigates how solar faculae contribute to north-south helioseismic travel time measurements by approximating the associated longitudinal flux using the Wilcox magnetogram's vertical field component. It suggests a correlation between the solar activity cycle and the travel time, with the time lagging the activity cycle by about 1-2 years, indicating a time lag in the associated flux's increase and decline. The study also considers the potential impact of electric current sheets on helioseismic travel time measurements, specifically regarding their lateral movement and the underlying convective zone's speed. Moreover, it examines the relationship between the travel time lag and the latitude of the underlying magnetic roots, specifically in relation to the latitude at which the magnetic field changes polarity between the north and south poles.

Researchers have employed analytical solutions and simulations to investigate the gravitational wave signal produced by cosmic strings and primordial magnetic fields within the frequency range of 1 nanohertz to 16 microhertz, as determined by the Pulsar Timing Network. They discovered that a power-law spectrum of cosmic strings with an index greater than 5/3 results in the dominant contribution to the expected signal. Furthermore, differing conditions in the generation of primordial magnetic fields either boosts or reduces the signal, relative to a reference scenario. The study's conclusions highlight that data analyses across multiple observation platforms should be synchronized, and that separate detectors should not be individually analyzed, due to the varied expectations based on the underlying physics. The researchers calculated the signal-to-noise ratio for a collection of magnetogenic strings and found that a network of deep and precise pulsar timing measurements may detect the gravitational wave signal produced by these cosmic strings, provided that the strain amplitude is substantial enough. In contrast, the expected signal from random primordial magnetic fields may be difficult to detect even at optimal conditions, as it is generally weaker than other potential sources within the given frequency range.

Light field technology has shown significant potential in various applications for its unique light field properties. A key feature of these properties is parallax, enabling adaptable compression approaches based on the level of parallax present in an image. Nevertheless, existing methods often fail to consider practical light field characteristics or efficiently utilize cues for effective compression. This study introduces a novel learning-based method for compressing light fields in a practical context, distinguishing itself from previous approaches through its focus on inherent light field properties. Moreover, the proposed method incorporates a feature that adapts to the specific geometry of the capture apparatus. Performance comparisons across diverse benchmark datasets, including synthetic and captured data, as well as newly created categories, display the superiority of our approach, both in terms of overall performance and specifically in scenarios with varying levels of parallax.

In a cross-lingual information retrieval framework, we investigate whether an unsupervised translational model can enhance semantic search across languages that it doesn't speak. This involves a challenge called Vector-Based Cross-Lingual Retrieval (VBCLIR). This problem has been studied by models that can learn and fine-tune without labels, using transfer learning as a key component. The question is how far we can take this approach. First, we show that an unsupervised model has the potential to greatly reduce the need for expensive label-based models. Next, we introduce an innovative solution that combines interactive and non-interactive models to power VBCLIR with reduced computational costs. Experimental results on the MS MARCO dataset demonstrate that our approach surpasses 11 different and state-of-the-art baselines, with an average of 3% better performance in Rank-N. This success shows that using non-interactive models to fine-tune and calibrate Rank-N can greatly improve VBCLIR overall performance and propagate positive search results from query to document ranking.

The increasing need for precise maps of essential services has driven the development of Generalized Boosted Regression Models as a leading approach for geographical estimation. However, the effectiveness of GBRMs and other spatial estimation methods in low and middle income countries has not been thoroughly explored. Our analysis involves evaluating eleven different techniques, including GBRMs, for small area estimation in Tanzania using two datasets. Our findings indicate that GBRMs, along with other machine learning-based methods, deliver the most reliable results. When comparing different techniques, we consider issues like computational simplicity, flexibility in data requirements, and the capacity to handle various types of data. Our research considers measures such as mean squared error, the amount of explanatory variables, and the computational time required for each method. Based on our findings, we offer recommendations for spatial estimation in low and middle income countries, emphasizing the importance of using design-based weights to ensure that the estimated values accurately reflect the population.

The classical Kelly betting strategy is a computational method used to determine optimal bet sizes at a two-option gambling table. This study adapts the method for a quantum setting where a coin toss equivalent is achieved through entangled particle observation, employing a continuous variable approach to tackle a formula previously deemed intractable by others.

Using the full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the density functional theory, we studied the electronic structure, stacking-dependent band arrangement, and band gaps of MoSi$_2$N$_4$, WSi$_2$N$_4$, TISi$_2$N$_4$, MoGe$_2$N$_4$, WGe$_2$N$_4$, TiGe$_2$N$_4$, MoSi$_2$P$_4$, WSi$_2$P$_4$, TIP$_2$N$_4$, MoGe$_2$P$_4$, WGe$_2$P$_4$, TiP$_2$N$_4$, MoSi$_2$As$_4$, WSi$_2$As$_4$, TIAS$_2$N$_4$, MoGe$_2$As$_4$, WGe$_2$As$_4$, TiAs$_2$N$_4$, MoSi$_2$As$_4$, WSi$_2$As$_4$, and TiAs$_2$P$_4$ with respect to their natural or inverse hexagonal structures. In our analysis, we identify that the quasiparticle band arrangement is not affected by stacking for these compounds, indicating that the ground state is 2D. Additionally, we find a common feature in the charge density of these compounds, which corresponds to a high exciton in the MoSi$_2$N$_4

The search for rare $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays has led to the identification of an anomalous signal at $125.7 \pm 11.4 \,(\text{stat.} ) \,^{+7.9}_{-5.9} \,(\text{syst.}) \,\mathrm{fb}\, (\mathrm{proton}\, \mathrm{branching}\, \mathrm{ratio})$ corresponding to a local significance of $2.4 \, \sigma$. The measured branching ratio is in line with a previous experiment and is compared to the theoretical predictions based on Standard Model and beyond its boundaries. The results were determined using data from proton-proton collisions at LHCb with center-of-mass energies of $7, 8$ and $13\,\mathrm{Te\!/\!}c^2$.

A theoretical model of how the solar system formed suggests that planetary material originates from short-lived, high-mass stars that previously existed. According to a new scenario, if we consider protostellar cloud breakdowns as a method for planet formation, then the first objects formed would be extremely dense, which in turn influences the formation of their surrounding disk structures. A numerical investigation reveals that planetary core formation efficiently begins even before the first stars have fully developed their outer layers. Furthermore, this experimental analysis indicates that disks formed from this process have a consistently inclined plane of solid material when compared to gas components, with the plane of the solar z-axis mirroring this orientation. Correspondingly, planets developing in these early disks are more likely to have an offset in their orbital patterns, particularly in regions near where radial accretion takes place and where extreme magnetic field influences affect gas movement. Observations of a particular type of two-star system, where the planets are closely aligned with each other, support this theoretical model as it fits the pattern of planetary arrangements observed across the universe.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observatories often use atmospheric models to correct these distortions before processing the captured data. These models, which are based on earlier research, were previously reviewed in a study (Saglia et al. 2021, paper I). In this paper, we outline, validate, and assess five atmospheric models suitable for correction at optical to near-infrared wavelengths (0.38 $\mu$m - 3.8 $\mu$m). Our correction techniques were tested on various telescopes, including those mounted on solid and movable platforms, and were influenced by altitude, weather conditions, wind, temperature, polar ice caps, and human activity. Consequently, a combination of the the truncated Gaussian and Mauna Kea models provided the most effective correction, and a hybrid version of these models performed well on various telescopes, especially when factoring in the height of the telescopes above the ground. Nonetheless, local environmental factors, such as pollution and temperature variations, can alter the atmospheric conditions, potentially leading to inaccuracies in the atmospheric models. Therefore, the best approach may be to monitor and adjust the atmospheric conditions in real-time using on-sky observations rather than solely relying on pre-established models.

This paper employs a refined hierarchical latent variable model to capture patterns in multi-period time series data, which exhibit sparse relationships across consecutive time frames. The traditional LSTMs in the neural network community and the hierarchical Bayesian model in the Bayesian method both utilize previously generated information to predict future values, but only the Bayesian method considers the uncertainty associated with those predictions. By adopting a refined hierarchical Bayesian model, we can simplify the computational requirements typically associated to avoid time complexity issues, which we then reframe as a Bayesian variational inference problem to optimize the model's parameters. We derive the variational posterior based on the refined model and propose an iterative algorithm to train the model, which achieves state-of-the-art results on various time series datasets. Moreover, we use a new dataset to examine the transparency and interpretability of our model, which can identify periodic patterns and uncertain prediction periods. Finally, we apply our model to the field of healthcare to analyze the connections between patient diagnoses and consecutive visits over time.

We establish connections between Stone duality, Pontryagin duality, and the logic $L_{\infty,\infty}$ by showing that corresponding dualities exist for compact abelian groups, real or complex numbers, and sets of natural numbers. The duality for real or complex numbers reflects the dualities established by Pontryagin duality and for $L_{\infty,\infty}$ is analogous to its situation in the complex numbers. In contrast, the situation for sets of natural numbers differs due to the non-existence of a dual compact abelian group. Instead, it is demonstrated that the natural numbers' dual is an additive group of left-cancellable relations, which corresponds to the first-order theory having a certain feature of being dense in its associated Stone space. Similarly, it is shown that the first-order theory of natural numbers relates to the dual of the integers' ($\mathbb{Z}$) compact abelian group via Pontryagin duality. Moreover, these results are encapsulated in a model class characterisation. The work also generalises to certain groups of measures.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing biased outcomes and uncontrolled data privacy. To address these issues, federated learning appears to present a compromise, enabling clients to train a model utilizing shared data while maintaining privacy. Nonetheless, existing studies on ethics in FL consider either fairness or privacy in isolation. This research, however, examines both concurrently, focusing on how to train models that are both equitable and private under FL. Based on the fairness definition $\mathcal{F}_{\infty}$, we formulate the first FL-based training framework, Fed-Fair-DP, to achieve simultaneously fair, differential privacy, and accurate models. By utilizing a novel layer-wise DP mechanism, we derive a privacy guarantee for Fed-Fair-DP. Furthermore, we propose the first empirical evaluation of fairness, accuracy, and privacy in FL settings, including two practical case studies. The results demonstrate that our framework can successfully achieve simultaneously fair, differential privacy, and accurate models, even outperforming baseline models in all three criteria.

We propose a supersymmetric expansion of a basic $U(1)_X$ model with a new and innovative distribution of weigt, $\lambda_{\phi}$. In this model, a new weigt between the standard model weigt $\phi$ and a $Z'$ field $\chi / \sqrt{2}$ is defined as $\phi$, with $\chi$ corresponding to a $U(1)_X$ charge of $x$. With $\chi$ acting as hidden weigt, this model explains how matter and dark matter come to equilibrium. With the lightest $\chi$ particle being neutral, this model leads to dark matter stability. With $\chi$ being part of a gauge symmetry that is spontaneously broken, this model introduces an innovative hidden weigt mechanism that is testable at the TeV scale. We explore the upper bound on $\lambda_{\phi}$ and the mass of $\chi$ in the context of the LHC second run. With $\chi$ being a messenger weigt, this model predicts the existence of $Z' \to \chi \chi$ decays, making it detectable in the LHC at high energies. With $\chi$ being part of a duality pair with $\tilde{B}$, this model predicts the existence of $Z' \to \tilde{B} \chi$ decays, also making it detectable in the LHC at high energies.
