In this research paper, we introduce an IRS-assisted wireless power transfer (WPT) network, combining the benefits of non-orthogonal multiple access and power transfer, linked to a central server via discrete cosines channels. To optimize this network's performance, we initially develop an optimization problem to achieve maximum throughput; however, this problem proves computationally complex due to IRS angle and user power reception ambiguity. To circumvent these complexities, we adopt a non-linear dimensionality reduction technique to convert data into a lower-dimensional format, reducing the optimization problem's complexity and implement an unsupervised deep learning (DL) method to learn and encode the ambiguity matrix. We then design an RL algorithm to exploit the properties of neural networks, using their gradient descent to iteratively find the optimal low-dimensional embedding for efficient network operation. Our simulation results confirm that the proposed DL-based methods execute three orders of magnitude faster than traditional optimization approaches, while achieving near-optimal performance.

For the first time, researchers used total absorption gamma spectroscopy to measure the Gamow-Teller strength distribution in $^{186}$Hg decaying into $^{186}$Au and compared it to theoretical QRPA calculations employing the SLy4 Skyrme force. The measured strength distribution, alongside the nuclei's half-lives, is best explained by incorporating a combination of proton and neutron transitions. We analyzed various factors contributing to the quasiparticle unfolding procedure and calculated the total strength associated with both the beta and double beta processes in $^{186}$Hg. The calculated maximum range for the feeding strength at $E_x$~2.1 MeV is specifically noteworthy. The calculated minimum range for the feeding strength at $E_x$~0.5 MeV is also significant. The combined theoretical and experimental results indicate that the isomer in $^{186}$Hg is structurally stable for an expected long period of several billion years before undergoing beta decay. We calculated the theoretical maximum range for the feeding strength at $E_x$~2843 keV and the theoretical minimum range for the feeding strength at $E_x$~1754 keV. The calculated minimum range for the feeding strength at $186$ keV is specifically noteworthy. The combined theoretical and experimental results indicate that the isomer in $^{186}$Hg is structurally stable for an expected long period of several billion years before undergoing beta decay.

Within the framework of a unified theory, a hidden sector with fermions whose fermionic nature is not revealed is introduced, which can interact with the standard model via dark substance-like dark matter. This interaction is further expanded to the standard model leptons through a portal mechanism. In turn, due to the portal interaction, the standard model leptons can undergo a significant transformation similar to leptogenesis, simultaneously impacting both dark matter stability and the observed baryon asymmetry. A more secure stability of dark matter is offered when it is coupled to the standard model leptons. This is because the same interactions that decay dark matter into hidden sector particles are counteracted by the standard model leptons, preventing dark matter direct detection constraints and establishing a stability time frame, which can be several decades. This phenomenon is demonstrated with 2 explicit models, which show that the lifetime of dark matter can be several decades. Furthermore, any dark matter annihilation constraints may be alleviated by the standard model leptons, allowing for a larger dark matter mass. This is illustrated in the case of a right-handed Majorana neutrino decaying into both standard model leptons and dark matter, both of which couple to the hidden sector fermions to a scalar. This result implies a larger mass range for dark matter, which can be as large as the GeV-TeV range.

The scarcity of comprehensive data hinders the effective learning control of intricate systems and those adapting to unpredictable changes. In this study, we demonstrate that gaining expertise in multiple modes of complex systems is achievable through a relatively small, universally constructed dataset. This dataset is generated without any prior knowledge of the systems' underlying dynamics, but is supported by straightforward, universally formulated observational specifications. Our proposed NeuroTopological Map, a neuro-fuzzy model with a systematized structure, enables efficient control of multi-modal dynamic systems and robust adaptation to unexpected changes, even when trained with the smallest of data sets consisting of only a few system inputs and outputs across multiple modes. The model was verified by applying it to a simulated quadrotor system with diverse initialization conditions.

Let $\lambda$ be a partition with $2\leq \lambda_1\leq \dots \leq \lambda_s\leq n$.
We construct an element $U^\lambda$ of the symmetric group $S_n$ as part of the Toda conformal field theory for $\mathfrak{sl}_3$.
This construction involves the orbit of the partition $\lambda$ under the action of the Weyl group associated with $\mathfrak{sl}_3$.
The element $U^\lambda$ is shown to satisfy specific relationships known as Ward identities.
These relationships are used to express $U^\lambda$ in terms of the elements of the parabolic subgroup corresponding to the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$-scythes of the partition $\lambda$.
These expressions can be viewed as a form of the fundamental lemma of Galois cohomology.
The element $U^\lambda$ is further shown to have connections to the stable cohomology of the Mora-Patel-Tymoze stack and the decorated Diophantine Simonovits-Kresch quiver.

Despite significant advancements in improving the diversity of generated images in GANs, a significant challenge remains in the mode collapse problem. A primary obstacle is the issue of overfitting in GANs, which is often exacerbated by overly simplified objective functions. In response, we are presenting a novel Relation GAN architecture, which leverages relation modules to enhance the diversity of generated images through a more comprehensive understanding of its variance. Specifically, our model incorporates triplet loss, introducing a new benchmark for state-of-the-art GANs to assess their ability to generate high-quality images with improved diversity and reduced mode collapse. Our experimental findings, encompassing both UniImage and FFHQ datasets, demonstrate that this new architecture outperforms existing GAN models, delivering state-of-the-art results and in-depth analysis.

We have successfully implemented an alternative approach to twin-field quantum key exchange without having to lock phases. This approach when compared to the standard method saw a 57% decrease in vacuum data bits and showcased tolerance to real-world noise levels that outperformed the standard method. Unlike standard techniques which rely on locking phases and thus are limited, our approach enables a broader understanding of quantum key exchange protocols that can function in diverse configurations. This breakthrough also opens up opportunities to study the fundamental properties of entangled states even in situations where measurement data is mixed.

We present a representation of the Toeplitz algebra $T_{\min}(\phi)$ with its symbol $\phi$ defined on either the Fock space or Hardy space within the complex unit vector space $\mathbb{C}^d$ consisting of $d$-dimensional functions with $d$ being any positive integer. To achieve this, three key concepts are explored in depth: the continuous functional calculus for symmetric Toeplitz operators on the Hardy space, the polynomial functional calculus for Toeplitz operators on the Fock space, and the equivalence principle showing that these two calculi share a common structure. By applying the continuous functional calculus for Hardy space and the polynomial functional calculus for Fock space, we conclude that $T_{\min}(\phi)$ is well-defined in a closed linear relationship within the closure of $\phi$-Fock space and the closure of $\phi$-Hardy space, respectively. We achieve this under the condition that the symbol $\phi$ exhibits radial symmetry in its point of zero and non-zero analyticity. We utilize the continuous functional calculus for Hardy space and the polynomial functional calculus for Fock space to establish operators within the closure of $\phi$-Fock space and the closure of $\phi$-Hardy space, and in conjunction with the equivalence principle, we discover that these two calculi generate equivalent Toeplitz algebras in the closure of $\phi$-Fock space and the closure of $\phi$

Real-world applications of object detection in computer vision are limited by current algorithms, which can only recognize a fixed set of objects. To overcome this limitation and improve object detection for everyday scenes, researchers have developed attention-based models. However, these systems have limitations of their own - they need extensive and costly annotations of image regions. To address this issue, the paper proposes a novel approach called PBL (Pseudo Box Label), which can generate reliable bounding box annotations for any object through a simplified text-to-box task. PBL involves text-to-box models learning to recognize words and their sizes based on existing annotated data, and then predicting boxes around target objects in new images. The predictions from PBL are used to enhance object detection models by substituting or combining them with detected bounding boxes. The approach was tested using a language model and YOLOv4, and resulted in significant improvements for every tested object category, showing that PBL can facilitate general object detection. Additionally, PBL can also be used as a standalone tool for identifying objects in images without any prior annotation, and it even works in video surveillance with a reasonable number of predictions per frame. A demonstration video is available at the link: https://tiny.vinodnarayan.com/pbl.

The presence of ionized, atomic, and photochemical regions within Rho Ophiuchus, influenced by a early B-type star (S1), has been identified using VLA and ALMA observations of Rho Ophiuchus in multiple molecular lines. These regions extend up to 53,000 AU in diameter and comprise ionized gas in a shell-like structure, approximately 9,500 to 18,000 AU in radius, primarily comprised of helium ionization by the star's Lyman limit. A photochemical model of gas in Rho Ophiuchus has shown that the region's radius can be scaled up by the star's R1 width, which is 9,500 AU, by a factor of three. This indicates that the Lyman continuum photon flux reaching the Rho Ophiuchus cloud is around one hundred times lower than the previous estimate. Emission from carbon and oxygen in the 158.2 micron line reveals that the star's R1 influence extends to 20,000 AU, extending beyond its ionized gas shell. A small, high-density cloud near S1 has also been identified, appearing to be tightly bounded by its photoevaporation process. A detailed comparison of the photoevaporation model predictions and observational measurements has shown a good fit for models created using variable initial mass functions in the range of one to three solar masses. Predictions indicate that the model will reach its escape stage within one to three thousand years. Measurements of the

Deep learning's prominent component, the transformer architecture, has seen substantial advancement in the fields of language and computer vision. A key transformer capability is generating factual text, which is critical for veracity in these areas. Recent years have observed a surge in the adoption of transformer-based models for veracity enhancement, leading to the creation of numerous techniques and applications. This study provides an in-depth review of the most recent transformer-based models developed specifically for veracity issues within NLP and CV tasks, focusing on pipeline distributions, optimization strategies, and parallel processing. It also explores the potential of these models to tackle related sub-problems, such as semantic representation and target identification, which are crucial to veracity. Ultimately, this review aims to identify the most challenging sub-problems and highlight promising areas for future veracity improvement.

Recent research has made notable achievements in constructing mortality prediction models based on hyperbolic long short term memory (HLSTM) networks, particularly for men in selected locations.  While these models take into account the temporal aspects of data, this research indicates that a more sophisticated approach is necessary to capture changes over time. Conversely, women's mortality trends exhibit fewer transformations over time and thus a simpler model is often more effective in this group. Therefore, developing separate models for men's and women's mortality forecasts may be the most accurate strategy. This study extends the HLSTM model to include factor models such as the factor model with hidden components and the model with adaptive and dynamic inputs derived from hidden components, both of which exhibit adaptive and dynamic behavior. Furthermore, an alternative model with time-invariant factor loadings was developed by freezing the loadings on training data. Results show that models with adaptive and dynamic factor loadings outperform the others, particularly for men's mortality forecasts in the United States and United Kingdom, while women's forecasts in the United States benefit from the model with time-invariant factor loadings.

The goal of neural architecture search (NAS) is to automatically design
high-performing neural networks for a given task. By treating network
design as a search space and employing an optimization strategy, NAS finds
effective architectures. However, it's challenging to balance exploration and
exploitation in the search process, particularly when the search space is
complex. In this research, we investigate how interference affects NAS, causing
the model to fail to generalize. We reveal that convergence issues are often
attributed to rich representation learning which hinders generalization. To
address this challenge, we propose a simple yet efficient approach that
significantly improves NAS's ability to generalize. Our experiments show that
our proposed method outperforms existing techniques and achieves better results
on well-known benchmarks.

Time series data in various fields like economics, finance, signal processing, computer networks, and astrophysics require analyzing series of data points over time to uncover important trends. In this process, experts typically apply both temporal and feature-based analysis techniques in conjunction with one another. To facilitate the second category, we introduce the R package 'theft' to provide feature-based analysis tools, specifically extracting relevant metrics from time series like the absolute conditional expectation, fouracm, f-1, TDD, TLOW, TPE, TPOS, and TWA features, which can then be used in subsequent machine learning processes. This paper presents the R functions for computing these features along with relevant example use cases. Additionally, we include a case study on the analysis of solar radiation data in a particular European city.

This research paper focuses on understanding the properties of groups with cubical geometry, which automatically results in uniformly convex spaces. Our primary finding reveals that for a group displaying this cubical trait, its boundary spaces are consistent if and only if the group itself is finite. This leads us to formulate a hypothesis stating that for a given boundary space, its associated group should be finite as well. To validate this theory, we confirm that the conjecture is valid in the context of spherical buildings. Additionally, our study involves analyzing the characteristics of boundary spaces resulting from infinite group structures.

Human-assisted translation can enhance the efficiency of automated translation by adjusting the output when necessary. Yet, to determine when corrections are needed, translators' reliability levels must be assessed. This study presents a novel Bayesian method to evaluate translators' reliability based on corrections provided by a crowd, and it simulates a translation memory to assess the translated text. Furthermore, a translation quality score is proposed to assess the translators' efficiency and accuracy. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through a theoretical example and an experiment involving real-world translations from a service provider.

Recent studies on random unitary systems have led to significant advancements in the understanding of non-Hermitian systems through the application of two fundamental tools: eigenvalue and eigenfunction analyses. To build upon this research, we undertake an in-depth examination of non-Hermitian systems from a quantum state perspective. By extending the concept of eigenstate and eigenchannel density of states to the study of non-Hermitian systems, we have found three key non-Hermitian characteristics that influence the behavior of quantum states in these systems. These characteristics are associated with long-term, mean, and short-term behavior of quantum states. To confirm our findings, we utilize two experimentally feasible methods: one that uses energy-dependent measurement strengths and another that involves measuring state-specific properties. Our work is particularly relevant to the study of single-photon optics and we have verified our findings in experiments involving parabolic and spherical microcavities. These experiments not only highlight the practical applications of our theory but also demonstrate its versatility.

The concept of "lottery tickets in deep networks" identifies that a pruned subnetwork from a larger, overpruned network can itself produce comparable results when properly initialized. We explored this concept by studying the characteristics of successful subnetworks from both convolutional and high-dimensional fully connected neural networks. Our research found that these optimal subnetworks often share similar activation behavior, functional relationship, and feature selection, regardless of the original network type. Moreover, our findings demonstrate that successful subnetworks from both types of networks often employ similar pattern-based feature extraction methods, which can be utilized to enhance pruned high-dimensional networks performance. Ultimately, our findings emphasize the importance of pruning technique details and data understanding in finding optimal subnetworks.

We introduce the concept of Anticipated Value (AV) for a lottery ticket, measuring the difference between the value of its winning tickets and the cost of purchasing tickets. Our comprehensive analysis of AV spans primary properties, secondary properties, and a comparison with the established Hit Number of a ticket. Additionally, we employ AV to examine when to purchase lottery tickets, taking into account the numbers on existing tickets. Notably, AV allows us to determine the numbers on new tickets to maximize the value of a purchase in a sequence of decisions. The computational efficiency of AV enables it to be effectively used in practical applications. Through AV, we also establish a connection to the field of prediction, revealing that the ticket's buyer has a perfect strategy if they can accurately forecast the ticket's winning numbers. Finally, AV allows us to adapt the existing idea of a 'hot' ticket to a broader category, implying that a ticket with consistently favorable properties for drawing should be classified as 'hot' and its owner should continue to purchase it.

The value of the anomalous dimension $\gamma_{N+3}$ for the $O(N)$ symmetric model's operator $\phi^Q$ has been determined at the six-loop level in the $O(\epsilon^{-1})$ expansion, where $\epsilon$ is the dimensionality of space. This finding allows for the calculation of the operator's anomalous dimension on the lattice, which can then be used to analyze self-dual operators in the $O(N)$ symmetric model.

Our research of the electron-phonon interaction in two-dimensional materials focuses on the effect of symmetric and asymmetric mechanisms. Using a tight-binding model and two different schemes - a finite-element method and the density functional perturbation theory - for two-dimensional materials, we investigate the coupling mechanisms and their influence on the characteristics of the two-dimensional materials' valleys. This study reveals that the coupling mechanisms significantly impact the characteristics, including valley Hall effect and valley Hall conductivity, and the asymmetric mechanism has a greater influence in cases where it leads to an increase in the 2D material's unit cell size along a particular direction. Moreover, it appears that the characteristics of the two-dimensional materials' valleys are sensitive to the type of the material's bond, and the asymmetric mechanism has a particular influence when the two different types of bonds are involved. This finding is particularly notable in cases of transition metal dichalcogenides, where the characteristics of the two-dimensional materials' valleys are influenced by the shift in the positions of the bond's atoms resulting from the asymmetric mechanism.

We took first place in the VisDA 2020 challenge by leveraging pre-trained models, specifically employing Contrastive Pretraining with Linear Classifiers (CPLC) to adapt to the challenge's unsupervised domain adaptation task. Our approach, described in detail within this abstract, will be reinforced through experimental results demonstrating its exceptional performance across several Visual Domain Adaptation tasks. These results will also showcase our model's ability to maintain a modest level of performance even under significant dataset manipulations, such as data augmentation and re-ranking. Moreover, we will examine the different sampling strategies within the underlying Contrastive Pretraining phase, specifically examining the impact of Uniform, Gaussian, and Cosine distributions. Interestingly, our findings reveal that Uniform sampling strategy yields the best outcome, which we will explain in the primary paper. Additionally, a supplementary section will examine the impact of Uniform sampling and explain its efficacy.

t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional representations, particularly effective in unsupervised learning for visualization purposes. Its core assumption relies on non-constrained data within Euclidean space, with ellipsoidal shapes allowed if the dataset's geometry is well-understood. However, in cases involving data with intrinsic spherical structures (like object orientations in rotation datasets or magnetization directions in iron-based materials), applying t-SNE can lead to distorted results. To address this issue, we present VMF-SNE, a novel negative sampling approach tailored to handle spherical data by taking advantage of a variational Bayes technique for generating approximate posterior distributions in Gaussian Finite Mixtures. Unlike other alternatives for dimensionality reduction on spheres, VMF-SNE offers a different strategy that does not involve gridding the sphere's surface or using neural networks. Instead, it capitalizes on the strength of the von Mises-Fisher distribution to create a significant advantage over alternatives with lower computational complexity, especially during embedding creation, and memory accessibility, leading to a substantial 1-D memory footprint reduction. In addition, VMF-SNE's negative sampling approach allows for a level of differentiability that other gradient-based optimization methods do not have, making it easier to implement. We compared VMF-SNE with the grid-based approach in terms of accuracy, differentiability, computational, and memory efficiency and found that it outperforms the grid method in all the mentioned aspects. We apply the coherent state representation in a comprehensive diagrammatic approach to analyze the properties of Fermi polarons in the weakly interacting Hubbard model across different interaction strengths and temperatures. In a two-dimensional lattice, particularly in the half-filled cuprate material, this method sheds new light on the observation that the effective mass exhibits a temperature-dependent increase, which converges to the strong interaction limit with rising interaction strengths. We investigate the origin of the temperature-dependent effective mass by examining diagrams of varying orders and find that it is primarily influenced by second-order interactions at all interaction strengths within this framework. Additionally, we calculate the critical temperature at which the quasiparticle residue plummets and compare it to the experimentally measured value in half-filled cuprate materials, yielding an estimate of the critical temperature that accounts for the observed trend.

Recent advancements in quantum computing from an theoretical to applied perspective hold significant promise for solving complex mathematics and physics models. The integration of quantum computing techniques is particularly important for addressing intricate quantum problems that exceed the processing capabilities of classical computers. The unique properties of fermions in quantum systems make them particularly challenging to model on a classical computer. The use of antibunching and state tomography in detecting Fermi polynomials allows for the observation of Fermi-Hartree-Bethe correlations in fermionic systems. The observation that these correlations serve as a precondition for obtaining accurate many-body wave functions through the Schmidt decomposition in quantum merging experiments highlights the importance of fermionic systems in understanding many-body interactions. The application of a digital-analog hybrid approach in emulating fermionic systems, characterized by a sudden death of entanglement in the digital section, is addressed using a quantum-walking based method for entanglement creation in the analog section. The combined digital-analog approach results in long-lived entanglement in the analog section which facilitates the accurate simulation of fermionic systems, characterized by antibunching and state tomography in the analog section. The efficiency of this method is illustrated by applying it to a simplified fermionic system, such as the system of two fermions in two sites, where theentanglement in the analog section is shown to last for multiple excitations in the digital section. We analyze the long-term behavior of several families of polynomial sequences, which originate from graph theory and are characterized by distinct construction methods. Specifically, our investigation focuses on sequences generated by the Jones polynomial, the Alexander polynomial, and the multivariate Higuchi polynomial, among others. By applying various mathematical tools, our results demonstrate that each of these polynomial sequences exhibits either a characteristic that defines them indefinitely or a behavior that causes them to eventually leave the realm of positive dimension. It is noteworthy that the multivariate Higuchi polynomial allows for a deeper understanding of its associated sequence through the use of elimination algebras.

Over time, the share of software engineers working remotely from their managers has increased significantly.  Managers who work remotely face unique challenges in leading their teams effectively.  This paper explores the relationship between remote work and the success of projects led by Scrum.  First, it investigated the success rates of Scrum projects through a quantitative analysis of 1,514 projects from the Benchmark database.  This established a positive correlation between remote work and project success.  A subsequent qualitative study of 23 practitioners provided insights into the underlying causes of this connection.  It became clear that successful remote work requires extra effort from managers to foster a strong, cohesive team.  This can be achieved through consistent communication, regular meetings, social events, and a sense of shared purpose.  Additionally, it is essential for remote managers to accurately assess the strengths and weaknesses of their team members and make informed decisions about task distribution and delegation.  Finally, it is beneficial for remote teams to collaborate on and meet shared goals during Retrospectives, allowing them to stay on the same page and work toward common objectives.

The study on the integer Gau-Wu value GW(I) of a integer matrix A, first introduced by Gau and Wu in 1988, has shown its significance in understanding some critical properties of matrices, including their trinitability and the Segre-Bart de Foresta classification. This work aims to investigate the GW(I) of 4x4 arrowhead matrices A where p is greater than or equal to 3, specifically those of the types (p,k,r) and (p,k,r,n) defined by Gullub and Van der Hofstad in 2004. These types include (p,k,r) with r greater than or equal to 2; (p,k,r,n) with n greater than or equal to 2; and (p,k) with p greater than 4. Here, the matrix A has p positive integer entries, its sum is (p-1)+k, its sum of squares is k+r times the square of a positive integer, and its sum of the products of any two entries is n times the square of a positive integer. Additionally, this work also derives the GW(I) of 3x3 arrowhead matrices A of the type (p,k) with p greater than 3.

The elliptic flow of electrons from decays of heavy-flavour hadrons, created in 5.02 TeV Pb-Pb collisions, was measured and was found to be about 0.05 with significant uncertainty. This result combined with data on elliptic flow of muons from the same decays was compared to model predictions, which included different calculations of the value of $\mu_B$ and the production mechanisms of heavy flavour. It was found that one particular model, ALICE, predicted the result would be around 0.04 which is close to the data found. This result may indicate that the production of heavy flavour in high energy collisions is influenced by the final stages of the expansion of the matter created. A plot comparing the data obtained for electrons and muons was also presented in the research.

Recent advances in topological data structures have led to the creation of new alpha-based methods for image segmentation that outperform established techniques in terms of performance and accuracy. This paper builds upon this work, exploring the use of persistent homology to enhance the detection of objects in images when the traditional gradient information is unclear or ambiguous. By combining gradient and color data in a single alpha structure, the proposed chromatic alpha structure offers the ability to adapt to a range of color distributions, thus improving the homography-based persistent homology detection method for complex, real-world image scenarios. The resulting detector has been rigorously tested across a diverse set of challenging, pseudo-real-world datasets created using synthetic and real images. These extensive tests demonstrate the proposed detector to be both more robust and accurate compared to the existing state-of-the-art gradient-based method. Furthermore, the supporting code and image datasets are available for others to build upon, expanding the foundations of homology-based detection capabilities.

We examine the degree of freedom (DoF) gain of optimal power control over binary power control in a network with multiple interferers, where each user has access to global channel information. It's discovered that with $K$ being the number of interferers, including the intended recipient, the extra DoF gain from using optimal power control over binary power control in this network is approximately $\sqrt{K}$ times a constant value, and this finding holds true even in networks where multiple receivers share the same intended signal. Moreover, the optimal power control that achieves these improved results involves users adjusting their transmission power based on the inverse of the number of interferers they intend to jam, and this power scaling method eliminates the need for users to adjust their transmission rates according to channel quality in order to minimize interference at other users. Before this, in similar network scenarios, a DoF gain of $\sqrt{K}$ was predicted through general principles. In contrast to previous studies, the current investigation looks at how power control algorithms perform in real-world networks where the number of interferers, including the intended recipient, can vary from 2 to an arbitrarily large number. Additionally, the current exploration highlights that optimal power control may not always outperform binary power control in Scenarios with small numbers of users ($K<10$).

Automated classification of sensory inputs into predetermined categories is an fundamental aspect of human decision-making systems, and this paper explores using an adaptive categorization approach to develop classifier models based on sensory data. These data are analyzed through both traditional and fuzzy formal concept analysis methods to determine concepts in two different spaces. Since the categories for classification are typically fixed and well-established, a novel framework combining formal concept analysis and Dempster-Shafer theory is proposed to leverage the obtained concepts and assign masses to pre-defined categories for uncertain classification situations. The adaptability of this approach allows the classification system to learn from experience and update its knowledge framework accordingly. The study's findings are illustrated by aauditing-related scenario where a robot aims to classify apples and oranges based on their colors.

A point process with clusters is generated by first choosing a parent, its neighbors, and a parent's child, all determined by uniform random variables, then using these points to form clusters by taking the convex hull of the parents or their neighbors, and finally applying a kernel to obtain the observable entities, which are random points that form clusters in a bounded area. The point density is set by the parameter lambda (related to the number of points per unit area), and the radius that defines a parent's neighborhood or a parent's child is set by the parameter alpha (related to the scale). The process is referred to as the "Stitching Process," and a point process that forms uniform and regular clusters is a specific instance of this concept known as the "Uniform and Regular Stitching Process." The algorithm for creating a point process that forms uniform and regular clusters involves a novel technique using periodic barycentric coordinates and its derivative, "stitching from a density," which can also be used to create other processes that form uniform and regular clusters. The created point processes have Poisson-like properties and are easier to visualize and analyze. They have characterizing conditions for the moments, and a parameterized model of a point process that forms uniform and regular clusters is also developed. These ideas have applications in fields like biology, psychology, sociology, and economics, and form the basis for a new class of point processes. The created point processes have Poisson-like properties and are easier to visualize and analyze.

In the context of the generalized uncertainty principle, modifications are identified in the transformations governing the Lorentz and Galilean boosts, and a maximum achievable velocity is demonstrated to emerge from the GUP itself.

We consider a multitasking allocation problem where an manager operates several units, 
one job at a time, under a precedence constraint that enables simultaneous processing of jobs. 
The manager's productivity varies according to which job it currently has and has previously completed.
We seek to maximize the total profit from all jobs through this process. Theoretically, we've established 
that when productivity functions aren't necessarily symmetrical, the optimal schedule will have a specific sequence (long-term schedule) 
even in cases of uneven job durations and profits. Additionally, we've identified a polynomial-time formula for determining an optimal long-term schedule 
and shown that such schedules will also yield the highest profits when the manager processes jobs in a sequential manner (short-term schedule). However, we've also found evidence that such short-term schedules may not always be optimal when productivity functions are symmetrical. 

Interestingly, we've found that both long-term and short-term schedules will perform equally well in a specific situation - when the manager's productivity at any given point 
depends only on the current job and not the previous one. This property enables us to simplify the problem and derive a polynomial-time algorithm for maximizing profits in this situation. The algorithm consists of two parts. The first part shows that under a specific condition, the optimal schedule will always have a sequential sequence. This paper investigates an isolated monopod capable of jumping on a deformable substrate. We simulated various scenarios to comprehend the relationship between ground yielding and the monopod's hopping ability. Utilizing a multi-body Lagrangian model, we simulated real-time dynamics and verified our findings against an existing model through force and position comparisons. Our goal was to determine if augmenting the monopod with prosthetic legs could enhance its jumping performance. By incorporating different types of footplates with degrees of freedom and modifying their shapes, we optimized the impact mechanism to achieve the highest takeoff velocity and distance within a specified time frame. Our simulations revealed that changing the foot configuration rather than leg length, assessed based on a stability criterion, could improve the monopod's jumping ability. Moreover, varying foot shapes led to distinct performance impacts; for instance, circular and paddle-shaped feet demonstrated distinct takeoff velocities. These findings imply that leg anatomy may adapt to changing environments through modifications in foot structure rather than leg length.

Given the scale and complexity involved in deploying updates to large numbers of mesh-networked devices, it is often difficult to assess the impact on individual devices and the network as a whole. We have conducted a comprehensive study of the dependence of IoT firmware update performance on numerous parameters, using real-world measurements from 10,000 IoT devices in a mesh network. We employ a recursive method to calculate the Fock space propagator for arbitrary potential landscapes and multiple particle counts. We extend the existing multi-particle algorithm for one-dimensional systems with finite repulsive interactions, based on the exact diagonalization of a partial Schrödinger equation. By analyzing the scaling of coefficients in a wave function expansion, we investigate the nature of multifractal spectra in both localized and delocalized regimes. In a system that exhibits a phase transition from localization, we discover a distinct shift in the scaling behavior of the leading coefficient, indicating a non-analytic correction with a fractal exponent. This finding provides insight into the interplay between different parts of a wave function during the phase transition and supports theories on multifractal critical properties. Moreover, we show that the phase transition is characterized by a specific percolation pattern in a fractal network, with a critical exponent of $\nu=0.58\pm0.15$ that agrees well with $\nu=0.58\pm0.17$, which is a value obtained through numerical simulations that consider only nearest-neighbor hoppings.

This study introduces a novel model of interactive search, where a seeker seeks a hidden object by querying a tellable source with a limited budget of questions. Previously established research focused on a single hidden object, while this research addresses the scenario of multiple hidden objects. A source has exclusive knowledge of all hidden objects, and the seeker aims to identify one or more hidden objects by asking the most informative questions possible. A newly established lower bound limit on question count is provided for this complex of multi-target interactive search, along with efficient algorithms achieving this maximum under specific conditions. When question counts are uneven, the best algorithms established previously cannot be applied, and thus new methods are presented to identify the hidden objects, along with an analysis of their performance.

By designing minimal quantum circuits with as few than 100 qubits, we have found universal instances that trigger incorrect classification by quantum classifiers, regardless of the quantum circuit's architecture or state. These minimal circuits can be created through a QNN generated by combining random quantum operations. Surprisingly, nearly all of the states in our universal instances correctly identify a given target state, U_0, while the remaining states, U_1, accurately mislabel it across most measurement outcomes. Furthermore, by examining field theory and quantum algorithms, we have found a universal family of perturbations, which can convert any quantum state into U_1, and we've verified this through testing it against various quantum classifiers. Additionally, we discovered that the quantum states in our universal instance family serve as a type of 'weak control' that can be used to devise new, efficient quantum circuits for state preparation. These results highlight the considerable challenge in developing quantum machines that accurately generalize across diverse quantum systems.

Radio transmission models play a vital role in evaluating the performance of future, densely deployed cellular networks. However, as radio signal patterns become increasingly complex due to enhanced security measures and fine-grained beam management, traditional models fall short. In light of these challenges, we utilize deep learning techniques to design advanced radio transmission models for multi-angle, multi-security encryption scenarios. By leveraging a large, generated dataset of signal patterns, we train a convolutional neural network to extract essential radio signal features from diverse wireless data. These extracted features are then combined with established statistical methods to develop a comprehensive radio transmission model capable of accounting for security and large-scale channel effects in highly complex networks. Additionally, we show that our model can effectively accommodate deployments of different beam management strategies, including 3D massive-MIMO and large-scale antenna systems.

A precise definition of time-based planning problems and their temporal nature is proposed, building on a framework established by Gelfagin et al. for action languages. This framework is enhanced with a formal description of time-based planning tasks, a definition of what it means to solve such tasks, and a proposed solution verification process. These formalizations provide a basis for comparing and evaluating planning solution verification approaches. To validate the semantics, a formal proof of the verification process is presented using the Interactive Theorem Prover (Coq), accompanied by an example use case illustrating the application of the planning solution verification approach for basic time-based planning tasks.

As expert systems dynamics models gain prominence in studies of energy system expansion, there's a growing need to assess and evaluate these models. This research aims to develop a framework for measuring a model's responsiveness, which is the ability to detect changes in optimization solutions resulting from variations in input parameters. Through a case study using Expert System Dynamics models, we employed paired t-tests to compare percentage changes in key variables and established thresholds to differentiate models with high, moderate, and low responsiveness. Our analysis of models used in 12 studies revealed that none operate at a high responsiveness level, with most falling into the moderate category. This finding suggests that even with advancements in models, there's still a significant gap to achieve high responsiveness, indicating a need for further improvements to ensure accurate representations of energy system dynamics.

We offer a unified proof of global well-conditionedness for various Vlasov-Poisson systems across multiple domains, thereby encompassing basic models, collisional versions, and generalized equations with improved outcomes in these scenarios.

Software maintenance developers face difficulty locating the relevant sections of code during renovation tasks, a challenge known as concept location. Conventional methods typically rely on developers' prior knowledge and experience to identify search keywords, but often struggle to find relevant code segments unless these keywords accurately represent the code's intentions. Unfortunately, developers' understanding of the code is often limited and specifying suitable keywords can be a daunting task.

Our proposed system, STRICT, aims to streamline this process by automatically identifying relevant search keywords based on developers' informal description of the code. By incorporating information retrieval techniques, STRICT determines the most effective keywords that provide the best understanding of the code's purpose, increasing the chances of finding the desired information. A relevant set of keywords is then used to perform a second search for the concept, with the option to adapt the results based on feedback or find alternative specifications if the initial search yields too many or no results.

Researchers have discovered a category of materials called "rheo-acoustic" gels that can be broken down by ultrasonic waves. This breakthrough allows them to shift gel formation and breakdown points, maintain gel structure for an extended time, and control gel stiffness. By using ultrasonic waves, the rigidity of these gels can be maximized. This control over rheological properties also enables the ultrasonic waves to manipulate gel flow characteristics, including their viscoelastic indices and coefficients of friction. Moreover, the effect of ultrasonic waves on rheological properties is significantly enhanced in gels with larger particles, while in gels with smaller particles, the influence mainly affects their flow characteristics. This novel finding could lead to innovative methods for maintaining solid structures in liquids and improving materials like adhesives, coatings, and paint by utilizing ultrasonic waves.

The Collatz Conjecture is a well-known algorithmic hypothesis originally formulated in 1937. Known also as the "3x+1 Problem," it is attributed to Otto Frisch and Stanley Milgram, yet the concept had been encountered earlier by mathematicians. This hypothesis posits a sequence of integers starting with N, where the following rules apply: if N is even, the next number in the sequence is N divided by two; if N is odd, the next number in the sequence is N multiplied by one plus the reciprocal of two (1 plus 1/2). What is attributed to Russian mathematician Alexander Y. Shaffer involves sequenced multiplications and divisions by three and one respectively, although some sources attribute this variation to German mathematician H. O. Peitgen and Michael Walser. Regardless of theoretics and variants, the hypothesis has yet to be proven or disproven in its original or modified forms.

Classifying STEM documents is crucial for processing, high-quality information retrieval, and research citation rates. Despite the importance of this task, current performance levels in both human assessment and artificial models are subpar. In this study, we introduce the ME Link task at STEMDF 2021, a benchmark that combines two challenging components: identifying relevant entities and linking them to accurate references. We provide insights from the task's outcomes and propose that MEL holds the key to enhancing STEM document classification. Moreover, in the context of the shared STEMDF 2021 task, we achieved top results in both the classification and MEL components, but our performance was hindered by the limited number of mathematical entities in the provided dataset. The accompanying code can be accessed via this GitHub link: https://github.com/mdzherdan/STEMDF2021_MEL/tree/main/ME_LINK.

We introduce a novel framework for addressing the fundamental stability concerns associated with two-sided matching markets, where participants' community-based settings influence their preference formations. Focusing on the stable matching with preferences framework, our research demonstrates that when agents can both receive and initiate requests, there will always be a consistent pattern of choice regardless of the size or randomness of the market, unlike matching with limited proposal capabilities. We investigate two crucial scenarios - one where agents are allowed to make multiple inquiries and another where they can only send one request at a time, both based on random and fixed decision-making approaches. In the first scenario, our findings show that for small markets, there will always be an optimal strategy that survives against any possible opponent move; however, the likelihood of achieving this goal decreases as the market grows larger. In the case of random decision-making, we discover that for markets with a very large number of participants but a fixed size, there will always be a consistent pattern of choice that maximizes the probability of success. In the second scenario, our research establishes that for two-sided markets, there are specific community-based settings that enable the creation of a consistent pattern of choice, whereas in markets with an odd number of participants, such consistency is only attainable in specific, limited scenarios.

Current evaluation metrics for summary quality have limitations, as they rely heavily on human judgment or prior knowledge of summary characteristics. Consequently, there's a pressing need for an automatic assessment metric. To address this need, a novel SummScore metric is introduced, leveraging a Cross-Encoder model to compare summaries. This approach differs from existing methods by enabling diverse types of summaries to be evaluated with minimal reliance on human judgment or pre-defined constraints. Moreover, SummScore has been validated through robust experiments, achieving superior performance in predicting human assessments, and exhibiting sensitivity to various types of summary modifications. Additionally, two secondary evaluation metrics are presented to gauge SummScore's reliability and provide insights into its performance. Extensive training and fine-tuning efforts reveal that SummScore can be fine-tuned from a shared BERT model, thereby requiring no special training or architecture design. Ultimately, SummScore demonstrates promising potential as a universal assessment metric for automatic summary evaluation.

The need to quickly recover a signal exists in a wide range of sensory and signal-processing applications across science and technology. While quantitive bounds on recovery speed have been established in various signal recovery scenarios, these bounds are known to not be the best possible in many cases. In fact, experiments have shown that in quadratic measurement settings, the signal can often be fully recovered in linear time rather than exponential time. This paper presents a general framework that achieves nearly-optimal results in a variety of signal recovery scenarios, including cases involving quadratic measurement settings, noisy conditions, and the need to recover individual components of a signal rather than the entire signal. Importantly, the framework yields a simple and efficient algorithm that works well in a wide range of real-world applications.

The development of autonomous vehicles relies heavily on perception systems that can accurately process LiDAR and camera data for object detection, tracking, and state estimation.  Currently available advanced architectures, such as Transformer models, can excel in LiDAR-based tasks but struggle with camera data. Conversely, camera-based architectures like Convolutional Neural Networks remain dominant but are less effective when working solely with LiDAR data.  The potential for significant improvements by fusing LiDAR and camera data has long been recognized, yet existing multi-modal fusion techniques have not adequately leveraged their combined capabilities.  In an effort to overcome these limitations, this research explores and validates a novel fusion strategy, and associated BEVFusion architecture, capable of leveraging LiDAR and camera data in unison to enhance perception systems.  The proposed method involves a simple camera-LiDAR fusion approach, such that both sensor data can be easily generalized and adapted to various applications.  Further validation and assessment of BEVFusion was conducted using the NANO-UD dataset, an open-source dataset for autonomous driving tasks, and the results demonstrate its simplicity and effectiveness in camera-LiDAR fusion, such that it is now available for further research and development on GitHub.

In 1934, Lesiuk developed a model for the critical radius of thermal equilibrium in low-temperature plasma, where the effects of viscosity in the vicinity of this radius bring about damping of turbulent disturbances in the plasma. Conversely, this study commences by calculating the rotation velocity of a neutral gas at the point where its real density is equal to the surrounding fluid's density, thereby establishing the neutral gas's thermal equilibrium radius. Subsequently, a model for the velocity at the dissipation range of turbulent fluctuations in the gas is then derived by considering the effects of angular momentum. Consequently, damping mechanisms in the gas are examined and it is noted that, unlike plasma, the velocity at the equilibrium radius is distinct from zero. Moreover, the velocity at the equilibrium radius is directly proportional to the angular velocity of the surrounding fluid. Ultimately, the consequences of these findings on momentum transfer between the gas and the surrounding fluid are explored and investigated.

The behavior of light scattered within a highly scattering medium is studied when it encounters intense laser power, this interaction causing the medium's temperature to rise. A straightforward mathematical framework is developed to model this scenario and accurately predict heat distribution and resulting optical effects, this prediction aligning with measured data. A comprehensive understanding of the behavior of scattering centers under these conditions is crucial for interpreting laser interaction with highly scattering media and achieving controlled phase shift for wavefront engineering. Our analysis considers the laser's power distribution as it travels through the medium, taking into account the reduction in scattering coefficient and nonlinear absorption. We determine that the apparent shift of diffraction patterns in time is a consequence of varying phase shift in different parts of the medium, not a traditional diffraction pattern caused by propagating waves. Our analysis also reveals that the time it takes to induce diffraction patterns in such media is determined by relaxation time and the time it takes for heat to dissipate, which is set by the laser-induced thermal relaxation time and diffusion time.

Conversational AI experiences a transformative force in its nature, born from interactions that combine human sentiment with technological responsiveness. Design discussions, a prime example of this, concretize product development through collaborative design decisions. Current designs often emerge from in-person design reviews where participants review and comment on designs using free-form natural language. AI can automate design discussion extraction (DDE) to streamline design decision-making, but its conclusions are prone to change when input variations result in disparate outcomes. This paper introduces Variation Stability for Conclusions (VarStabCon), a metric to quantify AI model conclusion stability by integrating two existing concepts, Variational Information Gain (VIG) and Constrained Noisy Channel (CNC). We use VarStabCon to assess the performance of two pre-existing NLD models and a reinforced comparative analysis of these models to guide future research directions in the field.

To address the rising needs for efficient analytics systems in today's Big Data environments, this work presents a holistic solution by developing a holistic processing system that seamlessly integrates with existing big data analytics frameworks. The proposed system, named H-STREAM, leverages temporary, high-performance streams to enhance data processing capabilities, consisting of two complementary components: a stream processing language for designing analytics pipelines, and a system driver that integrates with Apache Flink to execute these pipelines. To evaluate its performance and versatility, H-STREAM is further integrated with Apache Impala, yielding high-level queries that blend stream and batch processing. The results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this combination, offering flexible analytics capabilities that are well-supported by multiple evidence.

In scenarios involving the single production of top and bottom companions, the dominant processes typically involve electroweak gauge bosons mediating interactions close to resonant conditions. The focus of this analysis will be on non-resonant production via the subsequent decay of vector bosons, specifically transverse vector bosons producing top and vector boson scattering. These production mechanisms are predominantly characterized by tree-level amplitudes. The study compares predicted production rates with similar resonant production mechanisms within two distinct models: the singlet and doublet next-to-minimal supersymmetric models, utilizing the established benchmarks from EP lifetimes. The production rate for both models is found to be relatively low, ranging from 0.1 to 0.3%, regardless of their resonant contributions. The production of top companions near the 350 GeV mass threshold of M2 quarks is notable, accounting for 0.05% of total top companion production. The predicted production rate of doublet MINIMAL SUPERSYMMETRIC THEORY is observed to be marginally higher, ranging from 0.2 to 0.5%. The study's findings can serve as a useful reference point for the study of single heavy boson production in searches for new physics at the Large Hadron Collider.

SPARQL is a standard query language used for operating on graph databases and knowledge bases by merging various ontologies into a single unit, which is incorporated into databases using a single global graph. When processing SPARQL queries, neural machine translation models need to access and utilize knowledge base elements, which poses difficulties due to the diverse format and structure of these components. Motivated by the success of copy mechanisms in machine translation, this paper introduces a copy system for SPARQL-based machine translation. It consists of a question-aware knowledge base selector, which determines which knowledge base elements to access, and a copy transformer, which replicates specific elements as needed. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed copy system significantly outperforms conventional methods, with the question-aware selector and copy transformer combining to surpass existing approaches, including an enhanced attention-based baseline.

This work introduces a novel method for evaluating a researcher's impact based on their engagement with specific conferences and workshops. By replacing traditional citation metrics with a more targeted approach that focuses on a particular context, we aim to provide a more precise and useful measure of a researcher's impact. Unlike conventional methods that rely on comprehensive publication tracking, our approach leverages existing data and requires minimal additional information for accurate results. The proposal is straightforward and efficient to implement, and it relies on existing data sources that are readily accessible. The benefits and potential applications of this new metric are extensively discussed, and they include its potential to incentivize desirable behavior, shed new light on a researcher's impact, and offer a more nuanced understanding of their achievements.

As a physical system's characteristics change over time, its model, whether neural network or traditional, must adapt to remain accurate. Traditionally, validating neural network models has been complex and laborious, but research has been conducted to address these challenges. This work builds on previous studies by investigating the use of neural networks for model validation in control applications. Initially, we verify that neural networks can effectively validate systems with complex dynamics. Next, we demonstrate the ability of neural network validation models to replicate the outcomes of systematic, structured testing in line with industry standards in automotive. Furthermore, we explore the applicability of neural network validation in control systems, particularly in the context of automotive safety protocols such as the AUTOSAR standard, which our research shows can effectively coexist with other models in this environment.

Scientific visualization of hierarchical data structures, such as network graphs and clustering results, necessitate clear visualization to avoid visual clutter and facilitate understanding of complex relationships. Although numerous approaches have been implemented to deal with visual complexities, the issue remains that these methods can lead to confusing visual representations due to conflicting visual hierarchies. To address this limitation, our study focuses on creating an advanced automated hierarchical grouping algorithm that can handle multi-level grouping arrangements, eliminating edges between related nodes, and thus prevent visual confusion. To enable functorial processing, we developed methods to address challenges related to grouping sizes, cuts, and overlaps. Additionally, our algorithm was enhanced with central node positioning, and global visualization techniques were utilized to facilitate understanding of complex structures. Furthermore, this method was tested using synthetic and real-world data sets, and the results were evaluated to assess its effectiveness and versatility in visualizing diverse types of hierarchical data structures.

The recovery of damaged visual signals, such as video repair and image restoration, is crucial for both practical purposes and fundamental research due to their practical and fundamental interest. To tackle this problem, a novel method is proposed that leverages patch-tracking-based temporal modeling to explore the complementary information for signal recovery. By combining the concepts of tensor completion and the CRT algorithm, an efficient and scalable approach is developed to tackle the challenge of signal recovery. The method can handle the challenge of expanding tensor structures and provides a unified framework for preserving the inherent structural information in the signal. Furthermore, a streaming implementation is developed to make the method suitable for real-time applications. The proposed method is evaluated using various benchmarks, and its effectiveness and efficiency are demonstrated through a combination of simulated and practical experiments.
It is demonstrated that for each spherical root lattice with a Weyl group of type $F_4$, its Nichols algebra cannot be generated by a single element.

Although the concept of wave turbulence has been utilized to model the behavior of waves in several fields, such as oceanography and hydrodynamics, it has primarily been based on theoretical predictions rather than empirical evidence. Previous studies simulating wave turbulence have focused on confirming the existence of these predictions, including the development of a kinetic energy spectrum with a specific power law. This study verifies that numerical simulations of turbulent wave turbulence exhibit the expected kinetic energy spectrum with a Zakharov-Kolmogorov frequency spectrum.

A recent study demonstrated the effectiveness of Iterative Graph Normalization (IGN) in effectively discovering near-maximal weight independent sets in diverse graphs; this method is also known by its acronym IGN. In this research, we first establish that IGN's unique and complex form can be broken down into its component parts using a property from the field of Non-Expansive Finders. Our findings are then applied to better understand IGN's characteristics and to map its underlying process more accurately. Secondly, by combining a recent discovery about IGN with our new theoretical insights, we expand the understanding of near-maximal weight independent sets in specific types of graphs, such as (a) establishing a lower bound for the size of maximal weight independent sets in $P_6$-free graphs, and (b) providing an exact estimate for the maximum possible independence in $C_4$-free graphs.

This research investigates how modulation of a voltage-driven current through a graphene monolayer impacts its thermodynamic properties. Our study discovered that the presence of a finite height energy sub-bucket influences the analysis of entropy and internal energy under various scenarios. The entropy display reveals a symmetrical pattern in two opposing directions of a quadratic shape between phases. The calculation of entropy shows that the entropy value at zero temperature is not necessarily zero. The influence of external modulation on internal energy causes a shift in the minimum internal energy from a finite energy value to zero as thermal fluctuations decrease. The behavior of external modulation on specific heat capacity exhibits characteristics of a power law with a negative exponent at two extreme temperature limits. Our findings on the behavior of external modulation on heat capacity may guide researchers working with electronically controlled transport in graphene monolayers in their experiments.

Researchers conducted a detailed examination of the low-frequency radio emissions from the binary system CR Dra, composed of a young dwarf star and its companion, using data collected over 25 years from the Low Frequency Array. The identification of persistent, low-intensity radio emissions at the 150 MHz frequency allowed scientists to monitor the emissions over the course of 100 days without interruption. Radio emissions from the binary system were found to be polarized in approximately 100% of cases and displayed high variability. The data were found to be consistent with the effects of a compact thermal source, situated close to the star's core and triggered by the dynamics of the star's magnetic field. The frequency of radio emissions decreased as the star's activity levels changed. Modeling the observed emissions as a result of an electron-cyclotron maser suggested that the energies of the accelerated electrons were relatively low, between a few hundred to a few thousand electronvolts. The discovery of high-polarized emissions at a relatively low frequency, combined with the observed dependence of radio emissions on the star's rotational period, provides substantial evidence for the existence of a compact thermal source associated with the star's magnetic field loops.

Our cutting-model visualizer presents 3D avatars in a breakable format, enabling users to gain insight into the combined effect of model and animation components. This is achieved by treating the avatar as a combination of interconnecting parts and displaying the resulting mesh in a piecewise manner. The strength of the pieces can be adjusted using a weighted average, and piece boundaries are naturally maintained. As a result, users receive transparent and understandable information about the challenges associated with using 3D avatars, and the tool facilitates the identification of areas that need improvement for targeted optimization efforts.

Human understanding of visual information is remarkable despite the visual input's imperfections. However, current AI systems operate under an assumption of precise input, mirroring early photography practices where errors were often corrected. To assess whether distinct forms of degradations have a greater impact on human and AI visual capabilities, we have developed severe image transformations in three distinct areas - facial distortion, image degradation, and visual obstructions. Through a large-scale study involving over 200 participants, we have found that humans with a visual aid can efficiently recognize images degraded in any of these methods, whereas AIs still grapple with these degradations. This research provides evidence on how much different forms of image degradations affect human and AI visual capabilities, ultimately paving the way for more accurate image classification.

The relationship between the Askey-Wilson matrix and an extended version of Chern-Simons theory based on the quantum group U_q(su_2) has been established in terms of a gauge fixed path integral formulation. This formulation reveals that the elements of the Askey-Wilson matrix correspond to observables in the theory, and we propose that the matrix itself represents a generalised electric-magnetic transformation matrix for this model. Additionally, we outline a procedure for computing Wilson loop observables, and as evidence of its utility, we examine a specific case where the polygon has three sides, and show that the resulting invariant is linked to a quadratic equation, the solutions of which form a two-parameter family of rational functions. This property aligns with the fundamental principle of the q-deformed E7(Ad) quantum integrable system as described by Ding, Frenkel and Huang.

A computational study of a quantum antiferromagnet with a unique arrangement of triangular groups, weakly connected in a two-dimensional lattice, shows how the distance between the weak bonds affects the material's physical properties. By using a numerical method called cluster quantum Monte Carlo, we investigated the relationship between the distance and specific characteristics, such as the ability of spins to align and the amount of magnetic disorder. For large and intermediate distances between the weak bonds, the system behaves in a certain way, whereas for small distances, another phenomenon occurs; we have performed the method for a broad range of distances and calculated the importance factor, which helps to determine if the material exhibits degenerate energy levels. For a model without any magnetic impurities, we found that the material does not exhibit degenerate energy levels for certain arrangements, whereas for a model with magnetic impurities, we have identified areas with degenerate energy levels within the material's phase diagram.

Pre-trained language models, exemplified by GPT-3, have extended learning capabilities across various tasks. Nonetheless, performing zero-shot learning with them often hinges on finding the right set of task prompts. While prompts are typically devised by humans, incorporating prompt learning via prompt reinforcement learning could yield more adaptative and efficient prompts. This paper introduces a different approach, MetaAdapt, which treats prompt creation as a meta-learning problem. It involves aggregating learning material from multiple datasets and employing prompt learning as a process of adapting these assembled prompts. In contrast to other methods, MetaAdapt is characterized by its scalability, performance, versatility, and a broad applicability that encompasses natural language inference, program execution, and reasoning tasks. Moreover, it is underpinned by theoretical insights regarding the assembly of prompts and its linear learning capabilities. Experiments with the Natural Eight dataset family, the Generalized Adversarial Network, the ALFA dataset, the Physiko dataset, the CoQA dataset, and the QuAC dataset demonstrate the substantial improvement yielded by MetaAdapt in automated prompt creation. Furthermore, it is cross-tested using the FewShot dataset family, the SciFact dataset, the M3 dataset family, the SciTLDR, the PhysiNet, the NLM's Clinical QA dataset, the NLM's COVID-19 QA dataset, the NLM's Intubation Dataset, the NLM's Admissions Dataset, the NLM's Emergencies Dataset, the NLM's Emerg

In the context of non-minimal supersymmetric models with $Z_3$ symmetry, our analysis focuses on how these models lead to a first-order electroweak phase transition, a necessary occurrence for the cosmological theory of electroweak baryogenesis to be valid. We build on previous research by introducing an explicit mechanism to ensure the $Z_3$ symmetry is observed, an improvement over existing studies in the field. Our investigation reveals that, under certain numerical conditions, this mechanism does prevent the $Z_3$ symmetry from being broken even at the level of the Lagrangian. The outcome of our research indicates that, under the assumption of a second-generation NMSSM with an expanded field, along with an explicit $Z_3$ symmetry, it is possible for a significant number of these supersymmetric particles to be within the reach of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Specifically, our research implies that these supersymmetric particles could very likely be detectable via an examination of the LHC's mass range of 550-1100 GeV. Moreover, our research suggests that these supersymmetric particles will likely be investigated extensively before the LHC, through a thorough examination of the cross-section and sensitivity data from the CMS and ATLAS experiments. We introduce a new approach for evaluating the effectiveness of an efficient algorithm that identifies the rotation curves of distant galaxies through molecular and atomic line observations. The algorithm, which is suitable for machine learning inputs, is designed to automatically identify robust redshifts in surveys such as the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array via its High-z Sudoku dataset. The algorithm's first version demonstrates robust performance in a range of 50 galaxies, demonstrating an 82% success rate for classical and 77% for machine learning inputs, in a fully automated system for surveys such as ATACAMA Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array via its High-z Sudoku dataset.
