The main conservation laws of a physical system are often determined by a free flow and its boundaries, with a specific example being the conservation of momentum - namely the wall forces and stress - in a fluid flow. These wall forces and stress are inherently linked to a flow's geometry and are governed by a mathematical framework that can be formalized as a first-order PDE on the boundary of the flow. This framework can be applied to both Neumann and Dirichlet boundary conditions. This paper will demonstrate that this formulation can be applied to the 2D compressible Navier-Stokes equations to recover well-known conservation laws. It will also use this framework to derive new conservation laws for general flows with arbitrary initial and boundary conditions, and with the assumption of general stress tensors that take into account the effects of superelasticity and surface tension. This approach will be based on a key observation about the relationship between a flow's geometry and its tangential direction at the boundary of the flow. It will also be demonstrated that the same technique can be applied to the Euler equations, as well as to both linear and nonlinear elasticity equations.

Accurately predicting Non-Performing Loans can help banks avoid potential losses by providing essential information for credit decisions, thereby enabling lenders to identify clients with a higher risk of default at an earlier stage. This research aims to compare the performance of several machine learning models for NPL prediction and explore the significance of specific features for decision-making in the banking sector. Our analysis was conducted using a dataset from an Indian commercial bank containing demographic and credit history information for clients. By exercising domain knowledge and incorporating data preprocessing strategies, we improved model accuracy. Our comparison of classification models, such as Random Forest, XGB, and SVM, against Deep Neural Networks, revealed that XGB achieved the best balance between precision and recall among the baseline models, with a precision of 0.8131 and recall of 0.8366. A more complex DNN model was trained to compare the effectiveness of simpler and more advanced approaches. The XGB model's superior performance may be due to its lower hyperparameter density and adaptability. Understanding the decision-making process of the XGB model helped us pin down the most influential features for NPL prediction, which can inform banks on the critical variables to consider when assessing loan applicants.

It is established that the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck trails, as specified in Theorem 4.4, are entirely composed of the complete homogeneous and elementary symmetric functions. Furthermore, the chromatic symmetric functions of trails in regions bounded by two horizontal lines, as described in Theorem 3.6, can also be expressed as a combination of these functions. These results are achieved through the application of q-rook theory, particularly by relating the symmetric functions of these Dyck trails to the q-rook polynomials of Ferrers doubles and anti-Ferrers doubles. The found connections hint at further advancements in symmetric function theory related to Dyck paths and L-labelings.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are a widely used technique for image recognition tasks. The Conv layer, defining the network's receptive field and extracting fundamental visual features, is crucial in CNNs. Traditional full-convolutional layers, however, only consider pixel relationships in a limited area and overlook global features. This restricts their ability to extract high-level global features from images. We address this limitation by introducing a new type of Conv layer - direction CNN - which incorporates orientation features to enhance visual recognition. Our experimental findings demonstrate that this new layer effectively improves the accuracy of standard CNNs. The source code for this research is available at https://github.com/Gradual-Student/D-CNN.

Using the tools of relative trace formulas, we investigate linear periods on groups of Lie type with a curved modification. This encompasses cases where the reductive group $G$ over an local field has a non-trivial center. Notably, this includes situations with groups like ${}^3D_4(v)$ and ${}^3A_1(v) \times Sp_{2n}(v)$. The findings show that the curved variants of these periods exist and are non-zero. Moreover, the research equates certain curved periods with the relative orbital integrals of certain curved functions on the double coset $I_{G(S)}(\sqrt{|G|}_S) \backslash G(S)$. Finally, by analyzing the curved transfer and factorization, we derive comparisons of periods on groups of residual dimension one and on arbitrary reductive groups. This generalizes the comparability of periods investigated by Qin-Shao-Wang.

We address the issue of significant flavor obstruction in the context of the QCD factorization formula for the top quark mass, and explore its connection with the $\hat r_{SF}$ parameter introduced in arXiv:2106.11617. By employing next-to-next-to-leading-order factorization and soft function evolution, we obtain an interplay between the light quark masses and the parameters governing the perturbative series. This allows us to circumvent the indeterminacy associated with $\hat r_{SF}$ in favor of a system of two undetermined constants. These constants are linked to specific Wilson coefficient renormalization constants and the pole masses of the light quarks. This framework can be further refined using the MS renormalization scheme, leading to a precise perturbative expansion for the top quark mass, and reducing the influence of light quark masses in the process.

Consider a graph $G$ and a subset $X$ of its vertices $V(G)$. A coloring of the graph's edges with respect to the vertex subset $X$ is defined as an assignment of colors to the edges incident with the vertices in $X$, provided the colors of the vertices do not determine this assignment. More specifically, for an edge $e = (x, y)$ in $G$, let $x \in X$ and $y \not\in X$. An edge $e'$ in $G$ is defined as an "extension" of $e$ if it connects a vertex in $X$ to a vertex not in $G$. An $e'$ extension of $e$ is said to have the same color as $e$ when assigned with a color with respect to the vertex subset $X$. A specific edge $e$ in $G$ is considered to match an extension $e'$ if both $e$ and the corresponding $e'$ have the same endpoints in $G$. For the vertex subset $X$ of a graph $G$, an edge subset ${\mathcal E}^* \subset G$ is defined to have the property that each edge in $G$ either matches to another in ${\mathcal E}^*$. A graph $G$ is said to have the property ${\mathcal F}(G,X,{\mathcal E}^*)$ with respect to a vertex subset $X

We present a hypercontractive inequality for functions within the weighted Berman space over a measure space equipped with a non-negative, countable measure. This hypercontractive inequality can be applied to establish the boundedness of certain operator $T_{\phi}$ associated with a non-decreasing function $\phi$, which is used in characterizing spaces with the bounded mean oscillation property across all possible subspaces of the weighted Berman space. Furthermore, our findings have practical implications in the context of quaternionic Taylor series expansions.

Currently, automated detection of COVID-19 from Computed Tomography (CT) scans largely relies on region-of-interest (ROI) analysis, which can be invasive and leads to biased results when using machine learning models. In this study, we present a novel approach using a two-stage neural network to identify COVID-19 directly from whole-chest scans, by employing a learning framework that is both supervised and transfer, to improve the accuracy and efficiency of pulmonary observations in chest radiographs and CT scans. We utilized 1855 pairs of chest CT scans and demographic information from patients at Mount Sinai Hospital in New York City to train a model that can accurately detect COVID-19 from low-dose scans and compare it to the current standard of care, which mostly relies on slice-by-slice manual analysis due to the low-dose quality leading to lower diagnostic accuracy. We achieved a high 84.4% COVID-19 detection accuracy on a set of 713 unseen patients from the same hospital, outperforming the current network of radiologists who reported an average accuracy of 81% on a matched set of 185 patients. This study showcases the capability of a two-stage capsule network to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of infectious disease detection, especially when using low-quality scans, providing valuable insights for clinical settings from the world's hardest-hit hospitals.

In the past ten years, there has been a significant surge in technological advancements, leading to an explosion of new small satellites launched into space, referring to them as "CubeSats." These satellites have presented both opportunities and challenges for the space industry, altering how launch services approach and provide their services. This paper examines the space industry's business model in relation to space utilization in low-earth orbit (LEO) and how it changes with the rising number of small satellites. It also evaluates the impact of new requirements from launch service providers and how these changes reflect the shift in the business model to better accommodate the new environment. Furthermore, the paper looks into emerging opportunities for small satellites and space waste in LEO during the next five years.

To tackle the challenge of mesh coarsening, where the mesh size needs to be reduced while maintaining high-quality results for complex CAD models with intricate geometries, researchers turned to topologically ideal meshes with limited elements. These ideal meshes possess desirable characteristics, such as organized node arrangements and robustness to geometric changes, making them suitable for numerous tasks. However, generating such meshes requires complex algorithms to handle high-dimensional variable spaces and complex constraints. To address this issue, a new method is presented that employs integer linear programming to produce high-order quadrilateral meshes under strict coherence conditions. By utilizing the mesh's topological organization, this approach simplifies the variable space and makes mesh coarsening more scalable, allowing it to handle large meshes with up to 100,000 elements on 16 GPU cores within a reasonable time frame. Furthermore, the method is particularly useful for applications that rely on linear solver performance, such as finite element methods, as it reduces the solution time by limiting the number of variables and constraints, often by two orders of magnitude.

The objective of this research was to develop mathematical expressions for the statistical characteristics of the sample correlation coefficient $\rho_j$ across $m$ randomly selected subsets $I_j$ of size $s$ from a set of $n$ data points. These expressions, known as moment functions, provide theoretical support for existing findings and can be utilized in future studies to obtain asymptotic distributions and other statistical characteristics. Our results cover scenarios with and without replacement, and we also generalize existing results on probability distributions.

We detail the scattering matrix method that encompasses all types of perturbative field theories. By applying this approach, we show how effective actions are derived from scattering matrices in two ways: via conformal anomalies in trees and through a perturbative formula for the one-loop effective action. Furthermore, we demonstrate that higher order loops can be calculated by systematically extending this formula, thereby allowing us to evaluate scattering amplitudes in theories with massless particles in general dimension. Several examples, including gauge theory and general relativity, illustrate the effectiveness of this framework for perturbative field theories.

We investigate the two- or three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations defined within a bounded region. The velocity and pressure are initially given as functions of space $v_0, w_0$ and a force is represented by $f_0$. This study specifically examines the case where the initial velocity has low regularity, specifically being in $v_0, w_0$ with $q$ close to 2 from below. In that scenario, controlling the solution by adding a small feedback term is generally not feasible. To address this, a small feedback term that takes into account all spatial derivatives of the velocity is added, specifically up to degree $k$. The term is proportional to $(v, w)_{k}$. This approach allows us to address the question whether adding such a small feedback term can stabilize the solution. The case where $k=0$ corresponds to the classical $L^2$-norm, which is known to be effective. However, for $k>0$, adding these higher degree terms may actually be counterproductive due to the decay rates of the relevant eigenvalues. Nonetheless, for $k=1$, a combination of these terms is shown to be effective. The main result of this study is a nearly sharp degree $k$-regularity result for the solutions.

The LitMind Lexicon is a practical reference tool for linguistic research purposes.
It can be accessed online at http://litmind.iis.sinica.edu.tw.
The lexicon contains definitions, part-of-speech information, example sentences, 
antonym correlations, synonym correlations, readability levels, and CVC morpheme information.
In addition to these features, the lexicon also offers search functionality using 
various criteria, such as word beginnings, approximate spellings, and part-of-speech categories.
The data in the lexicon is derived from the 2018 Corpus of Contemporary Chinese released 
by the Chinese Information Processing Society: CC corpus: 4.71 billion characters, 53 million sentences, 
and the 2019 Taiwan Literature Corpus: 6.26 billion characters, 350 million sentences.
Examples of newly-added words in the LLL are also presented. The LLL has also been used 
in various NLP systems for n-gram NLP model pre-training and word embedding learning.
Furthermore, the LLL has been applied to query suggestion and text normalization.

When a recommender system provides an explanation, it's crucial that it's consistent and accurate. A valid explanation should not only make sense but also align with the decision-making process. Since decision-making mechanisms in recommendation systems are often difficult to interpret, explanations that incorporate random elements may not enhance user trust. In this research, we introduce the concept of adherence, a new metric to evaluate the validity of explanatory techniques. By applying this metric, we analyze the efficacy of four existing explanation methods in enhancing trust, focusing specifically on KNN-based and LIME-based approaches to recommender systems. Surprisingly, our study indicates that explanations generated by LIME may undermine confidence in rare or unconventional recommendations. Consequently, we propose a new method, Consistent LIME, to improve the fidelity of LIME-based explanations through data-driven approaches. Experimental outcomes confirm that our proposed method adheres to the definition of a valid explanation and can boost user trust in atypical suggestions.

Theoretical investigation was conducted on the energy-level modifications within InAs quantum wells that are exposed to atmospheric conditions and surrounded by passivating oxide and germanium layers. The results indicate that the energy positioning of the confined states is significantly influenced by the interaction with the exterior environments. To maintain a superconducting state in the quantum well, characterized by a single confined state, an optimal passivation thickness of approximately 3.1 nm of germanium is required when it is deposited on the valence band maximum. Conversely, a thicker germanium deposition of approximately 3.4 nm is needed when it is deposited on the conduction band minimum, both cases being near the surface of the InAs layer. Further investigation into the influence of computational grid fineness and the importance of considering multiple environments on the positioning of the confined states is also discussed.

We show that local inspections, a crucial function in many learning applications such as classification and clustering, can be crucial in robust learning. By allowing the inspector to gather information-specific insights, we find that robustness can be significantly improved even with limited insight availability. In contrast to the traditional classification setting, we find that local inspections are particularly beneficial for clustering tasks. Moreover, we create a realistic scenario in which robust learning with local inspections significantly outperforms adversarial learning and standard identification.

Our previous research significantly sped up Sinkhorn iteration by taking advantage of a kernel matrix's inherent properties, transforming its $O(N^2)$ complexity to $O(N)$ time. This paper delves deeper into kernel matrix characteristics by defining and applying two key concepts, Lower Collinear Triangular Matrix and Upper Collinear Triangular Matrix. These concepts lead to the development of two algorithms that can compute kernel matrix columns or rows in $O(N)$ time. Based on this breakthrough, a new algorithm is proposed that can calculate the Sinkhorn iteration with an optimal transport cost in $O(KN)$ time, making it the first to achieve subquadratic complexity. This breakthrough is attributed to the $O(N)$ time complexity of inverting a lower/upper collinear triangular matrix with an $N \times N$ kernel matrix. This new algorithm is suitable for large-scale optimal transport problems and has been successfully tested on 256 and 512 GPU, surpassing existing solutions.

The young stellar object AU Microscopii is studied using James Webb Space Telescope's imaging data in the ultraviolet wavelength. New data from the optical filter at 1234 cm-1 show properties consistent with other mid-infrared data, indicating a predominantly passive, weakly retroreflected disk in dormancy. However, an unusual 1234 cm-1 feature, found in the Frost et al catalogue, is not associated with disk passive materials or ice substructures. 

Highly correlated far-UV and near-UV flux variations during flare events show that both star photons and wind collisions provide significant UV emission. This correlation holds for both main star and circumstellar medium UV emissions, but only the star's UV emission dominates bright flares. 

Comparing observed ultraviolet radiation to exoplanet habitability indices shows that AU Mic's easterly wind has key characteristics similar to those proposed for habitability, but its northwestern wind has opposite properties. 

Data on AU Mic b and c analogs reveal a 710 K rock planet type, with surface features like volcanoes, crust fractures, and carbon dioxide ice. 

Future EUV space telescopes can detect planeteres and the AU Mic exoplanet b and c are near habitability thresholds.

We've developed an innovative method to determine a charged particle's experience of drag as it loses energy due to the absorption by a material medium. Our approach is based on an iterative method that incorporates calculations of the electromagnetic current and pressure across thin layers of the medium. For particles with constant net charge and a non-fractional electric dipole moment, our results reveal that the drag experience by such particles is akin to those with pure magnetic fields. Specifically, the drag's angle and magnitude are independent of the dipole moment and the medium's properties, solely dependent on the particle's charge. Furthermore, we discover that the drag experience by polarized charged particles is diminished by a factor equivalent to the Einstein-Lorentz mass correction for unmagnetized dipoles. Our findings also encompass the peculiar case where the electromagnetic field is self-generated by the charged particle. We demonstrate that the principles applied to resistive medium drag are equally applicable to superconducting dipoles, even at the speed of light.

For unevenly distributed classification data, traditional nearest neighbor classification approaches are vulnerable to the underprediction of the minority class, resulting in lower accuracy and more biased forecasts. This issue is especially critical in the underrepresented minority class, which necessitates more precise prediction for effective initial assessments and subsequent actions in classification applications. To tackle this challenge, we have developed a novel method based on the underlying mechanics of nearest neighbor classification and the central limit theorem. This approach utilizes the combination of normally distributed approximations of the majority and minority classes to generate a decision boundary, resulting in a classification rule. Unlike other methods for handling unbalanced data, our approach does not involve weighting, resampling, or other forms of data manipulation, nor does it incorporate a kernel. Notably, it retains the data-driven, automatic decision making and transparency that are characteristic of the original nearest neighbor classification. Furthermore, it offers asymptotic consistency and adaptive behavior, making it a powerful tool capable of handling a range of complex classification scenarios. To formally validate the proposed method, we have established mathematical results, while numerical experiments have been conducted using various real-world and synthetic datasets to compare its performance with other relevant classification algorithms.

We derived the most luminous Quasar Luminosity Function (QSLF) in the redshift range of 4.0 to 5.5 using data from the most comprehensive dataset released by the SkyMapper telescope: 375 ultra-bright Quasars, 271 of which were new discoveries, primarily from a thorough examination of the Southern Quasar Survey. This extensive data, offering 78 magnitude variations, was analyzed in conjunction with the multi-color data of 2032 Quasars between z=4.0 to 5.5 and z=4.0 to 6.0 to create a comprehensive magnitude range of 360-460, allowing us to accurately predict the QSLF with a magnitude range of 450-460. Our analysis revealed that the QSLF peak occurred at a magnitude range of 450-460 for z=4.0 to 5.5 while comparing with the data of z=4.0 to 6.0, also, it showed that the QSLF slope changed at a magnitude of 460 when comparing with the data of z=4.0 to 5.5 and z=4.0 to 6.0, however, our analysis didn't show such variation with a magnitude range of 460 for z=5.0. Our analysis with all the data showed that there were 7 Quasars with a magnitude of 460 while none were found with a magnitude of 470

We have discovered that the interaction between a quantum dot and a superconducting island can be sensed by measuring changes in capacitance caused by gates. This interaction leads to either a quantum dot single-cooperative tunneling event or a dual-cooperative multi-cooperative tunneling event, both of which are initially disabled by the s-wave pairing in the superconducting island. However, if the quantum dot has a spin-degenerate state, a magnetic impurity can form between them, enabled by a finite exchange coupling that overcomes the barrier to tunneling. This enabled exchange coupling is then detected as a visible capacitance increase in the event branch that was previously hidden. Moreover, our results reveal that the induced exchange coupling can be modified by applying an additional gate, effectively changing the band structure and thus the height of the barrier to tunneling. This enables control of the single-cooperative tunneling event that was previously not accessible and reveals the single-cooperative tunneling event to be highly sensitive to local states within the band.

Our research focuses on the contraction behaviour of entropic discontinuities in systems of conservation laws, with a particular interest in their relationship with the standardised norms defined by the Invariant Manifold Theory and the Lax-Friedrichs and Lax-Hopf schemes. We aim to understand how these norms contract under various iterations of the Lax-Friedrichs and Lax-Hopf difference operators and explore their potential use in designing efficient algorithms for numerical simulations.

There has been a growing interest in generating novel views of a given scene for single RGB images due to their potential in real-world applications, including augmented reality and editing. Conventional methods typically employ learning-based techniques, but these can produce unrealistic results or lack the ability to consistently generate views of a scene from a different perspective. We present a new approach called DiffDreamer, a conditional diffusion model that can realistically imagine and accurately represent novel views of a given scene from a given perspective. Our model is unique as it can consistently and precisely generate new views from different angles. We demonstrate the efficacy of our model through comparative studies on datasets containing cars, chairs, and tables, showing significant improvements in quality and realism of novel views generated compared to existing approaches.

We've developed a unique, data-driven approach that uses optimization to model and analyze complex systems, which are represented as graphs. Our method relies on a historical dataset to identify the underlying network structure, and it uses this information to create a predictive model for forecasting future outcomes. This framework has been successfully tested using simulated epidemic data, and the results show that it outperforms other existing methods in accuracy. Additionally, it outperforms other existing methods in accuracy and outperforms previous models in terms of accuracy, speed, and ability to handle unknown parameters. Furthermore, it is adaptable to a wide variety of issues. For instance, it is adaptable to a wide variety of scenarios. For demonstration purposes, we have also shown its ability to forecast, optimize, and control epidemiological processes. For demonstration purposes, we have also shown its ability to forecast, optimize, and control processes in real-time.

The dynamics of a thin liquid layer on a fiber influenced by gravity are examined, particularly when subject to perturbations. Consideration is given to scenarios where the liquid layer is attached to the fiber with a finite coefficient of static friction. Analytical conclusions about the onset of instability in such systems, specifically the Rayleigh-Plateau instability, are drawn when the perturbation frequency is in the range of a characteristic fiber movement frequency. This analysis shows that a combination of gravitational force and friction causes the liquid layer to break apart more quickly compared to systems where the perturbation frequency is much higher or lower. Numerical simulations have demonstrated that these analytical conclusions accurately represent the observed system behavior.

We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for the Hunter-Saxton equation, focusing on $h$-measures and their relationship with Lipschitz perturbations. Our work establishes that certain non-trivial solutions exhibit temporal $h$-stability, provides conditions under which this property can be applied, and differentiates between absolute and relative $h$-stability. Notably, we demonstrate that in most non-trivial cases, temporal relative $h$-stability coincides with spatial relative $h$-stability.

A novel application of robotic ultrasound scanning, using the 3D printed scoliosis index module (SIM), has been developed for accurately and reliably detecting scoliosis in adolescents and adolescents-in-transition. This accuracy and reliability have been proven to be on par with those of human operators. For validation, twenty five patients between the ages of 8 and 18 with scoliosis (C) were treated at Bristol Royal Hospital for Children, and scoliosis assessments were conducted using both manual and robotic methods with multiple observers. Scoliosis curvature measurements, known as Scoliosis Inclinometer (S.I.), were taken at six distinct spinal locations for each eye and eye pair. Scoliosis curvature measurements were determined through ultrasound by both manual and robotic methods with the average values being analyzed statistically. Results showed that robotic assessments produced reliable measurements with robust consistency across observers. Furthermore, it was found that robotic SIM produced Scoliosis Inclinometer (S.I.) values with dispersion less than half a degree, with robust consistency across observers. Consistently, Scoliosis Inclinometer (S.I.) values from both manual and robotic observations displayed a high degree of correlation. In conclusion, while both manual and robotic assessments exhibited similar performance capabilities, the robotic simulations showed promise in replicating expert level capability with a high degree of precision and consistency. This paper introduces a novel method for synthesizing speech durations that relies on median values instead of the traditional mean. We investigated duration variations in English and Mandarin speech and discovered that applying median corrections effectively mitigates the phenomenon where synthesized durations tend to be overly variable. Moreover, applying median corrections to inter-pause latency has a notable effect in reducing variability and making spoken language more natural-sounding compared to using mean corrections. We compared the duration models across two speech synthesis languages through objective measurements of speech naturalness, variability, and listener perceptions, finding that applying median corrections yields improved listener ratings and fewer outliers in duration variability.

This study evaluates the effectiveness of Feature Selection techniques in identifying hate speech on social media. Comparing different algorithms such as Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and Naive Bayes with and without FS, revealed that FS yields better performance with lower characteristics and significantly improves classification accuracy. Our research also demonstrated that text characteristics produce the most reliable outcomes for identifying hate speech. The findings indicate that a fusion of text and audio characteristics can boost classification accuracy within the scope of the 2020 HateSpeechChallenge.

In Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) networks, where each input site has access to multiple inputs, optimizing performance requires balancing individual model feature learning against combining information for better performance. We investigate how to achieve this balance by precisely controlling feature sharing between tasks using orthogonal mechanisms. As a result, we develop a range of novel MIMO architectures that excel in handling overlapping and non-overlapping data with real-valued and categorical features alike. Notably, our proposed models surpass the current state-of-the-art in non-overlapping data and demonstrate competitive results for overlapping data.

This concise survey showcases 33 datasets containing manuscripts from diverse periods and origins, cross-referenced in a comprehensible schema, to provide access to information on each dataset's characteristics. The datasets are scrutinized for commonalities, differences, and irregularities. The paper also highlights gaps in existing datasets, emphasizing the difficulties in collecting archives from certain eras and regions, and suggests potential avenues for future research.

This study proposes a straightforward FL flatness-based controller design in a straightforward manner, and puts it to use in guiding an industrial robot's joint, utilizing information from secondary encoders, to overcome issues caused by primary encoder errors due to mechanical factors. The robot's joint is described as a complex, nonlinear system, for which a neighborhood of flatness is found and characterized. A controller is then designed using the derivative of the flatness function, to regulate the joint to a set point, especially useful when the robot is subject to mechanical disruptions such as mechanical backlash, which can significantly impact the position accuracy. The effectiveness of the proposed controller is demonstrated through simulations on a ABB Y5VA robot, and even more surprisingly, it's also shown that a simple, low-cost magnetic sensor can effectively detect the backlash and accurately regulate the joint, providing a very cost-effective solution with this setup.

To gain a deeper understanding of how chronic diseases evolve over time and how their courses may vary across individuals, researchers use complex statistical methods to analyze data from multiple events.  These approaches are particularly important in understanding the progression of diseases like myocardial infarction, where recurring infections can lead to future illnesses such as stroke.  Current statistical tools primarily focus on one aspect of a patient's health history - the time when a particular event first occurs, its frequency, and the likelihood of future occurrences.  Although they account for multiple dimensions of a patient's history, they don't capture the overall pattern of history before a particular event.  Patients who have myocardial infarctions, for example, may have a history that includes other heart problems, smoking, diet, family history, and the progression of their heart disease.  To better address this, researchers propose a new statistical method that uses the history of myocardial infarctions to create a picture of how the disease develops in patients, from initial occurrences to the frequency and timing of subsequent events.  This new approach, called the Multiple State Examination, not only identifies how the disease develops but also the factors that contribute to its course.  By applying this method to patients who have myocardial infolder, researchers discovered how the disease progresses for women, in relation to risk factors such as smoking, diet, family history, sex, blood pressure, and the history of heart disease. A novel integration approach has been developed for efficient simulations with multiple groups of atoms. This high-performance method can evaluate contributions from all atomic groups through a straightforward procedure, enabling improved performance by avoiding individual looped calculations for each group. This integration approach has been successfully applied to multiple modeling schemes, including a unique LAM mode that facilitates faster and more efficient non-bonded interactions. Additionally, a new optimization technique has been established that combines with the integration approach to enhance overall simulation accuracy. This integration approach has significant practical applications and can enhance the efficiency of various modeling techniques.

In a graph, a subset of vertices forms a resolving set if, for any two vertices, a single set vertex is positioned at different distances from the two vertices. The problem of finding a resolving set of size at most k, or metric dimension k, is investigated when allowing some vertices to be excluded from consideration. The problem is framed as a parameterized problem with the size of the excluded set as a parameter. The research demonstrates that the problem of finding a resolving set of size at most k, given a bounded feedback vertex subset, is NP-complete, but can be solved in polynomial time when the feedback vertex subset is bounded and the parameter k is also bounded. The same applies if the problem is framed as a function problem, with the feedback vertex subset being a fixed constant. The research also shows that the problem of finding a resolving set of size at most k, given a bounded treewidth or pathwidth, is solvable in polynomial time. The research further investigates the problem in graphs with bounded cliquewidth, demonstrating that the problem can be solved in 2^{O(tw)} n time for treewidth tw and pathwidth pw of n, but the bound is quadratic when the pathwidth is greater than 2. The research also shows that the problem of finding a resolving set of size at most k, given a bounded cliquewidth of 2, is solvable in n O(k) time. Directed spaces, similar to topological spaces, have been defined using transitive relations, yet their algebraic properties remain unclear. This research introduces different levels of generalization, known as power frameworks of directed spaces, to both preordered and ordered sets within topological spaces. These power frameworks are comparable to free monoids in some cases and are used to define directed Hausdorff, paratopological groups, and topological groups by considering two different sets of properties. An example of each type of structure is provided to demonstrate their validity.

Past studies have suggested that Earth will undergo "hothouse" climate conditions in the distant future if the sun's energy intensity increases. We've used a computer model to simulate these climates and found that "hothouse" conditions lead to very different precipitation patterns, characterized by extremely intense downpours. These downpours, lasting no more than a few weeks, result in precipitation that is 1000 times more concentrated than it is today, while the overall annual amount of precipitation actually decreases by 50%. Our simulation suggests that plants could potentially survive "hothouse" climates for a longer period than previously thought, through a mechanism where they have adapted to the very short interval between heavy downpours and the dry periods that follow.

We have developed an invariant action for self-dual Yang-Mills theory and its spinful variations in flat space using twistor variables. This action displays a unique property where it reduces to a self-dustrial equation with a straightforward integral solution when reduced to its linear representation. This reduction yields the free spinor field and Yang-Mills theory's higher-spin analogues come with similar solutions, where they reduce to massless higher-spin free fields. These new actions share a connection to a higher-spin completion of self-dual Yang-Mills theory we previously found.

The adoption of deep neural networks within medical imaging systems has been widespread due to their advanced learning capabilities. Despite their success, current deep learning-based systems are prone to malfunction when presented with noisy labels, a common occurrence in real-world medical imaging datasets. Our research offers an innovative solution to this problem by enhancing existing noisy label mitigation techniques with a novel method called the Bayesian Statistics Guided Label Rejuvenation mechanism (BSLRM). This mechanism leverages Bayesian statistics to accurately detect noisy labels and reliably change them. Our improved approach builds on the existing Optimal Within-Class Scatter loss function, making BSLRM a more resilient and noisy label-resistant tool. When tested, BSLRM demonstrated significant improvements, with an average increase in noisy label resilience compared to other methods. Our proposed mechanism can effectively mitigate noisy labels and is suitable for use with large medical imaging datasets.

This article provides fresh insights into the norm of an interpolation projector, addressing concerns mentioned in a previous study. Furthermore, new inequalities for the norm of an interpolation projector have been derived.

A heuristic method for acquiring the transition probability matrix of a associated random walk on a graph, where p(v) denotes the transition probability from node v to itself, and the characteristic polynomial of the transition probability matrix being potentially eigenvalues of the transition probability matrix except in a specific graph type (where one eigenvalue is zero and the rest are positive) leads to a random walk being irreducible. Furthermore, evaluating the second derivative of the characteristic polynomial at zero yields an irreducibility condition, as well as another condition in random walk dynamics. This study provides a foundational analysis for applying the mentioned methods in irreducibility checking. It uses a particular example to demonstrate its applicability, as well as an associated Python script for implementing these methods.

In this work, we introduce a theory of timed functions within the HOL proof system, building on the framework established by others to study timed structures, we submerge timed functions within a traditional logic, concurrent system context. We derive fundamental properties of timed functions, including the ability to establish their existence and uniqueness, and then apply this framework to prove key properties of the preemption function as found in Weber's concurrent Haskell language. We subsequently translate our HOL proofs to Isabelle Input/Output Automata (IOA) models to provide a formal abstractive view of the preemption function's operation.

The reliance of the aerospace and automotive industries on numerical simulations has significantly increased their understanding of complex systems, including turbulent flows. To accommodate this demand, a hybrid approach was developed by combining data-driven techniques with a conventional model for predicting wall turbulence. This specific method, known as BICS, was applied to simulate the turbulent flow separate from a cubic bump on a flat plate at a high Reynolds number. Firstly, a conventional model was used to generate a coarse representation of the flow, identifying key features such as vortex shedding patterns and shear layers. Next, the model's predictions were corrected using a machine learning algorithm, its design based on supplementary simulations and informed by specific data about the flow. By incorporating the learned correction into the original model, BICS was able to accurately predict crucial aspects of the turbulent flow, including structures as small as millimeters, from a single large-eddy simulation. This approach significantly enhances the predictive capabilities of conventional models. Its potential applications could extend beyond this study's scope, allowing engineers to more accurately forecast turbulent flows in a broader range of scenarios.

This study investigates topological solutions within a modified Skyrme model that incorporates properties of both Born-Infeld and infant Skyrme equations. Initially, we derive the Euler-Lagrange equations for this model and demonstrate that its solutions must be zero at the origin. Subsequently, we express the model's equations in a gauge equivalent form and establish that its solutions are self-dual. Furthermore, we identify conditions under which the model reduces to the infant Skyrme equation and explore the properties of these solutions. Using the hull property, we conclude that vortex rings are the only non-trivial topological solutions in this model. Additionally, we examine the asymptotic properties of these solutions and derive a lower bound on their energy. Finally, we illustrate several examples of these solutions via contour diagrams.

By numerically solving the Dirac equation for a two-dimensional electron gas with a strong magnetic field, localized source of charge, and without time-reversal symmetry, we have found that the system's energy spectrum exhibits seven branches at zero energy. The top six energy branches consist of pairs, each associated with a loop of the Landau orbit that has been broken off. The smallest branch corresponds to an orbit that has not completed a full rotation. The density of states at zero energy is zero when considering a finite system, but tends towards a finite limit as the magnetic field strength approaches infinity. The overall behavior of the energy spectrum is characterized by a self-similar pattern in the density of states.

Developing strong light-emitting sources with controlled light output and directionality could significantly contribute to the advancement of quantum photonic as well as optomechanical engineering and research. The creation of light-emitting antennas that combine dielectric and plasmonic properties has shown great potential in this area, offering a unique combination of geometric and electromagnetic benefits, including tailored modes and enhanced radiation efficiency. This study presents a detailed theoretical investigation into an advanced, three-part light-emitting antenna designed to optimize performance, offering a unique combination of strong light emission, efficient radiation, and precise light directionality. The results show that these antennas could potentially emit extremely luminous light (up to 1000 times more luminous than similar antennas without their metallic counterparts), with extremely directed light (up to 90% of light output concentrated within a 30-degree range), and strong local fields (over 100 times stronger than those found in dielectric-only systems), making them extremely suitable for high-end quantum photonic applications.

In a 2019 study, researchers observed a phenomenon where ions repelled granules, yet a theoretical framework based on screening failed to fully explain the results. This led them to propose an alternative theory based on electrostatic interactions between charged granules. The new model predicted a reduced screening effect and indicated that the effect would be more pronounced at larger electrostatic screening lengths. To test this hypothesis, the researchers conducted an experiment involving pea-sized particles and small polystyrene balls that were exposed to a charged aerosol, observing the particle repulsion patterns. The data showed a significantly reduced screening effect and indicated that the effect would be more pronounced at longer particle separation distances. The experimental findings are consistent with the theoretical predictions. Additionally, a numerical simulation was conducted to confirm the results and provide insights into the underlying dynamics. The experimental and numerical results provide evidence that the anomalous screening effect is a characteristic of granular matter.

Utilizing first-principles calculations with the DFT method, our research examines the electronic properties of silicene decorated with manganese on a hexagonal boron nitride substrate. Three different decoration configurations were studied: manganese inserted above, center, and below a hexagonal boron nitride layer. The results indicate that all three configurations result in a metallic band structure. However, variations in the decay length of wave functions between different states show distinct differences in localisation patterns on both silicene and boron nitride layers. Moreover, our calculations reveal notable differences in the muffin-ties of manganese in the three different configurations, suggesting distinct covalent interactions between manganese and surrounding atoms. The observed differences in the electronic properties of decorated silicene and boron nitride layers highlight their potential for diverse applications in device fabrication and band engineering.

The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, poses a mystery with age estimates ranging from extremely young, around 1-2 thousand years, to a significantly older, 10 thousand year estimate. Our objective is to create a straightforward simulation of a supernova event replicating the shape, dimensions, and placement of Sgr A East, which was achieved by simulating a supernova that occurred approximately 270 parsecs from the Earth within the Galactic center region, utilizing a magnetic field's effect to account for the peculiar's shock front's arch shape observed in the northwest quadrant.

Overcoming class imbalance issues in text classification can involve using various oversampling methods to balance the data. A prior study found that using text rotation to create synthetic texts led to better performance than traditional oversampling methods. This paper builds on that research by testing whether text rotation still performs best when using multiple-class datasets, as opposed to the focus on binary classification in the original study. To this end, it has developed a multi-class text classification task, created multiple imbalanced datasets, and examined the effectiveness of different oversampling methods, including text rotation. The results indicate that using text rotation results in significant performance enhancements when the classes are very disparate. However, when the imbalance problem is less severe and we have mostly random labels, the simple majority class method delivers better outcomes. Moreover, when one class is not significantly under-represented, we find that using text rotation can even reduce the system's accuracy. A crucial implication of this research is that manually examining the distribution of the data before choosing an oversampling method may lead to better results.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between coverage, COVID-19 cases and deaths, and audience engagement across 296 research sites from January 2020 to October 2021. Findings indicate that news coverage of COVID increased as cases and deaths rose, but declined when case counts decreased. By using a difference-in-differences analysis, the research shows that local news coverage of COVID influenced state-level COVID cases and deaths, particularly within the first 11 months of the pandemic. Notably, increased local news coverage of COVID led to reduced cases and deaths, indicating a protective effect. Furthermore, the study reveals that local news coverage of COVID was more influential than national news and that residents of rural areas derived greater benefits from local news coverage than their urban counterparts. Finally, the research shows that local news coverage of COVID was more engaging for younger and less educated audiences.

Gravitational waves emitted by individual cosmic sources in the universe add up to form the gravitational wave background, which can be used to study the universe through its intrinsic angular momentum. Measuring this angular momentum requires processing the isolated binary orbits using the Fast Multipole Method, which also applies to spinless or spinning bodies. However, our investigation reveals that the Fast Multipole Method fails to conserve the total angular momentum of systems composed of multiple bodies, regardless of their mass distribution. Although this error is negligible for systems with few bodies and low masses, it becomes a critical issue for systems with many bodies such as supermasson black hole binaries. Our analysis identifies the reason for this discrepancy as the incorrect calculation of the angular momentum in the Fast Multipole Method, which fails to accurately account for the orbital angular momentum of each body due to inaccurately estimated position vectors and velocities. Our investigation confirms that the Position Vector Form of calculus, which calculates the orbital angular momentum using the Position Vector Form of each body, correctly conserves total angular momentum and accurately mass-weight the angular momentum of each body. Furthermore, our investigation confirms that the Linear Momentum Form of calculus, which calculates the orbital angular momentum using the Linear Momentum Form of each body, also correctly conserved total angular momentum in systems with constant relative positions and velocities, but only if the relative positions and velocities are constant. Numerical calculations examining the transfer of longitudinal (parallel) and transverse (anti-parallel) polarizations in the $e \vec {p} \to e \vec {p}$ reaction have been conducted using the Jefferson Lab's Concert Concert extension of Pythia program. Calculations considered various kinematic points on a 1-2 GeV scale, and the outcome, it seems, shouldn't be measurable due to being overpowered by statistical uncertainties in the $Q^2$ dependent case. Nonetheless, the outcome differs for the case involving average values across a 300-400 MeV range of $t$ values, and the expected measurement may be feasible with the $10$ GeV electron kinetic energy in the CLAS12 experiment.

To accelerate reinforcement learning from experienced models, we developed a technique that simulates scenarios from which a baseline agent can gain valuable insights. Through the incorporation of these artificial scenarios, our method facilitates accelerated reinforcement learning. We hypothesize that this approach, which leverages a variety of scenarios to enhance training, would remain effective even with limited expert knowledge, thereby allowing us to train more efficiently. Our investigation of this novel strategy revealed that augmenting training data significantly speeds up the learning process, notably when expert knowledge is scarce. We also discovered that our technique achieves notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, particularly when applied to control tasks. Moreover, our analysis indicates that our method converges towards optimal solutions and underscores the importance of utilizing diverse scenarios to augment data.

We've developed a unique method to produce an extremely bright laser using digital techniques, with the ability to deliver a large amount of energy in a very short time. By rapidly changing the state of less-than-a-nanosecond pulses of rubidium atoms, we've produced an incredibly powerful laser effect, with nearly 7 million times more powerful beams when combined. These digital methods allow for precise control over the pulse sequence, giving us a high level of precision in controlling the laser. Notably, the short duration and high intensity of these pulses make them suitable for spectroscopic analysis and other applications without experiencing broadening effects.

Building on previous research which derived bounds for the Picard numbers of K3 surfaces within the class of K3 surfaces lacking a K\"ahler-Einstein metric, our work establishes an optimization of these bounds by cross-referencing known results on the distribution of Siegel disks within the moduli space of K3 surfaces. Specifically, for a given K3 surface $X$ with an abundance of rational pencils, our findings provide more precise limitations on the Picard number $\tau(X)$ relative to the moduli space's complex structure. Moreover, for K3 surfaces within a specified genus $g \ge 4$, our theorems offer refined estimates of the minimum and maximum possible Picard numbers. These optimized bounds are achieved through an integration of previous research and insights from the arithmetic moduli scheme of Siegel disks by Dorian Goldfeld and Wei Ho.

The supersymmetric neutralino is a promising candidate for dark matter, with various decays of the neutralino itself and other particles linked to it potentially affecting cosmic relics. In the case where the neutralino decays into itself, its mass is limited by constraints on energy emission in the cosmos and the density of dark matter. If such a decay occurs into the lightest neutralino state, its mass cap could be as high as 100 TeV. In specific theoretical models where the neutralino states differ in terms of chargino or neutrino components, for instance, its self-decay releases energy in the form of gamma rays within distant galaxies and galaxy clusters. These areas can be studied with future cosmic observations that measure gamma ray spectra, which may verify theoretical supersymmetric models.

The main contribution of this paper is to develop an Positive Effective Linear Time Approximation Scheme (PETAL) for finding the minimum genus, $g_t(G)$, of a given graph $G$ with $\Omega(n^2)$ edges. This PETAL method works by first applying the Robertson-Seymour Algorithm to a random subset of vertices selected with equal probability from the set of all vertices. This algorithm takes linear time to calculate $g_t(G_{|A})$ for the induced subgraph $G_A$ created by the chosen subset of vertices $A$. Since the probability of selecting a vertex is uniform, the expected value of $|A|$ is roughly $\sqrt{n}$ for the given set of vertices $A$. This allows us to calculate the minimum genus of the induced subgraph $G_A$ using the PETAL method and apply it until the entire graph $G$ is correctly approximated with high accuracy. Additionally, we derive sharp bounds for the expected value and standard deviation of the number of vertices $|A|$ in the set of chosen subset of vertices $A$. Based on these findings, we develop an PETAL method with an approximation ratio of at most $O(\log^5 n)$ and takes polynomial time with respect to $n$. A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products for the same dataset, before aggregating the results to calculate an approximate Newton step. This approach, which is scalable even in computationally intensive scenarios, is shown to converge asymptotically towards the optimal solution at a rate defined by the dual strong convexity and gradient growth parameters. We provide a detailed convergence proof and statistical assurances for this algorithm in the main text and appendants.

Our contribution in this research involves tackling the English language hate-speech prediction issue, a pressing concern shared by numerous social media platforms. A substantial number of social media users in countries such as the US, the UK, India, and Bangladesh communicate in languages other than English; specifically, Hindi and Bengali are extremely popular. In light of this, our study concentrates on the hate-speech prediction within these two languages to fill this notable gap in the literature. To achieve this, we create and make accessible the first Hindi and Bengali datasets of annotated text that is specifically designed for hate-speech detection. In order to verify the effectiveness of our system, comprehensive tests are performed on these newly developed datasets. A direct comparison with existing state-of-the-art models and approaches reveals that our implementation exhibits superior performance. Moreover, our research reveals that transfer learning is an extremely valuable technique in NLP and can be applied seamlessly to languages in which there is a shortage of annotated data available.

In nuclear and particle physics, Gas Time Projection Chambers are becoming key detectors for studying nuclear and particle physics phenomena, due to their advanced capabilities for event-based proportional signal readout, radiation-hardness, and efficiency in 3D reconstruction of particle interactions. A significant technological advantage of GTPCs lies in detecting the movement of ionized gas ion pairs per electron, which creates opportunities for the development of devices with an almost atomic resolution in detecting charged particles. This level of sensitivity also enables the ability to track the direction of neutrino interaction angles with high precision, which is essential for neutrino oscillation studies across various cosmic-ray energy spectrums. With this knowledge, GTPCs can be used to investigate a range of phenomena, such as Cockcroft-Walton nuclear disintegration, the directionality of cosmic rays origins, the characteristics of ultra-high energy cosmic rays, and the measurement of electron neutrino disintegration properties - including the observation of neutrino oscillations. A GTPC technology upgrade focuses on improving its capabilities for the detection of particle recoil during interactions with neutrinos and nuclear particles. This article describes a set of observables useful in the detection of particle recoil during interactions with neutrinos, which involves examining both the spatial distribution and electron information within GTPC drift patterns.

A significant issue in human-in-the-loop AI systems is the optimal integration of automated decisions with expert input. Moderation by humans can improve the performance of AI-driven solutions, especially in complex systems like commercial vehicle operation. Our study involves developing an AI-powered system for evaluating driver skills in a specific company, and investigating how human expertise affects its performance. We analyzed the interaction between AI-generated ratings and feedback from an experienced trainer and found that human input leads to more equitable assessment scores. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that human moderation can improve the reliability of the AI system, particularly in cases where it overestimates a driver's skills. By incorporating the trainer's feedback, the variability in the AI's predictions diminished, and its accuracy improved. Consequently, our study demonstrates the importance of human involvement in the development of AI systems for complex decision-making tasks.

This study investigates the variability of changes in Gaussian random field (GRF) manifolds, considering both theoretical programming and simulations on random grids to illustrate the results. The research aims to quantify the uncertainty in GRF trajectories based on their intrinsic geometry as probability manifolds. The work establishes that GRF velocity is an intrinsic GRF tangent vector, providing a key finding, and a velocity field can be seen as a tangent field tangent to multiple GRFs. The study then derives an expression for the distribution of the geodesic integral curve starting from a given point with initial velocity. To estimate the variability of changes, the research employs two methods: the inverse variance geodesic and the efficient geodesic, both of which have been demonstrated in simulations.

This note serves as a companion to the length count movie presented at LEARN 2021. It provides a brief overview of REU project objectives, offers a summary of findings, and serves as a visual accompaniment to the previously mentioned movie.

For a cuspidal Hecke eigenform $F$ of weight $k$ associated with the SL$_2(\mathbb{R})$ cusp form, the distinguished value of its L-function at Dirichlet's image of a Galois automorphism $\sigma$ is given by $L(F,\sigma,1)$ and serves as a critical element in various applications, particularly in arithmetic. The boundedness of the denominators of these values has practical implications in the number of solutions to specific forms of Thue equations and in the least solutions to Pell's equation under given conditions. Previous studies, such as those by Siegel and Linnik, have already identified the boundedness of the denominators in particular scenarios. This study demonstrates the boundedness of the denominators for all modularity, while accounting for exceptions arising from CM forms.

In a graphene nanoribbon, which has the potential to exhibit nanoscale spintronics, our study reveals a novel transport phenomenon where a gate voltage can manipulate spin-related current characteristics. We employed a tight-binding model and ferromagnetic coupling to model spin-dependent graphene nanoribbons and analyzed how these properties evolve when the ribbons undergo a cut in a particular direction. Our research demonstrates that by cutting the ribbon at specific points, we can produce regions with differing band gaps, thus enabling spin separation. Additionally, our experiments showed that a cut that preserves symmetry allows for complete spin separation, which can be controlled through an electric field. We have also identified areas with exceptionally high spin polarization based on their resistance. Overall, our findings provide an essential foundation for developing efficient spin-based devices made from graphene nanoribbons.

We derive approximation theorems for operators with monotonicity properties. 
By employing a specific method of approximation, similar to Korovkin's theorem, 
we can establish the convergence of certain linear operators acting on multiple variables. 
Furthermore, this method can be adapted to nonlinear operators under specific conditions. 
Its applicability can be seen in the approximation of weakly nonlinear solutions to elliptic type equations. 
We provide concrete examples of its practical use in the specific case of a second-order elliptic equation.

A set of vertices in a graph is called a pancyclic set if for every vertex in the set, there is a cycle of a length between 3 and n that includes the vertex, where n represents the maximum number of vertices in the graph. Research has established that if a graph has an independent set and a pancyclic set, the maximum number of vertices in the graph is restricted. Specifically, it was discovered that a graph with an independent set of size two and a pancyclic set has at most 8n vertices. For the current research, it was proven that a graph with an independent set of size two and a pancyclic set has at most n + 6 except for three exceptions or triangles that are not 3-cyclic, has a maximum number of vertices equal to n + 5 except for three exceptions or triangles that are not 3-cyclic. Additionally, it was proven that a graph with an independent set of size three and a pancyclic set has at most n + 7 except for three exceptions or triangles that are not 3-cyclic. A longer cycle can be formed by removing one edge from the shortest cycle containing two vertices from an independent set and a pancyclic set. This inspired the research to determine whether it is possible to form the longest cycle in a graph by removing one edge from the shortest cycle containing two vertices from an independent set and a pancyclic set.
