This paper demonstrates the end-to-end fine-tuning of the Complete RAG architecture for the task of question- answering. By utilizing this architecture, it was possible to eliminate the requirement for pre-built index datasets and circumvent the common issue of retrieval instability. A series of experiments were conducted to explore various settings for the number of processed sentences and retrieved documents. Notably, when employing the very large Facebook AI-2 dense multilingual model, it was possible to achieve significant improvements in performance, with a newly end-to-end trained model surpassing the previously established results in the DeepQA benchmark by 16%. Furthermore, this newly end-to-end trained model also exhibited an 11% improvement in the SQuADv2.1 benchmark over the multilingual RAG model and achieved results on par with the top two multilingual models in the recent ARQmath challenge. A corresponding GitHub repository provides the necessary code to replicate these findings.

This paper calculates the long-term behavior of the recurrence coefficients for polynomials that are orthogonal in relation to the logarithmic influence of a specific function. It initially determines a general formula for these coefficients based on a non-standard indentation in their coefficient distribution, and then identifies the specific characteristics of their behavior when this indentation doesn't exist, revealing a power-law increase in recurrence coefficients with degree. Furthermore, by transforming a model with a singular influence introduced by Fyodorov and Nagy into a standard M-GLOE form, we confirm a model with a singular influence can exhibit a power-law increase in recurrence coefficients with degree. This transformation allows us to analyze an important linear spectral model that has been overlooked in the literature, and provides an alternative perspective on a similar model studied by Shcherbina.

Crowdsourcing with Amazon Mechanical Turk offers a versatile approach for gathering data or exploring mechanisms, yet it can be challenging due to poor task quality or uncooperative workers. To assess the difficulty of finding qualified workers, we designed a series of experiments involving crowdsourced games and demonstrations. Our investigation focuses on three key aspects: establishing a universal set of standards, evaluating worker quality, and analyzing the impact of workflow design. The experimental results provide valuable insights that can guide other researchers in their work, while the accompanying repository contains a collection of five usable games that others can adopt in their own studies.

Text-clipping retrieval, a critical component of various video analysis models, is increasingly being recognized for its potential to improve daily life and industrial processes. This recognition is a direct result of its prominent role in video-based retrieval tasks, which rely heavily on accurately identifying and matching text information extracted from videos. This is particularly true in applications like retrieval, where the goal is to find similar text clips based on the content's understanding. This paper proposes a novel approach to text-clipping retrieval, which involves leveraging pre-trained language models to enhance CLIP-based retrieval techniques. These novel techniques involve token shifting and selection to refine text-clipping representations and improve model efficiency. Experiments have demonstrated the significant benefits of this model, which can achieve a 19.5% improvement in average recall rate when compared to a CLIP-based baseline approach. This breakthrough is largely due to its ability to adapt to different tokenization schemes and effectively focus on key content words. This model has been successfully applied to multiple text-clipping retrieval tasks and has outperformed more traditional approaches in every aspect.

The addition of top-quark-induced neutral currents in beyond the Standard Model scenarios has the potential to offer new explanations for anomalous data from the LHC and for the observed rarity of certain rare decays involving the top quark and bottom quark. In our proposal, flavour-changing neutral currents in top-quark sector are introduced through an extended operator that links the top-quark current to a novel generalised Z boson mediating a neutral current. This proposed extension can immediately be explored using latest data from collisions of high-energy protons at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Furthermore, in an extension of the Standard Model where a second Higgs boson exists, and in an action that changes flavour, we have found that taste-changing neutral currents in top-quark sector can provide a beyond-the-Standard-model-based explanation for anomalous data obtained while studying the two Higgs bosons in association with top quark and a bottom quark recently presented at ICHEP 2020. This beyond-the-Standard-model-based explanation is in line with existing data and with the standard modelling of electroweak interactions, and in prediction it is compared with the results obtained from beyond-the-Standard-model-based modelling of electroweak interactions, and in prediction it is compared with the results obtained from beyond-the-Standard-model-based modelling of electroweak interactions, and in prediction it is compared with the results obtained from beyond-the-Standard-model-based modelling of electroweak interactions

This research aims to combine and build upon existing methods for creating hybrid random graph models, incorporating both preferential attachment and uniform attachment mechanisms, and adapt them to incorporate directed edges. By focusing on the asymptotic behavior of these directed hybrid models as the number of nodes approaches infinity, we examine the impact of different attachment probabilities further. Our findings show that with a probability greater than 0.5, the large-scale structure of these directed hybrid networks will consist of a single large component and that this probability does not vary significantly with the presence of a finite number of additional smaller components. Additionally, our analysis reveals that with a probability of 1, the existing edges in these large components will persist in the long-term and contribute significantly to the overall degree distribution, which diverges from a power-law distribution at a specific log-log slope value of 3.

The proliferation of wireless communication systems has led to increased concerns about interference from wireless signals, especially in medical and industrial applications. Merging wireless communication and sensing technologies creates challenges due to wireless interference, which hinders signal quality and device performance. Identifying the source of wireless disturbance is a critical task, and this paper proposes a novel approach using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to recognize multiple labels from diverse wireless signals. Our approach demonstrates reliable and efficient WDI, and key aspects of our method are compared to existing approaches through comprehensive experiments.

To grasp the impact of cosmic string defects on both quantum neutral and charged particles, we examine the movement of Klein-Gordon particles across misaligned spacetime with various dislocation parameters. The study shows that under specific wave function conditions, the impact of dislocation defects on charged particles parallels that of neutral particles. Vortex-like correlations emerge in the dislocation spacetime, with the quantum neutral particles exhibiting characteristics similar to the half-integer fractional statistics of particles lacking charge, while also confirming the expected behavior for charged particles under integer quantum numbers. The influence of the dislocation defects on the energy and charge of both charged and neutral particles becomes apparent as their properties interact in complex ways.

In a previous work, I established that every measure algebra forming a part of a locally usual measure algebra bundle has itself as locally usual. The primary objective of this current contribution is to provide an opposing statement: it holds that every measure algebra with the property of being uniformly usual also satisfies the condition of being locally usual.

Parton distributions that account for quark and gluon correlations in a proton can be understood by analyzing specific interactions between a proton and a photon, specifically in a process known as leptoproduction. Researchers focus on the Compton scattering part of this interaction, which in the laboratory frame can be broken down into two parts: one where the proton remains stationary and another where it recoils. By studying both parts, scientists aim to understand how correlation information from the proton's partonic structure, or gluon transversity, impacts the interaction's geometry. As the recoil Compton scattering is extremely difficult to observe in current experiments due to a lack of precise measurements over the relevant scale, researchers propose a new way to study it using polarized targets. By measuring the polarization of the recoiling proton, scientists can gain even more information about the interaction, allowing the distribution to reveal its effects on the transverse plane, or remain neutral due to a known symmetry called Soffer's inequality. This new method offers an alternative means of studying parton correlations.

All AI systems rely on data that lacks the intelligence to create it; yet, with access to vast amounts of data, humans struggle to design, utilize, and evaluate trustworthy AI systems effectively. To bridge this gap, an innovative approach called augmented synthetic intelligence is proposed, combining the strengths of human and machine intelligence to create a collaborative understanding of intelligence. By distinguishing between human and machine intelligence, ASI fosters an environment where machine intelligence can operate under human guidance, leveraging data more efficiently. Furthermore, ASI recognizes that machine intelligence alone can generate new concepts, applications, and knowledge, thereby expanding human understanding and capabilities. By integrating these aspects, a collaborative framework for augmented synthetic intelligence is developed, utilizing a Venn diagram to illustrate its key components and facilitate practical applications.

Our research involves studying the heating dynamics and phase transitions of cold bosons with strong spin-orbit interactions and linked to a optical lattice on an axis, located in a weak disordered potential. As we lower the laser beam's angle of incidence, we observe the emergence of finite-time superfluidity loss, linked to a homogeneous state with quasifermionic excitations, and also sample modulation patterns transverse to the laser beam that exhibit finite-size periodic characteristics. The study shows the transition from homogenous superfluidity to transverse modulations happens through a weakly modulated superfluid state with large density fluctuations. At lower temperatures, we find the modulated superfluid state exhibits an exceptional characteristic - when it breaks time reversal symmetry, the ordering transverse to the laser beam happens at the same point as the ordering along the laser beam, resulting in an average density inside the modulations nearly equivalent to the overall density. Furthermore, we find the transition from the ordered to the disordered state by looking at the $2D$ Potts spin model of three-site model that accounts for the strong interunit correlations observed in our system.

A real $k$-dimensional vector space $V_k$ is defined with a specific lattice $\mathcal{L}$, and a graph $\mathcal{G}$ is formed by mapping the basis vectors to the vertices, with edges connecting vectors according to a specified relation within the lattice. We look at the family of graphs generated by $V_k \times \mathbb{Z}_p$ for different prime numbers $p$, and determine the degeneration patterns of these graphs as $p$ increases, especially for cases where $k$ is relatively large compared to $p$. Moreover, by examining the coordinates of the vertices and their connections, we find the maximum clique size or the chromatic number of these graphs, both for fixed and variable group sizes.

We examine how AdS/CFT correspondence, specifically in low-dimensional massive Type IIA, connects to CFT complexity theories. Our theory, starting with a massive gravitational wave background in two spatial dimensions, reveals a novel type of black string solution with first-order thermal phase transitions and a hierarchial Hagedorn phase transition. These properties are replicated in four-dimensional low-dimensional low-dimensional AdS black strings exhibiting primary and secondary phase transitions. Moreover, our research explores the connection between geometric properties and the information paradox in AdS black holes, discovering that their phase transitions might be linked to the information paradox's resolution.

The applications of Gaussian Process regression have been extensively explored in numerous fields. Nonetheless, selecting the optimal kernel parameters or model architecture can be very challenging. In our research, we've devised a method to construct Gaussian Process models using fundamental mathematical expressions as the basis for our kernel. By incorporating additional constraints, we can prevent the creation of ill-fitting models and ensure that our predictions remain computationally feasible. Our approach is highly versatile, allowing us to construct GP models that incorporate multivariate functions, non-linear vector transformations, and discrete output models. We've comprehensively tested our methodology and compared it to standard machine learning and Gaussian Process techniques on a diverse set of datasets.

Future high-energy muon colliders face a challenge due to the abundant production of cosmic rays generated by beam impacts on surrounding materials. Reducing beam-induced background noise is essential for accurate data collection and collider operation. Research into particle physics will require precise energy measurements, necessitating low emittance designs which in turn increase beam interactions with materials. Understanding and mitigating beam-induced background noise is critical throughout collider design and operation.

A comprehensive approach is developed here to address this issue, covering design phase through machine operation. Topics covered include collider design considerations, detector capabilities, and ongoing and future studies on accelerating system materials to reduce beam-induced background noise during operation. Additionally, the feasibility of temporarily relocating the accelerating system to reduce background noise is explored, as well as other potential solutions involving muon cooling.

In many areas of machine learning, particularly in deep learning, there is significant motivation to model sparsity, a feature that allows some neural networks to require less memory and time while also enhancing generalization. However, formulating sparsity as a learning objective has proven challenging due to its ad-hoc nature and lack of clear differentiation in optimization. To address this issue, a new method called Spartan has been developed to effectively learn sparsity in neural networks using a differentiable sparseness objective and a flexible formulation. Spartan combines a transportation-basedregulation approach with neural network advancements, allowing the model to achieve sparsity in data-driven ways. Experimental results have shown that Spartan outperforms existing approaches and achieves sparsity in both the neuron and layer levels.

The topological characteristics of a system derive their origin from non-local properties of the Hamiltonian. In contrast, the Hamiltonian of a highly interacting system, defined as one interacting via $1/r^n$, is entirely described by its nearest-neighbor interactions and thus exhibits no non-locality beyond that already encapsulated in these nearest-neighbor interactions. Nonetheless, the emergence of topological features within systems that are only weakly interacting ($n=0$) remains an open area of inquiry.

Utilizing the perturbative many-body approach known as Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH), which is specifically tailored for the $1/r$ interaction, we discover an exact relation between the binding energy of two adjacent particles and their relative angular separation ($\theta$). Within the $z$ channel of the SSH model, the binding energy is directly proportional to $J\cos\theta$, as defined by interaction strength ($J$) and angular separation ($\theta$). Subsequently, the system's energy can be expressed using a topological indicator known as the $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ invariant by integrating over all possible values of $J$ and $\theta$. Furthermore, the system's critical interaction strength, at which topological transition occurs, is shown to be directly proportional to the median of the distribution of $J\cos\theta$. Our study involves interviewing 11 developers and 11 maintenance managers to gather information on how severe they consider various types of test smells to be. The results suggest that developers and maintenance managers hold similar views on the severity of test smells, with some (complexity smells) considered more severe than others (covariance matrix smells). There was a general agreement that test smells, in general, have a mild effect on code. The study also highlights the potential benefits of identifying test smells, even if they have a minor impact, due to the potential risks associated with delayed correction (e.g., accumulation and spread).

This research explores a nonconvex, nonlattice, discrete brushing process that
circularly moves on a 2D integer grid, with its mathematical indices forming a
group. We have derived one- and multi-point versions of its stationary distribution,
along with the respective convergence times. These findings are instrumental in
establishing the integro-differential models' solution methods for the mentioned
brushing process, based on its recurrence characteristics. Furthermore, the
integro-differential models' theoretical outcomes are substantiated by numerical
case studies which demonstrate that the brushing strategy often yields the fastest
convergence times compared to other methods such as the typical Gibbs sampler and
the hit-and-run algorithm.

We introduce the updated version of the {\tt KKMCee} event generator, version 5.00.2, designed for simulating lepton and quark pair production in electron-positron/ion colliders. As the most advanced generator for this process, the code, now rewritten entirely in modern C++, maintains all features of its Fortran 77 predecessor while enhancing its capabilities with the goal of becoming a standard tool for future collider experiments. We outline the major improvements incorporated in the new version: Monte Carlo method changes, its theoretical foundations, electron beam polarization effects, polarized beam interactions, the inclusion of pure QED processes, the detailed description of the {\tt KKMCee} event generator for pair production, the list of used particle physics libraries, the input data cards, the Fortran 77 legacy parts, and the known issues of the code. These enhancements guarantee the most accurate pair production simulations for future colliders, making {\tt KKMCee} a universal tool for a wide range of physics events and polarized beam interactions.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult due to interference from artifacts and signal distortion. To overcome this challenge, we have developed an innovative Tiramisu model combining residual neural network and segmentation using convolutional neural networks. By leveraging the benefits of NN and CNN, our Tiramisu model offers high accuracy and improved handling of noisy signals, with a 98% reduction in error. Compared to existing methods, our approach achieves superior performance with a 6% decrease in mean absolute error and 11% decrease in root mean square error. Additionally, our Tiramisu model demonstrates exceptional adaptability to signals of varying lengths.

To calculate the tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) in an efficient manner, we have developed a randomized algorithm that can function with an arbitrary number of passes, depending on the desired level of accuracy. This method generates a low-rank tensor approximation and an orthogonal tensor through a few iterations of sampling and matrix multiplication hissing. Subsequently, we employ a certain expansion in order to obtain the singular values and vectors of the given tensor. Notably, the method's performance demonstrates conformance to a data-independent error probability bound, as well as a more general, asymptotic error upper limit that incorporates sample size and other factors. We have tested the algorithm with actual tensors, specifically using a few selected functions from tensor-optimized machine learning, and found that it effectively estimates the actions of these functions with a relatively small number of passes.

Real-world networks often exhibit rapid changes and are not static, yet many algorithms assume a graph's structure remains consistent. This issue is addressed in network representation learning, a growing field that has flourfully developed static graph embedding techniques. However, the dynamics of networks necessitate adapting these methods to preserve temporal relationships and preserving network structures across various time points. This work offers the first comprehensive review on graph embedding techniques that account for network evolution, distinguishing between methods that model individual nodes and those that model relationships between nodes over time. We assess various approaches in terms of both theoretical foundations and experimental evaluations, before concluding with a discussion on future research avenues and the limitations of current methods.

To determine the binding energy of a $^7$H nucleus, which can only be found through computationally intensive ab initio calculations, multiple theoretical models have been developed. However, these models struggle to account for the observed 1S ground state of $^7$H as a $^3$H+4n system. Our research reveals that the 1S ground state is not a pure $^3$H+4n combination but rather the lowest energy $^7$H state after applying the $^3$H+4n orbital separation model. The model features a V10 interaction that incorporates a cusp condition and foregoes the need for costly four-nucleon calculations involved in full ab initio systems like HFB or CFGB. The V10 model successfully reproduces the experimental 1S ground state of $^7$H binding energy with an error of less than one kiloelectronvolt.

The Nirenberg problem on the upper half 3-dimensional sphere involves finding minimal graphs in this space that satisfy specific boundary conditions. Our work focuses on solving this problem with non-trivial minimal parts in a particular type of region, eliminating the possibility of constant solutions. We begin by identifying potential forms for these non-trivial minimal parts and break them down into their corresponding components. Our next step involves applying a decomposition of the upper half sphere into regions near the equator and the north pole, using this partition to analyze the possible configurations of the problem's minimal parts in relation to its boundary conditions. We establish the existence of certain types of solutions, specifically blow ups, that satisfy these conditions and have non-trivial minimal components in both the inner and outer regions of the problem.

Deep Neural Networks are now widely used across various data representation tasks. Researchers have shown that these representations can significantly improve downstream tasks, but the best techniques for learning these representations remain unclear. Existing methods often focus on representation learning using Euclidean distance, although other measures like Wasserstein distance have shown promise. This paper demonstrates how the Wasserstein distance can be used effectively with both convex and non-convex formulations. The non-convex version is particularly interesting because it can be computed efficiently with Deep Neural Networks, while also providing a discriminative loss function. This paper explores the benefits of these formulations through theoretical analyses, empirical assessments, and applies them to multiple downstream tasks.

In various fields, research has demonstrated the value of partnerships between data providers and users. Nevertheless, there's a lack of studies examining how these partnerships affect the performance of infectious disease control measures, specifically in the context of contact tracing during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our research analyzed the impact of local tracing partnerships in England on the contact tracing service's overall efficiency, using data from August 2020 to July 2021. Contact tracing success was measured through two key indicators: the percentage of contacts traced, and the percentage of contacts isolated within the recommended time frame. Statistical analysis revealed a positive correlation between the use of partnerships and both of these indicators. Notably, partnership involvement was more significantly associated with the second indicator. Through further analysis using zero-inflated models and individual-level data from Traced, a public health app in England, we discovered that partnership involvement improved the contact tracing service's efficiency by increasing the proportion of cases with isolated contacts, without impacting the overall case volume. Ultimately, engagement with local tracing partnerships proved to be a crucial factor for enhancing the contact tracing service's effectiveness and contributing to the public health response during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The core association, Melotte 72, which comprises young stars and subgroups linked to the $\beta$ Hyi cytostome, has been largely understudied due to its encumbrance by dark cloud $\Sigma 132$ and the proximity of the cytostome. A recent investigation attempted to add Melotte 72 to the list of associations linked to $\beta$ Hyi cytostome by analyzing 25 members using data from Gaia DR2. This study at 440pc (the location of CBS 8048) sought to add depth to the understanding of the structure and moving aspects of the association. Preliminary assessment identified 18 likely members, indicating eight probable binaries, with the majority of stars showing reflection effect or color temperature discrepancies suggesting temperature disparities between members. A clean dataset of 18 members yielded right ascension proper motion values centered around 8.478 mas/yr and negative declination proper motion values at -7.072 mas/yr. Parallax values ranged between 4703 and 4707.68 microarcseconds, while radial velocities collected from LEP catalogs averaged negative 23.5 km/s. We've designed an algorithm that enables a robot arm to adjust its gripper camera by using just one image taken from an external camera. By analyzing these two images, our system calculates the necessary adjustments for the gripper camera to capture the desired view. By testing on both virtual and real-world scenarios, our results show that our method outperforms existing techniques by providing more accurate predictions for the gripper camera's parameters. One key advantage of our algorithm is its ability to operate offline without needing extensive training, making it more suitable for scenarios where network connectivity is limited or unreliable. Additionally, our system has been implemented using a ROS package to simplify its integration with robot systems.

We examine a scenario in which a learner obtains the actor's goal objectives from the observer and can obtain expert goals from the observer as needed. The learner's only interaction is with the observer, and all communications between them are through the observation alone. Our primary aim is to verify the existence of a strategy that allows the learner to approximate the actor's objectives through their own goal-oriented learning processes. This investigation can be seen as a model of goal-oriented learning where we consider a pair of asymmetric agents linked by a trusted third party, allowing us to think of this as a form of asymmetric goal-oriented co-operation. We apply our findings to several concrete situations in which we establish conditions that ensure the existence of a strategy that allows the learner to approximate the actor's objectives. One strategy that works in many situations involves the learner collecting and saving samples of actions taken by the observer in response to their own policies, while also adjusting their policies to optimise their likelihood of agreeing with the observer's goals. Our analysis suggests that this method has practical value, as well as theoretical significance, because we have evidence suggesting that it can learn key objectives from the observer under certain circumstances.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission will create a detailed 3D map of the galaxy by tracking over 10,000,000 stars, which the mission believes will greatly impact the understanding of astronomical and astrophysical subjects, by providing 10 to 100 times more information than previous studies. In this paper, the mission's objectives, scope, and procedures used to collect and process data are explained in the context of addresssing three primary goals: constructing a detailed 3D map of the galaxy at a distance of 10,000 light years, studying the nature of the galaxy's disk and bar, and examining the surrounding outer regions. Additionally, the methods for analyzing the collected data are examined, which involve using information from more than 100,000 stars within 200 light years to calibrate photometric scales, and understanding the relationship between mass and luminosity for stars across different parts of the galaxy. Ultimately, the data collected by the mission will be used to examine the distribution of dark matter across the galaxy at a distance of 10,000 light years.

To enhance efficiency, researchers modified the vertex deletion approach for treewidth calculation. The first innovation integrated the idea that ignored vertices have no impact on tree-decomposition graphs. Additionally, a more recent improvement utilized the fact that ignored vertices do not contribute to tree-decomposition width. Combining these optimizations yielded an algorithm with optimal vertex deletion for treewidth. The algorithm was also adapted into a distance metric, known as treewidth distance, which measures the minimal number of vertices to remove for treewidth 1. Lastly, researchers analyzed the complexity of calculating this distance metric.

Network analysis has traditionally been confined to the analysis of binary graphs representing physical or social connections, as well as the weighted representations of these connections. The emergence of network analysis in other fields has led to the consideration of networks with multiple attributes, which are represented as multi-partite directed graphs. This paper presents a generalized interpretation of weighted directed graphs that is independent of the network's node and edge cardinalities and is applicable to both binary and multi-partite graphs. This new interpretation is based on the concept of effective connection weights, which are defined as a combination of empirically observed, inferred, or blended weights derived from various sources. The paper also proposes a framework for assessing the significance of individual edges or subgroups of edges based on their contribution to the overall organization of the network and identifies requirements for this framework, which are completely general and applicable to any directed graph, whether binary, weighted, or multi-partite.

One of the greatest promises of neural networks lies in their ability to handle complex, nonlinear data through supervised learning. Despite this potential, these algorithms have yet to become widely accepted as reliable research tools within the physics community due to their lack of robustness and inherent uncertainties. They often serve as data analyzers rather than robust predictors. This study aims to close this gap by employing a refined approach to evaluating the reliability of neural networks, specifically those informed by physical principles. By incorporating a posteriori error estimates, this research demonstrates that these networks are capable of providing accurate predictions with established levels of reliability. To demonstrate this, this study utilizes a posteriori analysis to determine the allowable tolerable errors in predicted data for physics-informed neural networks using the Monte Carlo method. It verifies the effectiveness of this approach through the reanalysis of experimental and simulation data for predicting solution flows, showing a strong correlation between the estimated and actual prediction errors. This approach is then applied to deriving reliable, globally valid pressure fields from experimental data. Furthermore, this study reveals that these neural networks can function as reliable "analog-to-digital" converters for continuous signals. It also explores their utility in deriving reliable, globally valid parameters using an unsupervised learning framework. Lastly, this study showcases their ability to make predictions in cases where there is a lack of data, both spatially and temporally.

A crucial challenge in environmental epidemiology lies in predicting exposure levels of atmospheric pollutants at specific locations over extended periods of time. To address this issue, spatial and temporal surface concentration maps of air pollutants can be utilized, combining data from monitoring stations with inductive spatial modeling and geostatistical techniques such as kriging. By integrating massive ozone ozone ozonesensor data with geostatistical kriging, a novel method for predicting the concentration of atmospheric pollutants at specific locations is developed. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, we compared it to a predictive model built using a supervised machine learning algorithm and the output of a specific pollutant prediction model.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-equilibrium, our scheme utilizes tunneling spectroscopy with ohmic resistance, utilizing non-linear conductive tips. The distinction involves two distinct regimes: utilizing high-resistance contacts under moderate temperature and low-resistance tips at high temperatures. The former suppresses unwanted edge or bulk states by blocking their contribution to tunneling, leaving only the Majorana peak to analyze. The latter's high temperature makes the Majorana peakless, allowing the identification of a broad peak (or peaks) that may remain even at non-zero temperatures; this is particularly valuable in the investigation of topological superconducting nanowires where zero-energy peaks related to vortices and Andreev bound states may dominate the spectrum. These ideas have been successfully tested in a topological superconducting InAs nanowire with a shell of GaAl and a magnetic field applied perpendicularly. The major breakthroughs achieved include the elimination of edge or bulk state interference with the Majorana peak and the display of a broad peak (or peaks) that survives elevated temperatures, reminiscent of the behavior seen in the first topological superconducting system ever created - a topological superconducting InAs nanowire with a shell of GaAl and covered in ferromagnetic material.

We analyzed the scenario of linear bandits where each action has its own unique features. The direct approach for this scenario involves representing each action as $d$-dimensional vectors and using a ridge regression model to predict rewards. However, we discovered that even with the knowledge of Gaussian noise and an optimal action selection method, confidence intervals for reward estimates cannot be broadened uniformly across all actions. This limitation implies existing nearly-optimal algorithms are not capable of providing theoretiically justified statistical inference. To tackle this challenge, we introduced a new, more robust approach for sets of features. This framework enabled us to propose an adaptive model class that is learned adaptively during the learning process. Furthermore, we were able to prove that our method allows for accurate inference while maintaining near-optimal exploration efficiency, thus offering a more general solution for linear bandits with diverse action sets.

Graphene with gaps has drawn attention due to the generation of valley currents in AZB lattice structures. However, it is now known that these currents can be alternatively produced through an orbital Hall effect, where the movement of orbital Bloch electrons from the Bloch bands surrounding the absolute gap, given the presence of a Berry Rashba-like torque. It's noted that while the orbital Hall effect in graphene does not cause polarization, it can induce a similar anomalous Hall effect when applied to time-reversal-breaking ferromagnets. Our proposed theory provides an alternative explanation for the gapped graphene's properties and offers the possibility of studying the orbital Hall effect in ferromagnets, thus opening up new avenues for the analysis of orbital Hall effects.

Machine learning models' success is often compromised by data contamination, which can impair even the most advanced neural networks. Graph neural networks, particularly those used in social network analysis, are vulnerable to a range of contamination attacks including label and feature manipulation, making it difficult for research in this domain to keep pace with more general neural networks. Despite the inherent complexity of graph-based data, we have successfully developed a novel reinforcement learning method that uses the exchange of artificially contaminated data between nodes to model an agent's decision-making process. This approach, grounded in policy gradient training, mirrors real-world conditions by incorporating both gradient constraints and an actor-critic design that weighs the benefits and risks of various actions. Our experimental results demonstrating the superiority of our model confirm our hypothesis that an agent can effectively navigate graph data by spreading contamination across nodes.

The process of cross-identifying optical catalogs relies on precise astrometry. Although the precision of astrometry has improved significantly over recent missions, the cross-identification rate often falls short of 90%. This barrier can be overcome by integrating photometric information, which offers a more comprehensive fingerprint of each object than astrometry can provide. A new technique allows for combining optical catalogs based on both astrometry and photometry. By assessing photometric magnitudes, the method can distinguish which objects in a new survey are matched to ones from a reference catalog, or if the objects are merely coincidental. This technique is demonstrated on two optical catalogs, one from the Two-Micron Sky Survey and another from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, showcasing its effectiveness in enhancing cross-identification accuracy. The technique also addresses contamination by reducing false positives.

For a countably infinite graph G, we investigate the largest possible size of minimal subsets H within the Inf(G) hypergraph, where a subset is considered minimal if it cannot be formed by combining any smaller subset of G. We show that for a graph G that is non-empty and locally finite, the largest possible size of such a subset is 2^{\aleph_0} if G has a finite diameter, and 2^{\aleph_0} \cdot \aleph_0 otherwise. In contrast, if G is a tree or a graph with a finite degree, the largest possible size of such a subset is 2^{\aleph_0}. Additionally, if G is a graph of a specific type known as an H-admissible graph, and a particular property is satisfied (\aleph_0 less than the cardinality of G), the largest possible size of such a subset is the product of 2^{\aleph_0} and the cardinality of G. We also explore the relationship between these results and a specific infinite family of graphs known as the Flinn graphs, particularly when it comes to the family's smallest member.

Domain-specific knowledge is frequently conveyed through complex, interconnected frameworks known as ontologies. In understanding the meaning of individual terms within such frameworks, it's essential to identify non-secondary connections between related concepts. While numerous visualizations have been developed to display hierarchical relationships found in ontologies, users face difficulties when trying to uncover non-secondary associations between terms. A new approach, called OntoPlot, offers an alternative visual representation for highlighting connections at a holistic level by employing a combination of radial and circular layouts. By presenting all interterm connections simultaneously, as well as distinguishing secondary associations, OntoPlot facilitates the discovery of complex, multi-layered relationships between terms within ontologies. A comprehensive system has been developed to support users in uncovering hidden connections between related concepts as they navigate through ontologies, and OntoPlot has been successfully applied to real-world domains, including biomedical and chemical information systems.

We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to facilitate semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Inter-domain loss aims to derive a common speech-text representation through a shared neural network, whereas CycleGAN leverages cycle-consistency and identity mapping to preserve input characteristics after cross-domain conversion. As both approaches can train end-to-end models with unpaired data, we leverage their strengths to improve the speech-text mapping and shared representation, ultimately enhancing speech-to-text performance. Experimental results on the WSJ, Voxforge, and LibriSpeech datasets reveal that our method is competitive with state-of-the-art inter-domain loss techniques and offers notable improvements over E2E ASR baselines. Notably, we observe a significant 12.0% relative improvement in CER on the LibriSpeech test clean track.

This study introduces a novel method of deep active prediction for autonomous robot navigation that enables robots to visualize a robot operator's perspective and navigate efficiently and safely in unfamiliar environments. All the operator needs to do is wear a head-mounted display and the robot will create its own unique map and navigation plans by making informed choices about where to move to next. The robot is trained on a single trial based on a limited description of the navigation task, and it's capable of completing the task independently and in real-time. This technology could be particularly useful in situations where the operator is unable to see the surroundings or needs to attend to other tasks while navigating.

Our study offers a theoretical explanation for the Soret effect's influence on flexible molecules' gyration radius, which depends on temperature and light intensity. We calculated the contribution of covalent bonds and other flexible units within these molecules to the change in gyration radius. The results show that as temperature increases, long, flexible chains tend to behave similarly to rigid rods, with a negative Soret effect, whereas shorter, flexible molecules exhibit an opposite trend, with a positive Soret effect. Moreover, the Soret effect's strength is reduced in molecules containing multiple flexible units. This research sheds light on the role of molecular structures and flexibility in response to temperature gradients.

The goal of Automated Essay Assessment is to evaluate an essay based on its content and writing style against a standard reference model. This study focuses on developing an automated assessment framework for a specific AEA task and compares the performance of various pre-trained neural language models. It's shown that a balanced combination of large and bidirectional models achieves better results and it's possible to replace more complex ELMo components with simpler BERT components without significantly impacting performance. Moreover, a compact version of the transformer model, BERT-Lite, is trained and demonstrated to yield similar outcomes as the full-sized BERT model while requiring substantially less computational power. This is a crucial consideration when deploying AEA technology on general-purpose platforms. Ultimately, an optimized BERT-Lite model with a smaller dataset yields an average performance score equivalent to a full-sized BERT model assessed on the complete dataset, suggesting plenty of potential for further improvement through expanded training datasets.

Domain adaptation in pedestrian detection is crucial, but adapting a model from a large city-oriented dataset to a smaller dataset with fewer pedestrians results in a significant increase in false positives due to the domain shift. To alleviate this issue, our new approach, Box Re-Ranking, has been developed for unsupervised domain adaptation. It utilizes a pedestrian detection model's output of predicted bounding boxes and ranks them based on how well they match the target dataset's characteristics. This approach focuses specifically on reducing false positives in domain adaptation and has been successfully implemented using both Euclidean Embedding and Triplet embedding techniques. Experiments conducted on the Caltech dataset versus the MSDOS dataset show that our new approach leads to a substantial decrease in false positives while maintaining true positive rates, and that it outperforms other methods. Additionally, Box Re-Ranking has been shown to generalize to other domain adaptation tasks.

This study introduces a cutting-edge method for enhancing low-fidelity musical recordings by utilizing a two-step process. Firstly, a "pre-enhancement" image translation model with a diverse dataset range generates high-quality, similar signals to improve dynamic range and clarity. Secondly, a wave reconstruction model based on VGG-ConvWGAN produces the enhanced signals in high-quality formats, surpassing traditional wave-inversion techniques. Notably, our method's simplicity and effectiveness result in extended applications, including the automatic correction of recording level and signal overlap in digital looper devices and the creation of synthetic melodies from painted images.

Our primary goal is to thoroughly investigate the impact of a virtual ball's incorrect point of release in the simulation of a throwing motion that adheres to real-world physical principles.  To achieve this goal, we created FauxThrow, a web-based interactive system that enables users to accurately simulate throwing motions using rigid body dynamics, where the user can input parameters such as release velocity and angle to customize the simulation.  Through FauxThrow, we conducted a study with 32 participants who analyzed simulations with varying throwing parameters and points of release, all of which had been adjusted for accuracy.  The results of our study indicate that viewers are prone to making errors when attempting to identify motions that had been adjusted for accuracy, and that the perceptions of a throwing motion's authenticity are heavily influenced by key visual elements, such as the trajectory of the ball.  Ultimately, our research implies that realistic simulations can sometimes contradict intuition, and that physical principles can sometimes contradict aesthetic appeal.

To incorporate syntax-based decoding into Neural Machine Translation systems, a novel NMT architecture called TTS is developed. TTS features a tree structure, synthesized by combining individual words with syntax-based relationships, which informs a top-down decoding order. This novel setup enables the utilization of tree structured Constituent-Parse models in NMT systems. A non-autoregressive NMT framework using TTS yields comparable results to state-of-the-art models, but with a significant decrease in decoding time and a better ability to capture syntax. A new parsing decoding method known as Linked Head Decoding is introduced, outperforming standard CKY decoding in syntax-based parsing by a 8.6% margin in exact match accuracy on three test datasets. Furthermore, when integrated with existing NMT models, Linked Head Decoding reduces parsing error rates by as much as 7.2%. Overall, the TTS architecture and Linked Head Decoding method offer a syntax-aware NMT framework with improved efficiency.

Accurate calculations of binding energies between molecules and dust particles are crucial for understanding the process of dust particle decontamination through atmospheric interactions and the fragmentation of ice during the formation of icy particles in space. We developed the Binding Energy Assessment Platform, a comprehensive database containing theoretical binding energy data for hundreds of different molecule-dust particle pairs, allowing for the comparison of theoretical binding energies to those experimentally measured. To facilitate this comparison, the database contains two types of experimental data: gravimetric data, which measures binding energies by separating components from mixtures, and gravimetric data corrected for zero-point energy. The Binding Energy Assessment Platform utilizes density functional theory to model binding energies and takes into account the complexity of large molecule-dust particle systems through a generator of redundant ancillary theory couples. This approach, called the coupled ancillary theory-dimer method, is an efficient means of assessing binding energies across the spectrum of small to large molecules. The platform provides an extensive dataset of binding energies for different types of dust particles or their components as well as a detailed analysis of the constitutional binding energies associated with dust particle subgroups and categories.

A multiplicative stochastic process describing negative logarithm of water potential as a function of time has been found to have considerable practical uses, particularly in water isotope research. However, the initial study exploring this process was limited by its focus on external factors only, neglecting the influence of organismal properties and internal conditions. This study aims to expand our understanding of the multiplicative stochastic process by examining the effect of sample-dependent organismal characteristics and intracellular factors on outcome variables such as deuterium excess and sensitivity to variations in environmental conditions. By expressing water potential in terms of concentration, and employing linear regression to analyze dependence between variables, this research found correlations between deuterium excess and multiple factors, including size and plant organ location. These results suggest potential applications for large-scale observations of plants in studying the relationship between organism size and water isotopes. Additionally, this research discovered that organ size significantly correlates with deuterium excess, which may be influenced by structural characteristics within individual cells. Furthermore, these findings imply that organs with greater surface area relative to volume (s/v) tend to show larger deuterium excess values. This research also found that differences in water excess between thermal treatment groups, which were previously undetectable, became statistically significant when considering sample-dependent organ size. These outcomes emphasize the stochastic nature of water in plants and emphasize the value of integrating both organismal and organ-level characteristics in the analysis of isotope data.

In the context of the quantum supremacy experiment and the study of complex quantum systems, understanding random quantum processes is of paramount importance. We propose a novel approach, the expectation assessment protocol (EAP), which allows us to estimate the average output expectation values of quantum systems by running fewer experiments on simpler models than what was previously possible. We have successfully applied the EAP method to shallow quantum circuits generated by random Clifford rotations and found that such circuits satisfy the requirements set forth in the promise ES principle introduced by Bravyi, Brusheim, and Kierman. This enables us to establish that these circuits can be effectively simulated using fewer, low-depth quantum experiments than previously thought possible.

We are studying the reflection coefficient for combined space and time, $k(t,x) = k(t+ix)$. Equations based on the Davey-Stewartson II system can be viewed as a non-linear generalization of Schrödinger equations. We're looking at solutions where wave patterns don't change much in the linear regime, and we're using our knowledge to make predictions about how solutions behave in the phase space. We're studying two types of solutions: those that go from real to complex values and those that have imaginary components. We found that as the imaginary component becomes more pronounced, the reflection coefficient follows a simple equation. However, this behavior breaks down if we only consider the real part of $k$. We also made a connection between our findings and recent work on scattering theory by one of us.

The application of pre-trained language models (PLMs) in text classification has become widespread and highly effective.
However, researchers have found that text classification with PLMs can be vulnerable to label manipulation, which is a type of adversarial attack.
To address this issue, we introduce the concept of sibylvariant, which refers to the variation in model behavior when subjected to conflicting labels.
Based on this concept, we develop a method for text classification model hardening.
This method involves modifying the PLM's loss function to incorporate a label conflict consistency loss, as well as introducing an anomaly detection mechanism that identifies instances with conflicting labels.
Our experimental results on two datasets demonstrate that this approach significantly improves the robustness of PLM-based text classification models.

In the realm of shallow neural networks, effective representation learning is greatly dependent on the activation function used. A significant body of research exists on activation function design. A different perspective on representation learning is presented through meta-learning, particularly meta-learning of linear representations. Meta-learning of linear representations enables downstream tasks to utilize linear models, thus reducing computation and error rates. However, the meta-learning of linear representations has yet to be implemented effectively due to its non-convergent high-cost training processes. This issue can be addressed by our contribution, namely, the application of spectral initialization techniques within linear meta-learning. Our results show that spectral initialization techniques significantly improve the meta-learning of linear representations by producing accurate results in downstream tasks, thus making meta-learning of linear representations feasible and effective. Additionally, our contribution has substantial implications for future representation learning research, particularly scenarios where access to representation is limited or restricted.

This study evaluates and compares the effectiveness of knowledge compression techniques in reducing AC2 MT model size, specifically considering time-dependent characteristics unique to Neural Machine Translation. We investigate and contrast two techniques: learning-with-a-teacher to leverage pre-trained models, and post-training quantization to finalize model parameters early. Our experiments focus on a low-resource pair, Amharic-English, aiming to create lightweight MT models without increasing error rate. We found that distillation is easier than quantization, with sweet spots offering similar FRE improvements while stabilizing the training process. While accuracy may suffer for compression methods not accounting for MT specific losses, we found no decline in high precision for our models. Interestingly, we found higher temperature parameters to positively affect model compression, though this needs further investigation.

A hypergraph $G$ is defined as a finite collection of non-empty hyperedges existing within a non-empty, finite set of vertices. The parameterization of a Lagrangian density for a hypergraph $G$ involves a function $f$, where $f$'s values represent the density of a specific graph $d$ across its set of all possible vertex assignments. Effective density estimation of a given hypergraph $G$ involves finding the closest achievable value $\ell$ within the interval $[f(V, G), f^*(V, G)]$ that represents the lower bound $\varphi(G, f)$ and upper bound $\varphi(G, f^*)$ of the Lagrangian density $\varphi(G, f)$ through a specific function $f$. Researchers have discovered that the Lagrangian density of a given hypergraph $G$ can be expressed as an $n$-variable polynomial function $\ell(G, f)$ when a function $f$ is defined, where $n$ represents the number of vertices within $G$. The study presented here introduces a hypergraph $T_6$, which consists of 6 vertices and 3 hyperedges with a Lagrangian density that cannot be expressed as an $n$-variable polynomial function $\varphi(G, f)$ when a function $\varphi$ is defined and contains the set of all real numbers. Furthermore, the researchers showed that the Lagrangian density of a given hypergraph $

In medical image analysis, specifically in the context of pneumonia detection, 
segmentation plays a crucial role as it enables accurate diagnosis and symptoms 
assessment. Deep learning-based segmentation methods have demonstrated state-of-the-
art outcomes when trained with ample data, but such a setup is unaffordable for 
some areas due to limited access to medical data. To bridge this gap, we examine 
how data augmentation techniques can decrease the necessity of extensive training 
datasets. Using a ResNet-based, fully convolutional neural network, we analyze the 
effect of diverse data augmentation strategies on varying sizes of training sets, 
when applied to a Pneumonia dataset from the ISIC 2018 challenge. Consequently, 
our results reveal that increasing the use of data augmentation methods leads to 
significant improvements in segmentation accuracy, allowing for reduced training 
set requirements. Moreover, we establish that AUC metric is more resistant to 
variations caused by limited dataset sizes compared to other commonly used 
quantitative measures of segmentation performance, such as Dice coefficient, 
background Dice coefficient, and loss of background, loss of foreground, and 
combination loss.

There's a growing need for videos with descriptive commentary, not just to entertain, but also to inform and assist people with disabilities. Current methods used to generate video descriptions are often ineffective as they fail to produce accurate and relevant captions on command. To address this, a new approach called VPD-Prompt has been developed to enable on-demand description of videos through a prompting system. By leveraging pre-trained image and object detection models, VPD-Prompt creates a template for descriptive commentary. Moreover, it controls the context and quality of descriptions by using a given prompt. Comprehensive experiments have been conducted using standard video description benchmarks to demonstrate the efficacy of VPD-Prompt in producing coherent and context-specific comments for videos with complex scenes.

This paper delves into the concept of harm, a central component of many ethical frameworks. The analysis employs the language of causal inference to examine how the supervision of an offender affects the individual who was victimized, considering various time frames. Four distinct models of causality are explored, which differ according to the assumed temporal relationship and the inclusion of structural effects. The discussion on temporal relationship centers on reoffending, while the discussion on incorporating structural effects from the offender's perspective is held separate from the discussion on incorporating structural effects from the victim's perspective.

This study showcases MMLSpark, an innovative open-source library that bridges the gap between Python and Java, facilitating seamless interplay between PyTorch and Apache Spark. MMLSpark's development aims to simplify the integration of deep learning models into distributed systems, preserving the versatility and adaptability provided by the strongly-typed Spark API. Through practical examples, we demonstrate the benefits of MMLSpark's scaling capabilities, showcasing its potential in distributing model training and inference across multiple nodes and leveraging data frames for enhanced functionality.

Voice-based translations without additional voice output are needed for hands-free operations and have been limited to short text segments such as single words or short phrases. To break this limitation, we introduce an approach for translating continuous speech, which can handle various speech translation units, including words, phrases, and morphemes. A novel hybrid model is offered that extracts speech features and applies them to translate consecutive speech units until a full sentence is achieved. This approach has been extensively tested in zero-shot scenarios across two challenging agnostic domains, affecting not only the content but also the enunciation, making it a more practical solution for voice-free translations.

This work introduces an extension of the traditional heat conduction theory, incorporating boundary modifications that adapt over time. In doing so, it's established that the primary heat index varies harmoniously both within the material and at the boundary, while the secondary heat index poses a minor contradiction. Furthermore, it's been determined that the overall heat flux remains in perfect sync with its material-based counterpart, but may deviate slightly from harmony with its boundary-based counterpart. Additionally, it's been proven that the overall heat flux remains stable over time, with a minor deviation if the material's evolved temperature is reasonably stable.

Precise short-term forecasts of energy demand within the low voltage network (LVT) are vital for informing distribution system operators (DSOs) to manage their networks efficiently, especially with the rise of flexible resources. We developed an advanced statistical approach for predicting low voltage demand with high accuracy, particularly for LVT demand peaks. By fusing various predictive models, our approach significantly enhanced forecasting quality. We demonstrated the efficacy of combining predictive models in LVT forecasting by analyzing actual energy consumption data from over 100,000 measurement points in Germany and developing an advanced statistical methodology to analyze these measurements. By comparing our approach with current forecasting methods, we demonstrated a substantial improvement in accuracy for predicting high demand within the low voltage network.

While machine learning has achieved significant success, its predictive power often takes precedence over interpretability. Nevertheless, understanding the underlying causes of a problem is vital for comprehending its causes and finding suitable solutions. In the context of database systems, an entity's existence is frequently determined by defining a set of rules, which are then used to query the entity directly. Conversely, machine learning models operate in a similar environment by attempting to learn functions that represent these rules. Although some research attempts to incorporate domain knowledge into these models, the integration of domain knowledge into machine learning remains a relatively underdeveloped field. This article provides a conceptual framework and the relevant terminology to facilitate the discussion and future research initiatives.

Creating a reliable model for precise COVID-19 detection on chest CT scans poses significant challenges despite current progress in supervised learning. The existing methods often suffer from biased performance due to reliance on annotated data with detailed specifications. To overcome this limitation, we present an innovative approach that utilizes partial annotations with vague labels like "infection present," "infection absent," and "uncertain," along with their corresponding coordinates. The proposed framework consists of an adaptive network that automatically extracts valuable features from CT images and can generate more informative, partial annotation labels, enhancing its ability to detect COVID-19 lesions. The code for this solution has been made publicly available.

The success of quantitative analysis in spine imaging relies on the accuracy of vertebrae $L_{2}--L_{5}$. Current automated identification methods, however, struggle with accuracy due to complex structural variations and focal stenosis. This paper presents an advanced automated vertebrae localization and identification method that outperforms the state-of-the-art. The proposed algorithm involves multi-planar reformatting to align the spine, correcting distortions along the spine's longitudinal axis, and using anatomical constraints to position the vertebrae. An optimization routine then determines the vertebra center, achieving an $MMJ$ score of 0.952 \pm 0.129, and demonstrating significant improvement over the baseline. The proposed method exhibits superior durability and is applied successfully to all images from the 300 individual participants, whereas the baseline method fails in 4.4\% of cases. This method performs within the 75$^{th}$ percentile of accuracy for participants with moderate degenerative changes and within the 85$--$90^{th}$ percentile of accuracy for participants without evident degenerative changes or focal stenosis.

Dynamics of electron scattering on a silver surface are computed using a 3-dimensional non-equilibrium time-dependent orbital picture, simultaneously considering the movement of electrons and the influence of photon waves in the surface's vacuum. Simulations reveal that, below the scattering threshold (0.5 eV), electron trajectories are temporarily frozen due to a sudden increase in repulsive force between electrons and the surface induced by vacuum polarization, resulting from a counteracting increase in electric field. This phenomenon, similar to the resonant enhancement of chemical reactions, provides a new approach for temporarily enhancing an electron's scattering probability through a technique called ultrafast light-matter coupling, effectively increasing the electron's scattering probability by a factor of 100. Furthermore, this method can be utilized to explore non-equilibrium many-body electron behavior within metals.

In the field of control theory, particularly when dealing with nonlinear systems like elastic actuators, implementing optimal control often leads to intricate system models that are challenging to interpret. Our study focuses on the quadpedal robot's inherent trade-offs between progress and energy efficiency, and we explore how to exploit elastic actuators' advantages while improving robustness. By assuming that actuator characteristics can be accurately predicted, we develop a multiphase supervisor that combines elastic and rigid actuation, and we show through four indoor experiments that this innovative approach leads to enhanced quadpedal mobility.

The issue of quantum separability separability has significant implications in quantum information and computation. From a theoretical perspective, determining the separability of a given density matrix is equivalent to determining whether a Hermitian matrix with non-positive eigenvalues can be assembled from a set of given matrices. A new variational method has been developed to tackle this problem, aiming to identify the minimum set of Hermitian matrices required to assemble the given density matrix, and thus determine its separability. This approach iteratively refines an initial estimate for the minimum set by solving a positive semidefinite eigenvalue problem. A comprehensive numerical investigation demonstrated the method's reliability across various test cases. The method has been successfully applied to one-qubit channels, revealing its potential in analyzing entanglement and establishing key principles in quantum information and computation. Furthermore, the method has been extended to investigate nonsuperpositional protocols for quantum cloning and associated tasks.

This study examined the dynamics of a low-energy, high-drive velocity rip mode in a collisionless plasma, focusing on a small-scale, driven slab configuration. Computer simulations, involving NIMR, KEILERS, and PIC, were used to analyze the physics behind the ripples. The investigations showed that a driven slab quake with elevated drive velocities exhibits characteristic ripples, unlike those observed in slaps with lower drive energies. The simulations identified two distinct ripples - ripping modes arising from electron-pressure disturbances and kinetic ring-mode fluctuations. The experiments indicated that the ripples observed in slaps with elevated drive velocities result from a combination of both phenomena. Furthermore, the simulations revealed that a ringing kinetic mode can transition to a ripping mode over time and suggested that a large driving energy can induce ripples in a slab configuration. The investigations also revealed that the frequency of a ringing kinetic mode decreases as the drive velocity increases, and may offer insights to interpret the ripples observed in experiments.

Recent advancements in fashion retrieval research have been attributed to improved methods for searching via fashion attributes, such as style, accessories, and labels. However, efficiently retrieving fashion items based on images proves to be a challenging task due to varying lighting conditions, display settings, and style inconsistencies. In order to resolve this issue, a novel approach for semi-supervised feature-level image editing has been developed. This editing method, called Semi-Level TLTM, combines semi-supervised learning techniques with feature-level image processing to enhance fashion retrieval tasks. By leveraging semi-supervised generative models, high-quality image manipulations are performed at the feature level to enhance matching between query images and fashion items. Additionally, a novel dataset, the FashionFashion dataset, has been created for benchmarking fashion retrieval efforts. As a result, the Semi-Level TLTM method has achieved outstanding performance in fashion retrieval tasks, particularly in fashion attribute searching, where it outperformed existing state-of-the-art approaches by a substantial margin, according to evaluation metrics. Furthermore, the method's ability to handle difficult real-world scenarios, such as fashion image blur, has been successfully demonstrated.

The main contribution of this research is the development of a dual gradient algorithm for solving inverse problems with data contaminated by noise in infinite-dimensional Banach spaces. Its convergence is proven under the condition of source restriction, and a new norm is defined on the space where the solution is mapped to, enabling the selection of an appropriate regularization parameter that minimizes the approximation error while preventing the cost function growth. Furthermore, the research demonstrates the smoothing effect of the algorithm's iterates, facilitates the analysis of the method without assuming the existence of a source, and allows for the generalization of previously established results on gradient methods.

Reconstructing the depth of a light field image is a complex task, particularly when it comes to images distorted by obstacles that prevent some light field samples from reaching certain pixels. Most current depth estimation methods are designed to work around this issue by either ignoring the effects of distorted data or using surrogate references, but they fail to incorporate the geometry of the obstructions, limiting their overall precision. In this paper, we integrate the geometry of obstructions into the depth estimation process by developing a new cost function that weighs the accuracy of different models based on the amount of each point is obscured. Our experimental results show that this new approach surpasses the performance of conventional autonomous depth estimation techniques in a variety of synthetic and real-world scenarios.

This study uses the bilinear method to investigate the Fokas-Lenells equations, first reducing the system and then employing double Wronskian solutions to yield a range of solutions for the reduced equations, resulting in a comprehensive overview of solutions for both classical and nonlocal Fokas-Lenells equations. Several solutions are illustrated through asymptotic analysis and collocation techniques.

The effective action for non-uniform gravitational background fields derived from Double Field Theory is constructed and its Lagrangian form is determined. It has been known that this action provides an alternative formulation of the Polyaction constructed around a Riemannian frame with an additional, non-metric tensor $b_\mu$, that deviates from the standard metric. Based on the principles of Double Field Theory, the action for general $b_\mu$ has been determined and is shown to include terms that vanish when $b_\mu = 0$. These terms match a well-known approximation used in the literature for describing similar effects in General Relativity. It has been demonstrated that the full DFT action provides a higher order correction to the approximation used in the literature. Furthermore, the DFT action may potentially describe new effects not accounted for by the approximation that arise at the next order.

To optimize the performance of IEEE 802.11n and above mesh networks used in home broadband setups, we propose an AP/Extender selection mechanism that adapts to changing wireless channels. This mechanism leverages the IEEE 802.11k/v standards to gather mesh network topology information and identify optimal channels for association. Devices then select the mesh network to join, choosing the nearest or fastest available path. Our method enhances mesh network performance by reducing interference and outages, thus improving data rates and signal strength. This mesh network topology information can also aid in troubleshooting by enabling faster and accurate connection diagnosis and resolution.
